raw_finding: STRUCTURE: 4 years, categorical, PGY-1 through PGY-4, June start (FREIDA field_start_date_june = 12, i.e. a June 12 start; field_accredited_length = 4). PGY-1 is an internal medicine year at Dell Med and is included in the match - 'the program only offers categorical positions, which means that matching to the program comes with a matched internship to the internal medicine program at Dell Medical School' and 'It is not necessary to submit a separate application to the Department of Internal Medicine for the preliminary year.' ACGME PATIENT-CARE MINIMA as published: 18 months clinical adult neurology; 6 months adult neurology inpatient; 6 months adult neurology outpatient; 3 months elective; 3 months child neurology; 1 month psychiatry; half a day per week continuity clinic neuroimaging experience; critical care unit/emergency department experience including acute neurosurgical management. (The 3 months of child neurology is a ROTATION inside this adult curriculum and is legitimate adult-program content; it is not the separate Child Neurology residency.) THE PROGRAM'S SIGNATURE FEATURE IS OUTPATIENT VOLUME, and it is quantified. FREIDA field_special_features, verbatim: 'We schedule residents for outpatient rotations a minimum of 50% of PGY2-4 blocks.' The Curriculum page frames the same point: 'The residencies differ from many neurology training programs in that the curriculum emphasizes outpatient neurology as much as hospital-based rotations. Residents learn by seeing patients, which means that residents run the ward teams and rounds as well as evaluate and care for outpatients.' FREIDA field_training_outpatient_clinic = 40% hospital outpatient and field_train_ambulatory_nonhospit = 10% non-hospital ambulatory. BLOCK AND CALL DESIGN: 'Each rotation block lasts two weeks with many outpatient blocks scheduled for back-to-back blocks to improve continuity. THE PROGRAM HAS NO 24-HOUR CALL.' Night float is used (FREIDA field_night_float = True, field_night_float_y1 = True). FREIDA field_beeper_home_call = [0,0,10,10] indicates home call appears only in PGY-3 and PGY-4. Average duty hours 60/week in year one, maximum 14 consecutive hours, one 24-hour off-duty period per week, 6 hours/week of structured didactics. PGY-1 (internal medicine): a 4+1 schedule - four weeks inpatient at Dell Seton Medical Center with some rotations at Ascension Seton Medical Center Austin, then one week of clinic. A four-week neurology block replaces an ICU block relative to other preliminary interns, giving early ward neurology exposure. Clinic weeks are at the CENTRAL TEXAS VETERANS HEALTH CARE SYSTEM covering urgent, specialty and primary care of adults. PGY-2: first neurology year. Neurological history and examination; EEG interpretation, lumbar puncture, CT and MRI of brain and spinal cord; common outpatient problems (headache, dizziness, neck and back pain, peripheral neuropathies) and emergencies (coma and mental status change, stroke, seizures). PGY-2s hold the pager and respond first to consults, with an IN-HOUSE NIGHT SENIOR for the first four months of the year providing direct observation and feedback; afterwards the senior and attending staff each consult by phone. Dedicated neurocritical care staffing 24/7 means junior residents do not manage NCC patients overnight. PGY-3: adds multiple sclerosis, neuromuscular disease, dementia, CNS infections, nervous system tumours, Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders; in-depth EEG, EMG, neuroradiology and neuropathology; paediatric history and examination skills. Adult residents spend a total of three months across PGY-3 and PGY-4 with child neurology faculty on inpatient consults and outpatient clinics. PGY-3/PGY-4 SENIOR ROLES ACROSS TWO DISTINCT HOSPITALS: seniors lead vascular and non-vascular inpatient teams at both Dell Seton and Ascension Seton, plus the neurocritical care service at Dell Seton. The two sites are deliberately differentiated - 'Ascension Seton Medical Center gives residents exposure to pure consultative neurology whereas the Dell Seton Medical Center services are a hybrid of both primary neurology patients and consults... Residents might expect to encounter complex cardiac conditions and neurologic complications of obstetrical disease at Ascension Seton Medical Center, whereas at Dell Seton Medical Center they may be more likely to be challenged by patients with complex rheumatologic and infectious diseases.' PGY-4: core and subspecialty rotations including psychiatry; ABPN preparation; new senior rotations comprising supervisory roles in the neurocritical care unit, a 'teaching senior' position coordinating educational conferences, and additional outpatient offerings including epilepsy and movement disorder rotations. DIDACTICS: protected time with attendings covering pagers for inpatient residents, and outpatient residents excused from clinical duties to attend. Weekly schedule - Monday: morning report (outpatient case) and stroke huddle, afternoon didactics lecture; Tuesday: grand rounds, noon didactics, chief rounds; Wednesday: stroke huddle, noon didactics, epilepsy conference; Thursday: morning report (inpatient case), noon didactics, teaching senior didactics; Friday: morning report (inpatient case) and stroke huddle, noon didactics. Monthly journal club, resident day and special lectures. BOOT CAMP: an end-of-PGY-1 intensive lecture series covering neurology and the evaluation and management of neurological emergencies, plus a dedicated neuromuscular bootcamp at the start of the year for all residents. SCHOLARSHIP AND SYSTEMS TRAINING: all residents participate in quality improvement and patient safety projects; research rotation is optional (FREIDA field_research_rotation = 'Optional'); all Dell Med residents complete 'Foundations in Care Transformation', part of Dell Med's signature GME curriculum 'Advancing Care Transformation', emphasising value-based care, quality improvement, health equity, leadership and health sy
conflict_notes: CONTRADICTION NOTED: the Curriculum page states 'The program has no 24-hour call', while FREIDA field_call_schedule (which the registry rendered as 'Year 1: Every fourth night for 4 week(s); Year 2: Other for 2 week(s); Year 3/4: Every eleventh night or more') describes call FREQUENCY, not call DURATION. These are reconcilable - frequent short call and night float are compatible with no 24-hour shifts - but a reader comparing the two fields could wrongly infer a conflict, so both are recorded. I found no published block-schedule image or PDF to read; the weekly conference table was recoverable as text.

WHAT IS REAL AND VERIFIABLE INSTEAD IS SAFETY-NET AND HEALTH-EQUITY STRUCTURE, which I report on program/institutional evidence and explicitly NOT on city demographics. (1) The primary teaching hospital, Dell Seton Medical Center at The University of Texas, is Travis County's SAFETY-NET HOSPITAL, opened in 2017 to replace Brackenridge, operating in partnership with Central Health, the county's public hospital district - a 210-bed urban safety-net academic hospital and the ONLY Level I Trauma Center serving an eleven-county Central Texas region. Residents on the Dell Seton services are therefore training on an indigent-and-uninsured-serving payer mix by structure, not by aspiration. (2) Dell Med states its GME training sites deliberately include 'safety-net clinics, urban faculty practice, VA clinic, as well as opportunities to volunteer in free clinics', with 'integrated professional development and health equity curricula into program didactics', and reports that its residents provide nearly 900,000 hours of care annually at over 60 clinics and hospitals across Central Texas. (3) Every Dell Med resident completes 'Foundations in Care Transformation' within the Advancing Care Transformation curriculum, which the Directors' Welcome says 'emphasizes value-based care, quality improvement, HEALTH EQUITY, leadership and other key competencies in health systems science' - registry 'Health Systems Leadership Curriculum: Yes' and 'Healthcare Economics Curriculum: Yes' confirmed. (4) Neurology residents rotate through the CENTRAL TEXAS VETERANS HEALTH CARE SYSTEM during PGY-1 clinic weeks. (5) GLOBAL HEALTH, registry 'Global Health Experience: Yes' confirmed: Ethan Meltzer 'helps lead the Dell Med neurology global health collaboration' through AMPATH Kenya, and Dell Med's Division of Global Health provides opportunities for students, residents and faculty in Sub-Saharan Africa AND LATIN AMERICA. (6) Resident-level orientation toward these values is visible and specific: among the 24 Dell Seton residents, Lidya Teshome 'hopes to integrate neurological care and global health to improve access to care to vulnerable populations', Isabel Miller lists palliative care, Naimah Sarwar works 'at the intersections of health equity, women's health and palliative care', and Neha Patel and others list health-equity interests. BOTTOM LINE FOR A FLUENT SPANISH SPEAKER: the program offers no formal mechanism to develop, certify or be deployed for Spanish-language clinical skill. Her bilingualism would be an asset she brings to a safety-net setting that will certainly use it, rather than a skill this program is structured to train, credential or reward.
conflict_notes: GOVERNANCE LAW 5 OBSERVED: I did not use Austin's or Travis County's Hispanic population share as evidence of anything, and no demographic statistic appears in this finding. Every claim above is a program, hospital or institutional fact. I also excluded a Dell Med news item about Spanish-language autism diagnosis, which is paediatric research and not adult residency curriculum. Confidence MEDIUM because the safety-net evidence is strong and well sourced while the Spanish-specific finding is a verified absence, which is inherently harder to prove than a presence.

value: 4-year categorical with in-house PGY-1; front-loaded inpatient PGY-2 tapering to 5 elective blocks in PGY-4; 10 months total elective time with an optional 6-month research block; weekly longitudinal continuity clinic that rotates subspecialty annually at a 1:1 faculty ratio; 2 Neuro-ICU blocks; outpatient procedural training (Botox, occipital nerve block, LP) plus ICU procedures; required research with formal methods/ethics certification; elected PGY-4 administrative chief resident.

raw_finding: STRUCTURE: four-year categorical, 13 four-week blocks per year. PGY-1 (in-house preliminary medicine): MICU, Neurology Consult Service (NCS), ID, Rheumatology, ED, Wards x3, Cardiology x2, Endocrinology, Nephrology, Nights x2, Neuromuscular Disorders - including three months on neurology services to orient before PGY-2. All 12 months must be completed before promotion. PGY-2 (most inpatient-heavy year): NCS x3, Neuromuscular Disorders x2, Stroke x3, plus outpatient blocks in Epilepsy, Dementia, and Movement Disorders, plus Neuro-ICU x1 and consult-liaison Psychiatry x1. PGY-3: NCS x2, MND, Neuro-Oncology x2 at MD Anderson, Stroke, Neuro-ICU, Pediatric Neurology x2 at Children's Memorial Hermann, Electives x3-4. PGY-4: NCS x2, NMD x2, Stroke x2, Pediatric Neurology x1, Electives x5, Outpatient Neurology. DESIGN PRINCIPLE, verbatim: 'With each year of training, the resident has fewer general neurology rotations and more specialty and elective rotations.' ELECTIVES: ten months total across training - EMG/NCV, Epilepsy/EEG, Neuropathology/ophthalmic pathology, Neuroradiology, Neuro-oncology, Neuro-ophthalmology, Pain management, Neuromuscular medicine, Sleep medicine, Research, and self-designed experiences with a written Goals and Objectives statement and PD approval. A six-month research block is possible in PGY-4 with PD approval. CONTINUITY: weekly half-day longitudinal clinic; residents see about four patients per week; faculty-to-resident ratio in clinic is 1:1 with no more than two residents per half-day session; residents spend a year in one continuity clinic then ROTATE TO ANOTHER subspecialty clinic. Three continuity tracks: San Jose Clinic (PGY-4 option), General Neurology Resident Continuity Clinic (PGY-4 not assigned to San Jose), and the resident MDA clinic (twice monthly, 2nd and 4th Fridays). PROCEDURES: in the general continuity clinic - Botox injection, occipital nerve block, lumbar puncture; in the Neuro-ICU - intubation and ventilator management, arterial and central line placement, emergent cardioversion during CPR. TEAMS: every inpatient team has at least one junior and one senior neurology resident; senior residents provide back-up call for the junior night-call resident. LEADERSHIP: one PGY-4 is elected administrative chief resident annually, acting as liaison between staff and residents and assisting in program development. DIDACTICS: Morning Report Wed/Thu 8am; Resident Lecture Series Mon-Thu at noon covering ABPN-required content; Professor's Rounds Wed 1:15-2:15pm with a volunteer patient examined by a chosen resident; Neurology Grand Rounds Fri noon; Pediatric Grand Rounds Fri 8am; PGY-3 Resident Basic Science Lectures; each PGY-4 delivers a Grand Rounds presentation. RESEARCH: required - residents receive certified training in research methods and ethics; FREIDA records Research Rotation = Required and Research Track = Yes. WORK HOURS (FREIDA): 80 hours/week average, 28 maximum consecutive hours in PGY-1, 1.00 twenty-four-hour off-duty period per week; Night Float = No; PGY-2 call every fourth night for 12 weeks; moonlighting not permitted. TRACKS (FREIDA): Clinician Educator = Yes; Health Systems Leadership and Healthcare Economics curricula = Yes; Primary Care, Hospitalist, Women's Health tracks = No; Osteopathic Recognition = No.
conflict_notes: Rotation grids were read from the raw page HTML rather than a summarization pass, so the block-by-block sequence is exact. NEGATIVE FINDINGS worth stating plainly: NO point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) curriculum is mentioned anywhere on the program page; there is NO night float system (call-based instead); moonlighting is NOT permitted; and FREIDA records Global Health Experience = No and Advanced Degree Training = No. The continuity-clinic design - rotating to a different subspecialty clinic each year at a 1:1 faculty ratio - is unusual and genuinely differentiating.

San Jose Clinic's own 2023 Impact Report documents its patient population as 80% Hispanic/Latino, 8% African American, 6% White/Non-Hispanic, 3% Asian, 0% American Indian, 3% declined - serving 3,921 patients across 33,150 visits, against a Houston uninsured rate of 26%. The same report documents an INSTITUTIONAL partnership, not merely a rotation agreement: Houston Methodist Hospital is listed as a San Jose Clinic donor in the $100,000-$499,999 tier, and Trevor M. Burt, EdD, MS, Vice President of System Education at Houston Methodist Hospital, serves on the San Jose Clinic board. The program frames the rotation as autonomy-building: 'the experience provides an opportunity for autonomy in a clinical setting with limited resources.' NEGATIVE EVIDENCE, equally important: the word 'Spanish' does not appear ANYWHERE on the residency program page (verified by exhaustive string search of the full raw HTML - zero occurrences). No bilingual care pathway, language-concordance initiative, interpreter-training component, or Spanish-language clinic is described by the program. The San Jose Clinic 2023 Impact Report likewise contains zero occurrences of 'Spanish', 'bilingual', or 'interpret'. FREIDA/registry records Medical Spanish Curriculum = 'No', which this independent search CONFIRMS.
conflict_notes: Per ticket rule, Houston/Harris County demographics were NOT used as evidence - the 80% Hispanic/Latino figure is the documented patient population of a clinic the program REQUIRES its residents to staff weekly, which is program-specific by construction. SEPARATE, WEAKER SIGNAL, flagged rather than counted: 4 of 29 current residents (the single largest school cluster) graduated from UT Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, a border-region, federally designated Hispanic-Serving Institution, and 1 from Tecnologico de Monterrey in Mexico. That is a school-origin observation about recruitment, NOT evidence of program-level Spanish-language services, and no inference about any individual's language ability, nationality, or ethnicity was drawn from it. NET ASSESSMENT for a Spanish-speaking, Latino-health-oriented applicant: the patient-population exposure is real and required; the institutional language infrastructure is undocumented and should be asked about directly.

raw_finding: This is the strongest single finding for Alejandra at this program, and it is supported by three independent official sources that agree. (1) INSTITUTIONAL RULE - TTUHSC House Staff Policies and Procedures, section 03.01.01(A): 'PGY-1 Level. Prior to an applicant's commencement of residency or training at the PGY-1 level, the Program Director shall verify that the applicant has passed USMLE, Step 1, or its equivalent, within the number of attempts permitted for Texas licensure, i.e., a maximum of 3 attempts for Step 1.' ONLY STEP 1 is named as an entry condition. Section 03.01.02(A) then sets the Step 2 deadline at the far end of intern year: 'No later than end date of the PGY-1 year contract, each resident must provide written verification ... of having passed USMLE Step 2, both CK and CS, or their equivalents ... AND having taken USMLE Step 3 at least one time.' A candidate can therefore match, sign, and begin PGY-1 at TTUHSC without a Step 2 CK result in hand, and has until roughly 30 June of the intern year to produce the pass. (2) PROGRAM RULE - the Neurology Application Process page sets no Step 2 gate at all and states 'No minimum score requirements'; it describes review as beginning only when a file is 'complete', with the required items being the ERAS application, personal statement, CV, three LORs, Dean's Letter, transcripts, photograph, and a 'USMLE and/or COMPLEX Exam Report' - which a Step-1-only report satisfies on its face. There is no published statement anywhere that Step 2 must be in hand before initial review, before an interview invitation, or before ranking. The practical mechanics also work in her favour: the program reviews on a rolling basis from 1 September through 31 December and interviews IN PERSON, so an application filed at ERAS opening with a mid-October 2026 CK score arriving during the interview window is timed normally rather than late. The one caution worth stating plainly is that 'no published barrier' is not the same as 'score will not matter once it arrives' - a rolling-review program that reads files from September can, in practice, form impressions before a mid-October score lands, and nothing published tells us how this program behaves in that situation.
conflict_notes: The House Staff P&P PDF served at the canonical URL carries an internal cover reading '2023-2024' with a footer 'Last Revised: September 27, 2024', while the GME Programs page hyperlinks to it under the label '2025-2026 House Staff Policies & Procedures'. raw_finding: ECFMG certification is required of international medical graduates and the ORIGINAL CERTIFICATE MUST BE PRESENTED AT THE INTERVIEW - an unusually early and unusually concrete deadline. The Application Process page's International Medical Graduate checklist reads, item by item: completed ERAS application; TTUHSC ERAS Addendum Form (only upon interview invitation); personal statement; current CV; three letters of recommendation; Program Director's letter/certification if there was previous US residency training; Dean's Letter; medical school transcripts; 'Notarized copy of diploma (only needed upon interview invitation)'; 'Clerkship Affidavit (only needed upon interview invitation)'; 'ECFMG Certificate (original needed at interview)'; USMLE and/or COMLEX exam report; wallet-sized photograph. The GME Admission Requirements page and House Staff P&P 01.07.1 restate the rule at institution level: an applicant who graduated from a school whose curriculum is merely 'accepted by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board as equivalent to that of a Texas medical school' must 'possess a valid certificate issued by the Education Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG)'. Both documents frame the gate as: each applicant must be a graduate of a medical school approved by the Texas Medical Board, OR of a THECB-equivalent school plus ECFMG certification.
conflict_notes: AMBIGUITY FLAG FOR ALEJANDRA (material, and the contract asks for exactly this). Universidad Central del Caribe School of Medicine is LCME-accredited and confers a US MD; its graduates are US medical graduates, are approved by the Texas Medical Board on the same footing as a mainland LCME school, are NOT eligible for ECFMG certification, and belong in the page's 'US Graduates' column. Nothing on this program's page says so explicitly - the page offers only a binary 'US Graduates' vs 'International Medical Graduate' split with no mention of Puerto Rico, LCME, or US territories anywhere. A coordinator screening on nationality-of-place rather than accreditation could mis-sort a UCC file into the IMG column and then flag it as missing an ECFMG certificate, a notarized diploma, and a Clerkship Affidavit that she cannot and should not supply. Recommended mitigation: state 'LCME-accredited US MD degree, Universidad Central del Caribe (Puerto Rico, USA)' prominently in the CV header and personal statement, and be ready to say it to the coordinator (Tiffany Williams, tiffany.l.williams@ttuhsc.edu, 806.743.3832, or NeurologyResidencyLubbock@ttuhsc.edu) before the interview date.

His declared clinical interests include Movement disorders, Parkinson's disease, Dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Balance function and Botox. He is the only movement-disorders subspecialist documented in the department. (B) DEDICATED CLINIC - YES as a named service line, NO as a separately branded centre. Both the departmental home page and the Texas Tech Physicians Lubbock Neurology clinic page list 'Parkinson's Disease, Tremors and Movement Disorders' as one of the clinic's named areas of care, alongside Alzheimer's/Dementia/Memory Loss, Autonomic Disorders, Dizziness, Epilepsy, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocritical Care, Neurointervention, the Neurophysiology Lab and Stroke. There is no separate movement-disorders centre webpage, no named DBS programme page, no advertised multidisciplinary PD clinic with PT/OT/speech, and no patient support-group listing. (C) FELLOWSHIP - NO. TTUHSC Lubbock's GME programme index lists 17 fellowships (Breast Oncology, Burn & Wound, Cardiovascular Diseases, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, GI, Geriatric Medicine, Heme/Onc, Hospice & Palliative, ID, Interventional Cardiology, Mohs, Nephrology, Pain Management, Pediatric Hospitalist, PCCM, Sports Medicine, Surgical Critical Care) and NOT ONE is a neurology fellowship of any kind, let alone movement disorders. (D) RESIDENT ELECTIVES - NOT NAMED. The published PGY-2/3/4 rotation template lists on-site electives as: additional exposure to any standard rotation, Geriatrics, Sleep Medicine, Neuro-Surgery, Intro to Private Practice, Rehabilitative Medicine, Research, Neuro-Ophthalmology, Neuro-Pathology and Neuro-Radiology. Movement Disorders is NOT a named elective. Exposure therefore comes through the 4 months of outpatient clinic in PGY-3/PGY-4 ('Outpatient Clinic (greater than two (2) Faculty)') and through electives negotiated as 'additional exposure to any standard rotation' - real, but not a protected, named block. (E) ACTIVE RESEARCH AND RESIDENT CO-AUTHORSHIP - YES, and documented in PubMed with residents as first authors. 'Mystery Case: Symptomatic isolated tongue tremor of cortical origin due to stroke', Neurology, 2020 Mar 31 - Thakolwiboon S, Ruthirago D, Laengvejkal P, Wilms H (three TTUHSC Lubbock neurology residents plus Wilms, in the specialty's flagship journal). 'Increased creativity associated with dopamine agonist therapy: A case report and short review of the literature', Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery, 2022 May - Thakolwiboon S, Karukote A, Julayanont P, Wilms H (a Parkinson's-therapy paper with residents). 'Acute necrotizing encephalopathy', Proceedings (Baylor University Medical Center), 2022 - Hernandez R, Ota R, Medina Y, Hernandez Y, Julayanont P, Wilms H. Wilms has 12 PubMed-indexed papers under a Texas Tech affiliation. CLINICAL DEPTH EVIDENCE: TTUHSC's own Daily Dose feature 'Parkinson's Disease Patient Regains Independence' (1 May 2018) documents Wilms managing a young-onset Parkinson's patient on an Abbott Infinity deep brain stimulation system, personally programming the device at each visit via the iPad platform, with the patient's medication burden reduced roughly 40 percent - so DBS PROGRAMMING is done in this clinic. The DBS IMPLANTATION in that case was performed in San Angelo by neurosurgeon Luis Duarte, M.D., i.e. off-site, which is the honest limit on the programme's DBS depth. TRIALS: a ClinicalTrials.gov sweep of Lubbock-site Parkinson's studies found no currently recruiting PD trial at TTUHSC; the Lubbock PD/MS trial activity that does exist is mostly at a private practice (Bhupesh Dihenia, M.D., P.A.) and at Covenant Medical Group, not at TTUHSC.
conflict_notes: Researched entirely independently of domain 17 as instructed. The honest summary for Alejandra: this is a real movement-disorders asset built around ONE endowed professor who does DBS programming and publishes with residents - materially more than 'the department treats Parkinson's' - but it is single-point-of-failure depth with no fellowship to progress into, no named elective to guarantee the rotation, and no on-site DBS surgery. If Wilms were to leave, the domain would empty out.

The department's own site likewise has no fellowship section - the neurology site tree is Letter from the Chair, Faculty & Staff, Neurophysiology Lab, Residency Program (Overview, Current Residents, Didactics, Monthly Rotations, Pictures, Benefits, Application Process, Where Are They Now), Neurointerventional Service, and the PM&R Division. CONSEQUENCE: residents who want subspecialty training must leave Lubbock. The department's own published alumni record shows they do so successfully - see domain 19 - but there is no internal fellowship pathway, no 'stay on as a fellow' option in either of Alejandra's two interest areas, and no in-house fellow layer above the residents on service.
conflict_notes: A genuine structural limitation, and it also leaves Katherine Rivas Sevilla's 'Resident Instructor 5th Year' status unexplained - there is no in-house ACGME neurology fellowship for her to be in. A secondary benefit of having no fellows: residents are the senior learners on every neurology service, so procedural and consult volume is not siphoned off to a fellow layer, which is consistent with the chair letter's emphasis on 'unrestricted access' to EEG, EMG/NCV, evoked potentials, TCD, autonomic and tilt-table testing.

raw_finding: Nine concrete, source-backed differentiators, each tied to a named mechanism, number, person or document rather than to adjectives. (1) TWO ENDOWED CHAIRS IN ALEJANDRA'S PRIMARY INTEREST sit on one person: Henrik Wilms holds the Abraham-Tarbox Chair in Neurodegenerative Diseases AND the CH-Foundation Chair in Parkinson's Disease Research, and his practice-plan subspecialty designation is literally 'Movement Disorders Neurology'. (2) DBS PROGRAMMING IS DONE IN THIS CLINIC - TTUHSC's own published patient story documents Wilms programming an Abbott Infinity deep brain stimulation system at each visit and a 40 percent medication reduction in a young-onset Parkinson's patient. (3) THE MS LEAD IS ALSO THE ASSOCIATE PROGRAM DIRECTOR AND INTERIM CHAIR - Mirla Avila, MS/Neuroimmunology, fellowship-trained at the Maxine Mesinger MS Comprehensive Care Center at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston; a resident whose interest is MS is being taught by the person who also runs the program. (4) CURRENT RESIDENTS ARE PUBLISHING NEUROIMMUNOLOGY WITH HER - 'Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Setting of Neurosarcoidosis', Clinical Case Reports, June 2025, first two authors Pichatorn Suppakitjanusant and Gwyn Srifuengfung, both still in the program, senior author Avila; and Wilms has resident-first-author movement-disorders work in Neurology (2020) and Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery (2022). (5) THE PROGRAM PROMOTES ITS OWN - the Program Director (Jannatul Ferdous, Class of 2017, Vanderbilt epilepsy fellowship) and the Interim Chair/APD (Mirla Avila, Class of 2016) are both graduates of this residency. (6) UNRESTRICTED NEURODIAGNOSTIC PROCEDURE ACCESS IS THE DEPARTMENT'S STATED STRATEGY, not a slogan - the chair letter names the specific modalities residents perform and interpret (32-channel video EEG, ambulatory and long-term monitoring, EMG, NCV, evoked potentials, TCD and diagnostic ultrasound, tilt-table, autonomic testing, Humphrey visual fields and OCT), the department owns the lab, and there are NO FELLOWS ABOVE THE RESIDENTS to absorb that volume (TTUHSC Lubbock has 17 fellowships and none in neurology). (7) A FULL NEUROINTERVENTIONAL SERVICE IN-HOUSE - Saif Bushnaq MD covers endovascular thrombectomy, aneurysm coiling and flow diversion, AVM/DAVF/CCF embolization, carotid and intracranial stenting and venous sinus stenting at a Level I trauma centre, which is unusual for a program this size. (8) CATCHMENT AND CASE MIX ARE QUANTIFIED - the department describes itself as 'the only academic neurologic center in the Texas South Plains, an area larger than New England', serving a 62-county area across West Texas, eastern New Mexico and southwestern Oklahoma, across two hospitals totalling more than 1,300 beds (University Medical Center, 301 beds, Lubbock County Hospital District, first hospital in Texas to receive Trauma One designation and home to the West Texas perinatal centre and regional burn centre; plus Covenant Medical Center). AeroCare flies roughly 400 patients a year into UMC and 520 into the Covenant system. (9) A HISTORICALLY STRONG FELLOWSHIP EXIT FOR IMG-HEAVY CLASSES - the classes of 2014-2018 placed named graduates at UT Southwestern, Vanderbilt, Cleveland Clinic (twice), University of Chicago, Mount Sinai, Mayo Clinic Rochester, Baylor Houston, SUNY Upstate, University of Florida and MGH/Harvard.

Every item above is tied to a named person, a named service, a named document, or a published number.

conflict_notes: TRAP CAUGHT AND REJECTED, and it is the direct analogue of the El Paso Foster medical-Spanish trap. A search for TTUHSC Spanish-language training surfaces the 'Confianza: Hispanic-Oriented Medicine Enrichment' programme, a federally designated HRSA-funded Hispanic Center of Excellence under the TTUHSC banner. Reading the page shows it is (a) located at TTUHSC PERMIAN BASIN (Odessa/Midland), a different campus roughly 140 miles from Lubbock, (b) aimed at FAMILY MEDICINE, explicitly built to 'recruit, train, and retain URM learners as rural and/or faculty primary care physicians' and to 'ensure/facilitate matriculation into the Permian Basin Family Medicine residency program', and (c) a pipeline programme for middle-school through medical-school learners plus family medicine residents. It has nothing to do with the Lubbock Adult Neurology residency and I have not counted it. Alejandra's fluent Spanish is a personal asset she would bring here rather than a capability this program has built - there is exactly one documented Spanish-speaking neurologist in the department, and being the second would likely make her clinically valuable, but that is an argument about her contribution, not about the program's Spanish/Latino infrastructure, which is essentially undeveloped at the residency level.

raw_finding: NO CURRENT RESIDENT, FACULTY MEMBER OR INSTITUTIONAL PARTNERSHIP CONNECTS THIS PROGRAM TO UNIVERSIDAD CENTRAL DEL CARIBE OR TO ANY PUERTO RICO MEDICAL SCHOOL, with one genuine historical exception. THE EXCEPTION: the department's own 'Where Are They Now' page records, for the Class of 2016, 'Angel O. Claudio - After Dr. Claudio graduates from our program, he plans to return to Puerto Rico and be in Private Practice.' That is the program's own published statement and it establishes (a) that the program has trained at least one physician with a stated Puerto Rico destination and (b) that the program considered it worth publishing. It does NOT establish where Dr Claudio attended medical school, and I did not infer it. WHAT I CHECKED AND FOUND NOTHING: no current resident is identifiable as a UCC, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico or San Juan Bautista graduate - but no resident's medical school is published at all (domain 12), so this is an absence of published evidence rather than a demonstrated absence; the ten faculty Digital Measures profiles show medical degrees from Germany (x1, plus a German PhD), South Korea (x2), Bangladesh (x1), Jordan (x1), Guatemala (x1), China (x1), and the United States (University of Texas-Houston, and UNTHSC TCOM for the PM&R DO) - none from Puerto Rico; the published alumni list for 2014-2020 names no Puerto Rico medical school; there is no affiliation agreement, visiting-student pathway, exchange or recruiting relationship with any Puerto Rico institution published on the program, department or GME pages. ELIGIBILITY MECHANICS, which is where this domain actually matters: the governing institutional rule is that 'Each applicant must be a graduate of a medical school that is approved by the Texas Medical Board or a medical school whose curriculum is accepted as equivalent to that of a Texas medical school by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board', with the ECFMG certificate required only of the latter group. UCC is LCME-accredited and therefore falls in the FIRST group - TMB-approved, no ECFMG, no notarized diploma, no clerkship affidavit, no J-1. The program's own Application Process page, however, presents only a binary 'US Graduates' versus 'International Medical Graduate' checklist and never mentions LCME, Puerto Rico or US territories, so the risk is mis-sorting by a reader rather than a substantive eligibility barrier.
conflict_notes: PARTIALLY_VERIFIED because the negative finding for current residents is only as strong as the (nonexistent) publication of resident medical schools. The one Puerto Rico data point is eight years old and is a destination, not an origin. Practical consequence for Alejandra: there is no UCC or Puerto Rico alumni network to leverage here, no faculty member who trained in Puerto Rico, and no program-side familiarity with UCC that can be assumed - she would be introducing her school to this program rather than building on a known relationship.

FREIDA/REGISTRY (conflicting): 'US MD Graduates Percent: 88.1%', 'DO Graduates Percent: 0.0%', 'IMG Graduates Percent: 11.9%'. 11.9% back-solves to 5/42 (5/42 = 11.905%), and the gender split 54.8%/45.2% back-solves to 23/42 and 19/42 - so FREIDA's demographic denominator is 42, not 44. AGGREGATOR (residencyadvisor, third value): 'MD 90%, U.S. IMG 5%, Non-U.S. IMG 6%' - which sums to 101% and is internally inconsistent on its face.
conflict_notes: Marked CONFLICT rather than VERIFIED because three sources disagree on IMG share, and the disagreement is material to an IMG applicant's read of this program. Three non-exclusive candidate explanations, none of which I can confirm: (1) FREIDA's 'IMG' category is commonly understood to include US CITIZENS who attended medical school outside the US - residencyadvisor's separate 'U.S. IMG 5%' bucket supports this reading, and such residents are indistinguishable on a roster that lists only school names; (2) FREIDA's snapshot (survey received 2025-07-09) covers a different cohort year than the current AY2026-2027 roster; (3) FREIDA's denominator is demonstrably 42 while the actual complement is 44. I did NOT infer nationality, citizenship, or ethnicity from any resident's name - classification is strictly by the accreditation/location of the named medical school. The 0% DO figure is the one point where all three sources agree (roster: 0 DO schools; FREIDA: 0.0%), and the registry's 'Osteopathic Recognition: No' is consistent.

conflict_notes: PARTIALLY_VERIFIED is the honest state: the safety-net training evidence is strong, specific and program-level (continuity clinics physically located in Parkland's ambulatory care center is a curricular fact, not a city statistic), but the Spanish-language and Latino-specific evidence is absent at the program level and only generic at the institutional level. (2) PROGRAM LEADERSHIP INVESTED IN THE SAFETY NET: the Residency Program Director, Corey Elam Goldsmith, M.D., concurrently serves as 'Chief of Neurology Outpatient Clinics at Ben Taub Hospital (Harris Health System)' — directly tying residency leadership to safety-net ambulatory neurology. (c) CONTAMINATION TRAP AVOIDED: a search for medical Spanish surfaced the BCM CHILD Neurology program as offering medical Spanish / non-English language instruction. raw_finding: Searched, in order of authority: (1) the program's own Residency Application Process page (lsom.uthscsa.edu, modified 2026-06-23) - it states ERAS-only submission, ECFMG/J-1 rules for IMGs, and the review criteria list, and says NOTHING about when USMLE results must be in hand; (2) the program's Residency Program Description page (modified 2026-08-27) - nothing; (3) the Residency Program landing page (modified 2026-06-23) - nothing; (4) the Resident Benefits and Compensation page - nothing; (5) the Office of GME policy manual index and the two governing PDFs, Policy 4.3 Resident Selection and Appointment (GMEC approved September 9, 2025) and Policy 3.3 Completion of USMLE Examinations (GMEC revised February 2015); (6) the GME International Residents policy page; (7) the FREIDA 2026 survey node's USMLE fields; (8) the GME residencies index. There is NO published applicant FAQ for this program. RESULT: the program publishes no Step 2 CK timing barrier of any kind - not with the application, not before initial review, not before interview invitation, not before ranking. The only institutional timing statement located is Policy 3.3's PGY-1-ENTRY expectation ('for appointment to a PGY1 position'), i.e. by July of the training year, roughly nine months AFTER Alejandra's mid-October 2026 score release. The FREIDA 2026 survey's interview-related flag field_usmle_step2_req_int is FALSE, which is the closest thing to an explicit 'not required for interview' datum and is consistent with the absence of published language. COUNTERVAILING OPERATIONAL FACT, which is about review sequencing rather than a Step 2 rule: the program states 'Applications will be reviewed as they become available in the ERAS system, and candidates will be invited in the order they are received and reviewed.' That is an explicitly ROLLING, first-in-first-reviewed process. Per the OPDA/CMSS Adult Neurology guide, ERAS applications open September 2, 2026 and programs begin reviewing September 23, 2026, with the typical neurology interview offer window running October 2026 - January 2027. So a file reaching this program in late September 2026 without a Step 2 CK score will be read on its other merits under a published policy that imposes no Step 2 gate, but it will be read early, and the score will land mid-October while interview offers are already being issued. There is no published mechanism for re-review after a score arrives, and none is promised.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No published rule was found stating when a Step 2 CK score must be in hand. Contact the program coordinator to confirm.
conflict_notes: RESEARCHED_NOT_FOUND here means 'searched thoroughly and the program publishes no timing rule'; it is NOT translated into 'not required.' The registry schema has no Step 2 timing field at all, so nothing was reused.

raw_finding: TWO INDEPENDENT LAYERS. (1) NAME-LEVEL, AY2026-27, denominator 37 - the only defensible name-level split is by published DEGREE SUFFIX: 4 DO (10.8%) and 33 MD (89.2%). The MD holders cannot be divided between US MD, Puerto Rico LCME, Caribbean offshore and other IMG because the program publishes no schools. (2) AGGREGATE, AY2025-26, denominator 34, from the FREIDA survey received 2026-07-08: field_pct_usmd = 47.1 (16/34), field_pct_img = 44.1 (15/34), field_pct_do = 8.8 (3/34), field_pct_female = 52.9 (18/34), field_pct_male = 47.1 (16/34). These three training-background shares sum to exactly 100.0 and each resolves to a whole resident out of 34, which is a strong internal consistency check that 34 was the survey denominator. INTERPRETATION: this is a genuinely IMG-heavy program - roughly 44% of residents are international graduates, an unusually high share for a university-based program, which in practice means the applicant pool this program actually ranks is broad rather than US-MD-dominated. FACULTY-SIDE COMPARATOR: FREIDA field_pct_ft_female = 44.00 (registry 42.90%). HOMEGROWN PIPELINE: the 2025 Annual Report reports 'a record four students from UT San Antonio Long School of Medicine' in the class recruited that year, and separately that 21 students took neurology electives with 11 applying to adult neurology - so a meaningful fraction of each class comes from the home medical school.
conflict_notes: Registry percentages (US MD 46.9%, IMG 46.9%, DO 6.2%, female 56.2%) are SUPERSEDED by the newer survey (47.1 / 44.1 / 8.8 / 52.9). Note the two layers have different denominators and different roster years and must not be merged.

raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY (Movement Disorders Faculty page, modified 2025-12-10): Okeanis Vaou, MD - Associate Professor/Clinical, Chief of the Division of Movement Disorders, Vice Chair for Faculty Development and Wellness, and Movement Disorders Fellowship Program Director (vaou@uthscsa.edu); Sarah Horn, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical AND the sitting Neurology Residency Program Director; Pablo Coss, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical (Class of 2020 graduate of this residency who returned as faculty); Leila Saadatpour, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical (Class of 2022 graduate of this residency who trained in Movement Disorders at Cleveland Clinic and returned); plus specialists Jessica Grimaldo and Kristen Matulis. Alicia Parker, MD and Leila Saadatpour, MD co-direct the CurePSP Center of Care. DEDICATED CLINIC AND PROGRAM: the section operates as the Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program (PDMDP) - 'Currently there are four fellowship trained movement disorders specialist, one movement disorders fellow in training, and two advanced practice providers.' The division states 'We are the only comprehensive Movement Disorders Center in the area of South Central Texas.' Named sub-clinics and designations: the Perry and Ruby Stevens Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence; a MIND Movement Disorder clinic 'for patients needing expedited evaluation of cognitive complaints in the setting of parkinsonism'; partner site for the Huntington Disease Society of America Center of Excellence Level 1 with UTHealth Houston; a 2025 CurePSP Center of Care designation covering PSP, CBD and MSA; and (via the Biggs Institute) a Lewy Body Dementia Association Research Center of Excellence designation. A Movement Disorders Clinic was established in Laredo, with Pablo Coss, MD travelling there regularly 'to better serve rural and underserved communities.' PROCEDURES AND THERAPIES: deep brain stimulation (with multidisciplinary DBS meetings and a 'DBS Connections' patient/caregiver program spanning preoperative education to long-term postoperative care), continuous levodopa pump, botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen pump management, and focused ultrasound discussed at the 2025 symposium. FELLOWSHIP: a two-year NON-ACGME adult Movement Disorders fellowship, one fellow selected per year, applied for through SF Match; year one clinical/procedural, year two adds research; available as a one-year clinical fellowship though the second year is recommended; requires completion of an ACGME-accredited Neurology residency and a full unrestricted Texas medical license; research conducted at the Perry and Ruby Stevens Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence and the Glenn Biggs Institute; curriculum includes didactics, journal club, multidisciplinary DBS meetings and video rounds. The fellowship was established in 2019 per the department's 50-year timeline. CURRENT FELLOWS (page modified 2026-07-10): TWO movement disorders fellows in post - Paro Bhaya, MD and Diana Petrosyan, MD. RESIDENT PIPELINE EVIDENCE: Brian Seegmiller (Class of 2025) entered the UT Health San Antonio Movement Disorders Fellowship; Pablo Coss (Class of 2020) did the same and is now faculty; Leila Saadatpour (Class of 2022) went to Cleveland Clinic Movement Disorders and returned as faculty; Hunberto Leal Bailey (Class of 2020) went to a Movement Disorder Fellowship at the University of Houston. RESIDENT ELECTIVES: the published elective menu explicitly includes 'Neurology general or subspecialty clinics,' and the PGY-2/3/4 block grid includes Clinical Practice (CP) blocks and multiple Elective blocks; the division states it provides 'active clinical education to medical students during their neurology rotation, neurology residents in training.' ACTIVE RESEARCH: participation in five Parkinson's Study Group (PSG) clinical trials plus industry-sponsored studies; named trials include ACP-204-012/013 (Lewy Body Dementia Psychosis), BIA 28 6156 (GBA1-variant PD), BHV8000-301 (early PD), BN44715 (IV prasinezumab, early PD), CAMELOT (antipsychotics in Lewy body disease), and induced-pluripotent-stem-cell genetics work. The program was 'the top recruiting site for PD GENEration in 2024 and 2025' and has been 'designated as a Super Site for PD GENEration, with the goal of recruiting a substantial number of patients with Parkinson's Disease, particularly those from a Hispanic background.' A dedicated study, 'Building a Health Coach Program,' is described as 'Coaching underserved communities and Hispanic minorities with Parkinson's Disease who lack resources and education about exercise and diet.' COMMUNITY: UT San Antonio's 2nd Annual Parkinson's Disease Symposium, a full-day free community symposium held March 2025 covering physical and speech therapy, exercise, freezing of gait, swallowing, caregiver support, Parkinson's disease in special populations, current research, DBS and focused ultrasound.
conflict_notes: This is one of the strongest movement-disorders findings possible short of an ACGME-accredited fellowship - the fellowship is explicitly non-ACGME, which matters for anyone who requires ACGME accreditation downstream (UCNS/Movement Disorders fellowships are commonly non-ACGME, so this is the field norm rather than a deficiency). The internal pipeline is demonstrated, not asserted: at least three graduates of this residency have gone into movement disorders and two are now on its faculty.

This is a prestigious designation granted to us by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS). We are only 1 of 8 centers in Texas with this title.' The 2025 Annual Report restates this as 'the first Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center in South Texas, a designation conferred by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS), and one of only eight centers in Texas to hold this distinction.' CLINIC HISTORY AND VOLUME: 'Dr Romero founded the clinic in 2011 with only 200 patients at the end of the year. Since then, we have seen tremendous success and growth treating over 2,000 patients with various neuroimmunologic disorders.' Care is now delivered at the Center for Brain Health, in coordination with physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, social work and neuropsychology, and in collaboration with urology/urogynecology and neuro-ophthalmology. CONDITIONS TREATED: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease (MOGAD), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosarcoidosis, neuropsychiatric lupus (NPSLE), neurologic manifestations of Sjogren's syndrome, and transverse myelitis. The department's historical Patient Care page notes the neuro-immunology program 'has focused on the neurological and psychiatric complications associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.' SERVICES: spasticity management including botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen pump management and splinting; dedicated infusion services for disease-modifying therapies (the Center for Brain Health houses a dedicated 12-chair non-oncology infusion suite); MRI at 1.5T and 3T, with the region's only 7-Tesla MRI available at the Center for Brain Health. FELLOWSHIP: a 12-month MS and Neuroimmunology fellowship, 'approved by the UT Health at San Antonio GME (Graduate Medical Education) department in 2022'; the fellow holds Faculty Development Position status and functions 'as licensed and fully privileged attending physicians within the Neurology Department'; salary funded by the fellow's own clinical productivity and billing. Curriculum: 10 four-hour blocks per week - six continuity clinic blocks at the MARC, 1-2 blocks a month in a subspecialty clinic at University Hospital where the fellow precepts neurology residents at their continuity clinic, one procedures block (botulinum toxin and baclofen pump), one elective block, one self-study/research block, plus inpatient autoimmune consults at University Hospital. Didactics: monthly autoimmune conference and monthly journal club. CURRENT FELLOWS: the department reports TWO neuroimmunology fellows - the 2025 Annual Report names 'Neuroimmunology fellows (2025-2026): Iryna Lobanova, MD, Eric Yeager, MD' and the Current Fellows page (modified 2026-07-10) lists Ashlynn Fajayan, DO and Vinutha Ganapathy, MD; the Annual Report notes 'Neuroimmunology and Clinical Neurophysiology taking two fellows.' RESIDENT PIPELINE: Eric Yeager (Class of 2025) went directly into the UT Health San Antonio Neuroimmunology Fellowship; Alejandra Duque Ramirez (Class of 2024) went to a Neuroimmunology Fellowship at the University of Chicago; Justin Rodriguez (Class of 2019) stayed as Clinical Instructor with neuroimmunology anticipated. RESIDENT TEACHING: 'Faculty members actively participate in the clinical education of medical students during their neurology clerkship rotation and the graduate medical education of neurology residents.' ACTIVE RESEARCH AND COMMUNITY: an active clinical trials program (named studies include Biomarker Validation, a longitudinal serum/CSF biomarker study, and BLOOMS, on a low-insulin lifestyle and the microbiome in MS); MS Education Day for Patients and Caregivers held September 2025; Texas Multiple Sclerosis Consortium lectures in partnership with Can Do MS and CMSC (Lyndsey Hale, MD); and - directly relevant to Alejandra - 'Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative Member, National Multiple Sclerosis Society Initiative - Tania Reyna, MD.' The division's stated mission includes 'evaluating, and addressing health disparities within our community.'
conflict_notes: The division is small in headcount (two attending physicians plus a PA-C), which is the one caveat - depth of named MS faculty is thinner than the movement-disorders division. Note the fellowship is non-ACGME (institutionally GME-approved in 2022), which is the norm for MS/neuroimmunology. Dr. Rebecca Romero, who founded the clinic in 2011 and formerly served as Associate Program Director, no longer appears on the current faculty page.

program_name: University of Texas Health Science Center San Antonio Joe and Teresa Lozano Long School of Medicine Program
summary: Not published. Program tracks graduates' board certification pass rates internally (FREIDA program-evaluation field) and builds board preparation into promotion standards, but publishes no figure.
raw_finding: No program-specific ABPN neurology board certification pass rate is published. Searched: the program's Residency Program page, Program Description page, Application Process page, Benefits and Compensation page, Where Did Our Residents Go page, the 2025 Neurology Annual Report PDF in full (a text search of the extracted document for 'board pass', 'ABPN', and 'certification pass' returned nothing), the department Education pages, the FREIDA 2026 survey node (210 fields; no board-pass-rate field exists in the survey schema), and general web search. WHAT IS PUBLISHED INSTEAD: the program states that board preparation is an explicit promotion standard - 'Exams - this includes a personal goal of scoring high enough to be able to show preparation to pass the written board exam. Oral board vignette case studies and patient presentations are set to aid the resident with their learning and preparation for studies with their certification exams. Those who need assistance will work with faculty in reading programs to enhance their preparation for their exams.' And FREIDA field_program_evaluation_2019 records that the program uses 'Graduates' board certification pass rates' as one of its three named program-evaluation instruments, alongside 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements' and 'Performance-based assessment scores (e.g. OSCE, patient or computer simulations)' - so the program tracks the metric internally but does not publish the number. ACGME's public program search, which is the other place a board pass rate would appear, is CAPTCHA-gated and was NOT circumvented per governance law 3.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · The program does not publish a board pass rate.
conflict_notes: Registry 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation = Yes' is a SEMANTIC_MISMATCH risk: it records that the program USES board pass rates as an evaluation instrument, not that a pass rate is published or known. Do not read that registry Yes as a performance figure.

raw_finding: This domain was tested hard for PROGRAM- AND INSTITUTION-LEVEL evidence, with city demographics explicitly excluded as non-evidence per governance law 5. WHAT WAS FOUND, in descending order of strength. (1) A NAMED SPANISH LANGUAGE CLINIC INSIDE THE DEPARTMENT. The 2025 Neurology Annual Report, in the Clinical Activities section for the department's primary clinical hub, lists among its specialized neuro-cognitive clinics: 'Spanish Language Clinic: Culturally and linguistically tailored care is at the heart of everything we do for Spanish-speaking patients. All services, from neuropsychological assessments to counseling, are provided in Spanish, and in 2025, we worked closely with the CAPAS Center to ensure that research and care are optimized for Hispanic/Latino families in South Texas.' This is a named, standing clinical service within the Department of Neurology's own annual report - not a city statistic and not a medical-school elective. (2) A FACULTY-LEVEL NATIONAL HISPANIC MS ROLE. The Neuroimmunology division's Community Engagement list names 'Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative Member, National Multiple Sclerosis Society Initiative - Tania Reyna, MD' - the Division Chief of Neuroimmunology and MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship Director holds a formal role in a national NMSS Hispanic/Latinx initiative. (3) A FUNDED HISPANIC-FOCUSED MOVEMENT DISORDERS RESEARCH PROGRAM. The Movement Disorders division reports being 'the top recruiting site for PD GENEration in 2024 and 2025' and 'designated as a Super Site for PD GENEration, with the goal of recruiting a substantial number of patients with Parkinson's Disease, particularly those from a Hispanic background,' plus a named study 'Building a Health Coach Program - Coaching underserved communities and Hispanic minorities with Parkinson's Disease who lack resources and education about exercise and diet,' and a separate project 'Increasing Recruitment in Diverse Parkinson's Disease Populations - Parkinson's Foundation PD GENEration Genetic Registry Community Outreach.' (4) AN NIA-DESIGNATED ADRC WITH AN EXPLICIT LATINO DEMENTIA-DISPARITIES MISSION. The Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's & Neurodegenerative Diseases, which sits inside this department's orbit and is where Movement Disorders and Behavioral Neurology fellows do research, is described in the Annual Report as having secured in 2025 'the renewal of its designation as a National Institute on Aging (NIA) Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC), extending its status as the only federally designated center of its kind in Texas,' and the report describes a companion social-science center whose 'primary mission is to identify why Hispanic communities in South Texas face disproportionate dementia risks and to develop public health strategies that address these disparities at the source.' (5) A SAFETY-NET CLINICAL PARTNER, WITH RESIDENTS PLACED IN IT. The program's primary clinical partner is University Health - the Bexar County Hospital District public health system, the third largest public health system in Texas - and the department operates a satellite clinic at the Robert B. Green Downtown Campus, University Health's historic downtown safety-net outpatient center. The PGY-1 longitudinal schedule places the resident's continuity clinic AT THE ROBERT B. GREEN CLINIC ('The resident will spend 1/2 day in the continuity clinic at the Robert B. Green Clinic'). The MS/Neuroimmunology fellowship curriculum states its University Hospital subspecialty clinic 'offers the opportunity for the fellow to precept neurology residents at their continuity clinic and interact with Medicaid and the underserved population.' (6) RURAL AND BORDER-REGION OUTREACH. A Movement Disorders Clinic was established in Laredo - a majority-Hispanic border city - with Pablo Coss, MD travelling there regularly 'to better serve rural and underserved communities'; the Biggs Institute also operates satellite clinics at UT Health Laredo and UT Health Hill Country; and the epilepsy program maintains 'a close collaborative relationship with the Epilepsy Foundation of Central and South Texas through our support of outreach clinics in the underserved communities of South Texas.' (7) DEPARTMENTAL MISSION LANGUAGE. The department's stated Vision is 'To optimize brain health for a diverse community'; its Values include 'Health Equity: We strive for the highest level of health for all people'; Community Engagement is one of its four stated mission pillars; and the Neuroimmunology division's mission explicitly includes 'evaluating, and addressing health disparities within our community.' WHAT WAS NOT FOUND, AND MUST NOT BE CLAIMED: there is NO formal Medical Spanish curriculum, Spanish-language track, language certification, or interpreter-training requirement published for the NEUROLOGY RESIDENCY. No neurology page, the 2025 Annual Report, and the FREIDA 2026 survey's offerings list all lack any language-instruction item.
conflict_notes: REGISTRY DEFECT CAUGHT - this is precisely the Stage A failure mode the contract warned about. The registry asserts 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: Yes'. The FREIDA survey received 2026-07-08 lists the program's resident/fellow offerings as exactly nine items - health systems leadership curriculum, interprofessional teamwork, debt management/financial counseling, USMLE Step 3 academic support, international experience/global health, resident/fellow retreats, off-campus electives, hospice/home care experience, and advanced degree training - and 'Instruction in medical Spanish or other non-English language' is NOT among them. Two decoys were found and rejected: (a) a Medical Spanish Interpretation & Translation elective that belongs to the UT Health San Antonio INTERNAL MEDICINE residency's 'Create Your Own Elective' menu, a different department; and (b) a CanopyLearn medical-Spanish license and a 'Latin American Health and Language' program that belong to UTHealth HOUSTON (med.uth.edu), a different institution. Neither was imported. The genuine Spanish/Latino case for this program is clinical, research and community-based, and it is strong - but it is NOT a language curriculum.

raw_finding: No Universidad Central del Caribe graduate, no Puerto Rico medical school graduate, and no Puerto Rico institutional tie was identified for this program. Searched: the current-residents roster (names and PGY only - no medical schools are published, so no resident can be traced to UCC or any other school; see domain 12), the thirteen-class Where Did Our Residents Go page (destinations only, no origin schools, and no Puerto Rico destination appears in any of the 2013-2025 classes), the Current Fellows page, all seven division faculty pages, the Department Leadership page, the full 2025 Neurology Annual Report PDF, and targeted web search pairing 'Universidad Central del Caribe' and 'Puerto Rico' with this program and its faculty. The only Puerto Rico connection surfaced anywhere in the institution was a Biggs Institute assistant professor holding graduate degrees from Ponce Health Sciences University - a PhD-track basic/clinical scientist, not a Neurology residency graduate, not a UCC graduate, and not evidence of a residency pipeline. ELIGIBILITY POSITION, which is the part that actually matters: institutional GME Policy 4.3 (September 2025) makes a graduate of an LCME-accredited medical school eligible on the first prong, with ECFMG certification required only of international medical school graduates. UCC is LCME-accredited, so Alejandra is a US MD graduate for this program's eligibility purposes and needs no ECFMG certificate and no visa. AMBIGUITY FLAGGED PER CONTRACT: the policy phrase is 'Graduate of medical school in the U.S. and Canada accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME) or the American Osteopathic Association (AOA)' - it does not name Puerto Rico or US territories explicitly, and no program or GME page examined mentions Puerto Rico anywhere. The LCME accreditation test is unambiguous on its face, but a one-line written confirmation from the program coordinator would remove any risk of an applicant-screening system mis-bucketing a Puerto Rico LCME school as international and applying the IMG J-1/ECFMG/USCE language to her file.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No Universidad Central del Caribe or Puerto Rico medical-school connection was found.
conflict_notes: 'Not identified' here is constrained by the fact that the program publishes no resident medical schools at all - absence of published UCC/PR graduates is therefore weak evidence of absence, not strong evidence. The FREIDA-reported 44.1% IMG share shows the program ranks broadly, which is context, not a Puerto Rico tie.

raw_finding: ACGME ID 1804821127 = 'San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program' in NEUROLOGY (Adult Neurology), sponsored by SAUSHEC, a Department of Defense / Defense Health Agency multi-service GME consortium. FREIDA renders the sponsor location as 'San Antonio Military Med Ctr, MCHE-ZDM-N, 3551 Roger Brooke Dr, JBSA Ft Sam Houston, TX 78234-4504'. The official DHA GME program page gives the residency's own contact address as 'Brooke Army Medical Center, Neurology Clinic, 1st floor, 3551 Roger Brooke Dr., JBSA Fort Sam Houston, TX 78234', phone 210-916-2203, fax 210-916-3833, email dha.jbsa.brooke-amc.list.saushec-neuro@health.mil, hours Mon-Fri 0730-1630. GEOGRAPHY (explicitly checked because the base name is misleading): JBSA Fort Sam Houston is in SAN ANTONIO, Bexar County, Texas. It is NOT in Houston. Houston is approximately 195-200 road miles east on I-10, roughly a 3-hour drive. The word 'Houston' in 'Fort Sam Houston' commemorates Sam Houston and has nothing to do with the city of Houston. PROGRAM STRUCTURE (the registry's '3 years' resolved): the official page's AT A GLANCE block states verbatim 'Program Length: 3 years (program starts at PGY2 level)' and 'Required Pre-Requisite Training: Medical school graduation, completion of PGY1 program in Internal Medicine. All applicants must be active duty members of the U.S. Military.' and 'Categorical Year in Specialty Required: No' and 'Total Approved Complement: 8' and 'Approved per Year (if applicable): N/A' and 'Dedicated Research Year Offered: No' and 'Medical Student Rotation Availability: 3rd and 4th year' and 'Additional Degree Concurrent with Training (e.g. MPH): No' and 'Program Type: Military Medical Center' and 'Accredited: Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME)'. So this is an ADVANCED (PGY-2 entry) Adult Neurology program of 3 ACGME-accredited years, requiring a separately obtained PGY-1 year, and that PGY-1 must be in INTERNAL MEDICINE specifically (narrower than the ACGME neurology program requirements, which permit a broader preliminary year). Total training is 4 years. The program's own text confirms the PGY numbering: 'our PGY2 residents often take 6-7 call shifts in a 4-week block, while our PGY4 residents often take 1-3 call shifts per 4-week block. Our PGY4 (chief residents)...'. An archived official BAMC page (captured 2019-12-08, page-modified stamp 2012) stated: 'SAUSHEC Neurology is an ACGME accredited training program and is the only Neurology Residency Training Program in the USAF. SAUSHEC Neurology is a 4-year residency program, including 1 year of internship. Yearly, Neurology accepts 2-3 AF applicants and may defer 1-2, depending on future needs of those services.' SERVICE OWNERSHIP: the Uniformed Services University Department of Neurology residency page lists SAUSHEC under 'AIR FORCE RESIDENCY CONTACTS' and states 'The second program is at San Antonio Military Medical Center in San Antonio, TX. This program is for Air Force applicants.' SAUSHEC institution-wide: 36 ACGME GME programs, 22 Graduate Allied Health Education programs, 766 residents, 360 inpatient beds (average daily census 250); training sites Brooke Army Medical Center (BAMC), Wilford Hall Ambulatory Surgical Center (JBSA-Lackland), and the Moreno Clinic; BAMC is the busiest hospital in the DoD and hosts its sole Level I trauma center and burn center. Neurology rotation sites: BAMC, Audie L. Murphy Veterans Affairs hospital, and University of Texas Health San Antonio (UTHSA).
conflict_notes: Registry 'Program Length: 3 years' is literally correct for the ACGME-accredited length but is materially misleading without the PGY-2 entry point; classed SEMANTIC_MISMATCH. Three different official ZIP/suite renderings were seen (78234-4504 sponsor record, 78234 program contact block, 78234-6200 on the archived legacy page) - preserved as a conflict rather than silently harmonized. The legacy 'only Neurology Residency Training Program in the USAF' claim is a 2012-era statement recovered from a 2019 Wayback capture of a domain (www.bamc.health.mil) that no longer resolves (DNS SERVFAIL as of this run); it is corroborated in substance, but not verbatim, by the current USUHS page.

The official DHA GME Application Information FAQ (Eligibility, page last updated 25 Aug 2026) asks 'If I am a non-U.S. citizen or other status such as legal resident (green card) am I eligible to apply?' and answers verbatim: 'No. All applicants must be U.S. citizens.' Note the answer excludes even lawful permanent residents, not merely visa holders. The same FAQ's Q1 limits eligibility to (a) persons affiliated with a U.S. Uniformed Service - 'Current Medical Corps officer authorized to apply by their Service' or persons 'Enrolled in the Uniformed Services University School of Medicine, Health Professions Scholarship Program, or Health Services Collegiate Program' - and (b) 'Civilian applicant to one of the few programs that have VA funded position(s)'. Because entry to this program requires a commission as a U.S. military Medical Corps officer, and commissioning requires U.S. citizenship, there is no visa pathway of any kind.
conflict_notes: The registry row carried no visa fields at all (one of the 127 unpopulated columns), so this domain is entirely fresh research. For a non-U.S.-citizen applicant this is an absolute bar, not a preference.

summary: Not published. No minimum, no pass/fail statement, no screening threshold. USMLE transcript is a required JGMESB document; no score standard published.
raw_finding: No USMLE Step 1 policy is published by this program anywhere I could reach. Checked: (1) the official DHA GME SAUSHEC Neurology program page - its 'Applicant Information, Rotation and Interview Opportunities' section covers medical-student rotations and interview logistics and says only 'In our candidates, we value potential for academic success, but also work ethic, ability to function well in a team, and many other factors which demonstrate potential for long-term success as a military officer and neurologist'; no score language, no Step policy. (2) FREIDA program 1804821127, 'Program & Work Schedule' view: the fields 'Medical Exam Licensing Requirements for Interview Consideration', 'Recommendation Letter Requirements' and 'Additional Eligibility Information' are rendered as bare headings with NO values - the program left them blank in the AMA survey (FREIDA record last updated 2/19/2026). (3) The DHA GME Application Information page and its four FAQ pages: no Step 1 language. (4) The Air Force Physician Education Branch GME Application Instructions page: it lists 'USMLE / COMLEX Transcript' among required application documents submitted by Medical School Officials, but states no minimum score, no pass/fail language, and no per-specialty threshold. Related but distinct fact: the Air Force Post-GME Assignments page requires a 'Step/Level 3 score report (taken by March 15 of PGY1)' and an 'Unrestricted state medical license (issued by March 15 of PGY2)' - that is a Step 3 timing rule for physicians already in Air Force GME, not an applicant Step 1 screening rule. Since Step 1 is now pass/fail, the only published requirement anywhere in this pipeline is that a USMLE transcript be furnished to the Joint Graduate Medical Education Selection Board.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · A Step 1 policy is not published.
conflict_notes: Searched and genuinely unpublished - NOT the same as 'no requirement'. Selection is by the Joint Service GME Selection Board, whose per-specialty scoring rubric lives in the CAC-restricted MODS system and the CAC-restricted HPERB document, which I did not and could not access.

program_name: San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program
summary: No published Step 2 CK minimum; no published statement that Step 2 CK is required for application. Program administers its own end-of-rotation written test to students applying to the residency.
raw_finding: No USMLE Step 2 CK minimum score, and no statement that Step 2 CK is required at all, is published by this program. There is no published 230/235/240-type cutoff. The functional screening mechanism is the Joint Graduate Medical Education Selection Board's internal ranking, whose criteria are not public. In addition, the program page describes a program-administered written examination given to audition rotators: 'Students applying to the neurology residency will also take a written test at the end of the rotation.' That program-specific written test - not a USMLE threshold - is the only published objective academic screen this program describes.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No minimum Step 2 CK score is published.
conflict_notes: Alejandra's 230-240 planning range cannot be compared against any published standard here because none exists. Note that the contract's Step 2 CK 235 figure is a planning midpoint, not a score.

program_name: San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program
summary: RESEARCHED_NOT_FOUND at program level. Program publishes no Step 2 timing. Surrounding JGMESB calendar: application window 1 Jul - 31 Aug 2026; supporting documents incl. USMLE transcript due 15 Oct 2026.
raw_finding: The five-way timing question (required with application / before initial review / before interview invitation / before ranking / no published timing) cannot be answered from this program's own publications because the program publishes no USMLE timing language at all. Every candidate source is empty on timing: the official program page says nothing; FREIDA's 'Medical Exam Licensing Requirements for Interview Consideration' field is blank; there is no program applicant FAQ; there is no ERAS participation and therefore no ERAS-linked timing convention. I deliberately did NOT infer timing from any minimum-score language, because there is none. What IS published is the surrounding military-match calendar, which is a different thing and must not be mistaken for a program Step 2 rule. Per the Air Force Physician Education Branch, for the 2026 JGMESB cycle: applications are submitted via MODS (military network only) or by fillable PDF to the Physician Education Branch organizational email during 'July 1 through August 31, 2026'; supporting forms and documents, which include the 'USMLE / COMLEX Transcript' submitted by Medical School Officials, are due 'up until the deadline of October 15, 2026'. If a Step 2 CK score exists by mid-October it can be routed into the file through the school; the Air Force also publishes a 'Score Report Letter Template' under 'For Medical Student Applicants', which is consistent with late-arriving score reports being accommodated administratively. That is an inference about the mechanism, not a published program rule, and I am labelling it as such. Hypothetically mapped onto Alejandra's calendar - Step 2 CK sat late September 2026, score mid-October 2026 - the score would land right at the JGMESB supporting-document deadline of 15 October. But this analysis is moot for her: she cannot submit a JGMESB application at all (see domain 9 and the classification). Step 2 timing is therefore not the binding constraint at this program; eligibility is.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No published rule was found stating when a Step 2 CK score must be in hand. Contact the program coordinator to confirm.
conflict_notes: RESEARCHED_NOT_FOUND is explicitly NOT being translated into 'not required'. The registry has no Step 2 timing field at all (known 196-column schema gap), so nothing could be reused here.

program_name: San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program
summary: No published YOG limit. Bounded instead by military rank/promotion restrictions and commissioning age criteria.
raw_finding: No year-of-graduation limit is published. The official program page states no YOG rule. FREIDA's eligibility fields are blank. The DHA GME Eligibility FAQ imposes no graduation-recency criterion. The Air Force Physician Education Branch page imposes AGE- and RANK-based restrictions instead of YOG-based ones, which is the structurally different way a military accession system bounds applicant vintage: applicants may not apply if they are 'Colonel, Colonel-select, or IPZ to Colonel at time of application to GME or will be IPZ to Colonel during GME training' or are 'Below the rank of Lieutenant Colonel passed over for promotion'. Separately, the general accession literature for Medical Corps commissioning applies maximum-age criteria at the point of commissioning. For an applicant already commissioned via HPSP or USUHS, the practical effect is that application normally occurs in the final year of medical school or from an intern/staff position, which compresses the realistic YOG window without any explicit YOG rule existing.
