program_name: San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program
value: No IMG-style USCE requirement (IMGs ineligible). Audition rotation strongly encouraged for HPSP/USUHS students. Civilian medical students MAY rotate with a National Agency Check with Inquiries, but rank below military students in priority and cannot apply to the residency afterward.
summary: No IMG-style USCE requirement (IMGs ineligible). Audition rotation strongly encouraged for HPSP/USUHS students. Civilian medical students MAY rotate with a National Agency Check with Inquiries, but rank below military students in priority and cannot apply to the residency afterward.
raw_finding: There is no stated U.S. clinical experience requirement as an IMG-screening device, because the program does not accept IMGs or civilians at all. What the program does publish is a strongly encouraged AUDITION ROTATION pathway, restricted by population. Verbatim from the official program page, under 'Interview Guidance': 'Medical student applicants from Health Professions Scholarship Program (HPSP) or Uniformed Services University for the Health Sciences (USUHS) are encouraged to complete an interview rotation at BAMC, during which they will spend several weeks working with the inpatient consult team and also gain exposure to outpatient clinic.' Interviews are scheduled by emailing dha.jbsa.brooke-amc.list.saushec-neuro@health.mil. The rotation itself: 'Third and Fourth year medical students rotating through the neurology service will have exposure to 3 weeks of inpatient neurology consults as well as 1 week of outpatient neurology', with daily pre-rounding, daily morning lectures, table-rounds presentations, an opportunity to join 'a neuromuscular multidisciplinary clinic on the first Tuesday of each month' seeing ALS, myotonic dystrophy and various myopathies, a structured daily curriculum, a reading list, a student talk, and - critically - 'Students applying to the neurology residency will also take a written test at the end of the rotation.' The SAUSHEC medical-student rotation page adds operational detail: hours 6:30 a.m. - 4 p.m. with one day off per week, no call/nights, inpatient consult team comprising 'an attending, 2 neurology residents, and a variable number of off-service rotators'. ROTATION ELIGIBILITY - the one genuinely open door: SAUSHEC's medical-student page states that HPSP students schedule audition rotations through Clinician Nexus (app.cliniciannexus.com/join), that 'NON-HPSP Students: All rotations must be requested through the Student Coordinator via email at usarmy.jbsa.medcom-bamc.mbx.saushec-clerkship@health.mil', and explicitly that 'Civilians, with no military affiliation, must initiate a National Agency Check with Inquiries through the BAMC Security Office as soon as possible, but no later than one month prior to rotation start date.' So a civilian U.S. medical student CAN rotate at SAUSHEC subject to a NACI background check and an affiliation agreement; they simply cannot then apply to the residency. Priority ordering is published: 'Interview season for fourth year Medical Students is from May to October each year. Rotation requests from fourth year military medical students intending to interview will be given the highest priority for consideration.' Requests open on a rolling nine-month horizon (e.g. a July rotation may be requested from November 1). The neurology program separately asks students to 'request your rotation as early as possible, especially for requests during peak months of June - September.'
conflict_notes: PARTIALLY_VERIFIED because 'USCE requirement' in the ordinary IMG sense does not map onto this program; I answered the closest substantive question (audition-rotation access) rather than forcing the field.

program_name: San Antonio Uniformed Services Health Education Consortium Program
value: ECFMG route closed: program is not in NRMP, so civilians (ECFMG-certified or not) may not apply. UCC/Puerto Rico graduates are LCME U.S. MD graduates and clear the degree criterion, but are blocked by the active-duty/commissioning requirement, not by school accreditation.
summary: ECFMG route closed: program is not in NRMP, so civilians (ECFMG-certified or not) may not apply. UCC/Puerto Rico graduates are LCME U.S. MD graduates and clear the degree criterion, but are blocked by the active-duty/commissioning requirement, not by school accreditation.
raw_finding: ECFMG certification does not create a pathway into this program. The DHA GME Eligibility FAQ (health.mil, last updated 25 Aug 2026) asks 'May applicants who are ECFMG certified apply?' and answers verbatim: 'ECFMG applicants may apply to those programs that accept civilian applicants for VA funded positions, subject to the requirements of the VA and NRMP.' The preceding question, 'Can civilian applicants apply to DHA GME programs?', answers: 'A few programs accept civilian applicants for Veterans Administration funded positions. These programs may be found on the National Residency Matching Program website. Applicants must be U.S. citizens and meet the requirements of the VA and NRMP. Please note if the program is not found in the NRMP, that means civilian applicants may NOT apply.' The DHA GME Application Information landing page states the same rule in its own words: 'A limited number of programs have civilian positions funded by the Veterans Administration, and these positions are competed in the National Residency Match Program. Eligible applicants may apply through the NRMP. If a DHA GME program is not listed in the NRMP, then civilian applicants are not eligible to apply.' SAUSHEC Neurology is NOT in the NRMP. FREIDA's Program Participation block for 1804821127 lists under 'Participates In': 'Other Matching Program - Code: Military Selection Board', and under "Doesn't Participate In": 'Main Match of the National Resident Matching Program (NRMP)', 'San Francisco Match', 'Advanced or Fellowship Match of NRMP', and 'ERAS'. Therefore the ECFMG route is closed here. The eligibility FAQ's Q1 does list, as a general degree criterion, 'Graduated from a medical school outside of the United States or Canada, and meet one of the following additional qualifications: a. Hold a currently-valid certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates prior to appointment; or, b. Hold a full and unrestricted license to practice medicine in a United States licensing jurisdiction in his or her current ACGME specialty-/subspecialty program' - but that criterion sits underneath the citizenship gate ('No. All applicants must be U.S. citizens.') and, for a civilian, underneath the NRMP-listing gate. DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO ALEJANDRA'S SCHOOL TYPE: Universidad Central del Caribe is LCME-accredited, so a UCC graduate satisfies the FAQ's first degree bullet - 'Graduated from a medical school in the United States or Canada, accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education' - and is NOT an ECFMG-route applicant at all. Puerto Rico is a U.S. jurisdiction and its LCME schools are U.S. MD schools. No published DHA GME or Air Force GME language treats Puerto Rico LCME schools ambiguously; I looked specifically and found no carve-out, qualifier, or footnote about Puerto Rico. The barrier for a UCC graduate is therefore NOT degree accreditation and NOT ECFMG - it is the commissioning/active-duty requirement.
conflict_notes: I checked explicitly for ambiguous Puerto Rico language in the DHA GME and Air Force GME eligibility text and found none - a small but genuinely useful negative finding given the contract's flag about ambiguous LCME-Puerto-Rico wording elsewhere.

raw_finding: Composition cannot be established. The defensible denominator is 8 - the current census, verified twice (official program page 'Total Approved Complement: 8'; FREIDA 'Program Size 8' with Year 1/2/3 = 3/3/2). But the medical school of every one of those 8 individuals is unpublished, so all 8 fall into the 'unknown' bucket. Partition: us_md 0 + us_do 0 + caribbean 0 + other_img 0 + unknown 8 = 8 = denominator. Overlay counts (not part of the partition): ucc_residents 0, puerto_rico_school_residents 0 - meaning none identified, not zero verified. Structural context that bounds but does not determine the answer: entry requires a U.S. military commission and U.S. citizenship, and the feeder populations named by DHA GME are USUHS, HPSP and HSCP. USUHS is an LCME-accredited U.S. MD school; HPSP scholarships are held at U.S. LCME and AOA-accredited schools. The applicant pool is therefore overwhelmingly U.S. MD and U.S. DO by construction, and 'caribbean' (offshore for-profit) and 'other_img' entrants are structurally near-impossible because ECFMG-route applicants can only enter DHA GME through VA-funded civilian positions in NRMP-listed programs, of which this program has none. I am recording that as reasoning about the pipeline, not as counts.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · Resident composition cannot be fully derived because the program does not publish medical schools for all residents.
conflict_notes: Bucket rule satisfied: the five mutually exclusive buckets sum exactly to the denominator of 8. Overlays are excluded from the sum. Zero in the overlays means 'none identified in an unpublished roster', not 'verified none'.

raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY: two fellowship-trained movement-disorders neurologists have been publicly attached to Brooke Army Medical Center. Maj (Dr.) William Hoffman - his official USU profile lists him as 'Attending Neurologist & Movement Disorders Specialist, Brooke Army Medical Center' and 'Medical Director, Joint Integrated Clinical Medicine, 59th Medical Wing, JB San Antonio, TX', with a 'Movement Disorders Fellowship, Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY' where he trained in deep brain stimulation and botulinum toxin injections. Maj (Dr.) Jessie Jacobson, DO - identified in the official 15 April 2025 BAMC/JBSA article as a BAMC neurologist and movement-disorder specialist, fellowship-trained in movement disorders. That article states flatly: 'Hoffman and Jacobson are currently the only two Air Force neurologists who specialize in movement disorders. Additionally, there are only a few movement disorders specialists within the San Antonio community.' DEDICATED CLINICAL SERVICE - DBS PROGRAMMING IS DONE IN-HOUSE. From the same official article, Jacobson describing the BAMC workflow: 'Initially, during the first stages of the DBS programming, we will see the patient one month after surgery, then every 3-4 months in the first year to make sure everything is optimized. After that they can come back once or twice a year to get it checked. We have a tablet, which will tell us all the information about the patient's device and the patient has a little tablet themselves, that will show them the battery life.' Hoffman on directional/closed-loop programming: 'With the tablet, I can do an analysis and see exactly what the brainwaves are and then we can target the simulation and steer it exactly to the brainwaves causing the symptoms.' Referral pathway is published: 'Tricare beneficiaries who are experiencing any of the symptoms of PD should talk with their primary care team to get a referral to the BAMC Neurology Clinic for evaluation.' ACTIVE RESEARCH: an early-onset Parkinson's disease study in active-duty service members. Hoffman: 'In our clinic, we're seeing increasing numbers of active-duty patients with Parkinson's disease which is concerning. To our knowledge, no one has actually researched early-onset Parkinson's disease in active-duty service members, but we know that this population has many of the risk factors of Parkinson's disease.' Design, in his words: 'Our study aims to do a very detailed, comprehensive investigation of these patients. We're going into their deployment history, where they've been stationed, their exposure history - testing for toxic exposures in their body. We'll do a range of other diagnostic tests; test their genetics and check their microbiome because certain types of gut bacteria changes are associated with the development of the disease.' Risk factors under study include head injuries, PTSD and chemical exposures. RESIDENT EXPOSURE: movement disorders is named in the program's published faculty subspecialty list. Procedural training explicitly includes botulinum toxin: 'We place an emphasis on procedural competency for the treatment of headaches, including botulinum toxin injections, nerve blocks, and more.' Two optional external courses in the program's published course list are movement-disorders-specific: 'Vanderbilt University Focus on Common Movement Disorders' and 'Vanderbilt University Neuromodulation Course'. Residents have 2 elective blocks per year in each of the three years (6 elective blocks total across residency) and the program states residents do not compete with fellows for procedures. FELLOWSHIP: there is NO movement disorders fellowship at SAUSHEC. The program states 'Because we do not have fellowship training, residents do not have to compete with fellows for these procedures'; the SAUSHEC program list contains 36 programs and no neurology subspecialty fellowship of any kind.
conflict_notes: CURRENCY CAVEAT on Jacobson: a civilian San Antonio practice (Dominion Neurology Associates) now presents her as practising there, so the 'two AF movement disorders neurologists at BAMC' statement may be an April-2025 snapshot rather than the September-2026 position. Hoffman's BAMC role is corroborated by his current official USU profile.

raw_finding: THERE ARE NO NEUROLOGY SUBSPECIALTY FELLOWSHIPS AT SAUSHEC. The program says so itself and treats it as a selling point: 'Because we do not have fellowship training, residents do not have to compete with fellows for these procedures as sometimes occurs at major academic centers.' The claim is corroborated structurally: the full SAUSHEC program directory on health.mil lists 36 programs - 16 residencies (Anesthesiology, Dermatology, Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine, Neurology, OB/GYN, Ophthalmology, Orthopaedic Surgery, Otolaryngology, Pathology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, Diagnostic Radiology, Surgery, Transitional Year, Urology) and 20 fellowships (Adolescent Medicine, Advanced Emergency Medicine Ultrasonography, Allergy/Immunology, Cardiovascular Disease, Cytopathology, EMS & Disaster Medicine, Endocrinology, Gastroenterology, Hematology & Medical Oncology, Infectious Disease, Neonatology & Perinatal Medicine, Nephrology, Nuclear Medicine, Pain Medicine, Pulmonary Critical Care, Musculoskeletal Radiology, Rheumatology, Sleep Medicine, Surgical Critical Care & Acute Care Surgery/Trauma, Undersea & Hyperbaric Medicine). Not one is a neurology subspecialty: no vascular neurology, no epilepsy, no clinical neurophysiology, no neuromuscular, no movement disorders, no neurocritical care, no neuroimmunology, no headache, no sleep-via-neurology-sponsorship. TWO ADJACENT SAUSHEC FELLOWSHIPS ARE REACHABLE FROM NEUROLOGY. Sleep Medicine: 'Program Length: 1 year', 'Total Approved Complement: 4', 'Approved per Year (if applicable): 4', 'Required Pre-Requisite Training: Medical school graduation, completion of residency eligible to pursue sleep medicine. All applicants must be active duty members of the U.S. Military.' - and 'The sleep disorders center at Wilford Hall Ambulatory Surgical Center is the largest in the Department of Defense with 16 beds capable of evaluating patients of all ages'. Pain Medicine is also sponsored at SAUSHEC, and the program page notes that 'Pain fellows' rotate through the neurology department. Both are military-only. WHAT THE PROGRAM SUBSTITUTES FOR FELLOWSHIP EXPOSURE - this is the program's own strategic argument and it is specific: 'We also provide robust neurophysiology training and practice which is unique amongst residency programs (and often reserved for fellowship training elsewhere in the country). Our graduates are able to perform electromyography and interpret electroencephalogram independently, and our residents routinely score above the national mean on an EMG test which is typically only administered to fellows.' Curricular backing: 3 EEG blocks and 3 EMG blocks across the three years, plus a required 'SAUSHEC Neurology Neurophysiology Course (PGY3)'. WIDER MILITARY CONTEXT (not SAUSHEC fellowships): the USU Department of Neurology lists 14 neurology subspecialty training areas available to military neurologists overall - Epilepsy, Neurophysiology, Sleep Medicine, Intraoperative monitoring, Headache, Interventional Neurology, Vascular Neurology, Neurocritical Care, Neuro-oncology, Pain Management, Neuro-ophthalmology, Neuro-immunology, Movement Disorders, Behavioral Neuroscience. Those are DoD-wide career options typically obtained through military-sponsored civilian fellowships (as Nelson, Elsbernd, Koehn and Hoffman each did - Penn State Hershey, Mayo Arizona, Barrow, Columbia respectively), NOT programs SAUSHEC sponsors.
conflict_notes: I deliberately did NOT import the USU 14-subspecialty list into this program's fellowship offerings - that list is DoD-wide career options, a classic contamination trap. The absence of in-house fellowships is a genuine double-edged finding: more procedures for residents, no internal subspecialty pipeline.

raw_finding: COMPENSATION IS MILITARY PAY, NOT A RESIDENT STIPEND - this is the single most important correction to the registry's salary fields. The official DHA GME Pay and Benefits page (last updated 30 June 2026) states: 'Residents and fellows who are uniformed officers in the Army, Navy, Air Force, or U.S. Public Health Service and are compensated at the level of O-3 or greater, depending on prior service', pointing to the DFAS pay tables at dfas.mil/militarymembers/payentitlements/Pay-Tables/. On top of basic pay: 'Basic Allowance for Housing is a stipend provided to every uniformed member' (San Antonio rate, non-taxable), plus Post-9/11 GI Bill education benefits transferable to immediate family, SGLI life insurance 'at low-cost up to a maximum of $500K', a military retirement plan, and after graduation eligibility for Incentive Pay and Board Certification Pay under Medical Special Pay. FREIDA's reported figures for 1804821127, which the registry mirrors: PGY-1 $0, PGY-2 $69,252, PGY-3 $75,000, PGY-4 $79,352 (FREIDA's Overview renders the range as '$0-$79K'). The $0 PGY-1 entry is NOT the usual FREIDA null-sentinel defect in this case - or at least not only that - because there is genuinely no PGY-1 year in this advanced program; either way, $0 must not be reported as a salary. The $69K-$79K figures are consistent with O-3 basic pay alone and therefore UNDERSTATE total compensation, because they exclude BAH (non-taxable, and substantial in Bexar County), BAS, and the federal tax advantage on allowances. I attempted to pull the exact 2026 O-3 basic pay line from militarypay.defense.gov; the table is served as a separate download and I did not capture the precise figures, so I am not quoting a number I did not verify. LEAVE: 'All military officers receive a total of 30 days of ordinary leave (vacation) annually. Residents and fellows may not be able to use all 30 days while in training because of more restrictive specialty training time requirements. Unused days accumulate for later use per military service policy.' FREIDA separately shows '15-20 Vacation Days' and 'negotiable sick days', which conflicts with the 30-day statutory figure - the difference is almost certainly usable-in-training days versus accrued days. Medical leave: 'While there no limit on the amount of illness or convalescent absences per year, those with frequent or lengthy absences may need to be extended in training.' Parental leave: 'Residents/fellows may receive up to 12 weeks of non-chargeable leave (for birth-parent this is additive to convalescent leave). This leave may be taken in one week increments up to a year after the birth or adoption of a child', plus non-chargeable maternity convalescent leave. HEALTH/DENTAL/LIABILITY/DISABILITY: TRICARE for member and immediate family (health, hospitalization, mental health); TRICARE dental at additional cost; 'All military medical corps officers are protected from personal liability for actions related to their official duties by federal statute. The relevant statute is the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), 28 U.S.C. 1346(b), 2671-2680'; all officers carry disability coverage through the services' disability evaluation system. The registry's FREIDA-derived benefit strings ('Major medical residents: Fully Paid by Institution', 'Dental: Available, Not Paid By Institution', 'Disability: Fully Paid by Institution', 'Major Medical Domestic Partners: Not Available') are consistent with TRICARE rules. Moonlighting: 'Program Allows Moonlighting (Beyond PGY-1): No'. SERVICE OBLIGATION - the true 'cost' term: per the DHA GME FAQ, 'For Military trainees, training in DHA GME programs incurs a service obligation that is served either concurrently or consecutively with other service obligations. Military trainees should contact their Service GME office for specifics. For civilian trainees funded by the VA, there is no service obligation.'
conflict_notes: Registry salary fields CONFIRMED as faithful copies of FREIDA but SEMANTIC_MISMATCH as descriptions of actual compensation. I did not report an exact 2026 O-3 basic pay figure because I could not open the DFAS/militarypay table itself in this run.

YEAR 3 (PGY-4): Clinic 3; Consults 2; EEG 1; EMG 1; Pediatric Neurology 2; Psychiatry 1; Traumatic Brain Injury/Rehabilitation 1; Elective 2. Totals across residency: 8 clinic, 11 consult, 3 EEG, 3 EMG, 3 pediatric neurology, 1 stroke, 1 neuroradiology, 1 neuropathology, 1 psychiatry, 1 TBI/rehab, 6 elective. (The three pediatric-neurology blocks are an ADULT program's rotation through child neurology and are legitimate adult-program curriculum data, not child-neurology-program content.) ELECTIVES named: 'EEG/Epilepsy Monitoring Unit at UTHSA', 'Neurocritical care at BAMC or UTHSA', 'Research elective', plus any other subspecialty-focused rotation. CONTINUITY CLINIC: 'Our residents receive an excellent mix of inpatient and outpatient clinical experience, including maintaining sole responsibility for their own outpatient continuity clinic.' DIDACTICS: 'resident-focused didactics Mon-Thurs from 8 - 9 a.m. On Thurs, we have additional clinic-wide didactics from 12 - 1 p.m.' - resident-led journal club, basic science, faculty lectures, textbook chapter reviews, QIPS, and military-unique/leadership topics. 'We also participate in Neurosciences Grand Rounds at UT Health San Antonio approximately twice monthly.' FREIDA records 6 structured didactic hours per week in the first year. CALL: home call in 24-hour periods, front-loaded - 'our PGY2 residents often take 6-7 call shifts in a 4-week block, while our PGY4 residents often take 1-3 call shifts per 4-week block. Our PGY4 (chief residents) additionally complete backup call responsibilities, during which they provide initial after-hours guidance to PGY2 and PGY3 residents.' FREIDA: no night float; moonlighting not allowed; average 60 hours/week on duty in the first year; maximum 36 consecutive hours; 1.50 twenty-four-hour off-duty periods per week; program start date July. REQUIRED COURSES: SAUSHEC Neurology Bootcamp (PGY2); SAUSHEC Neurology Neurophysiology Course (PGY3); Smirniotopoulos Washington Neuroradiology Review (PGY3); Dr. Kenneth M. Earle Memorial Neuropathology Review (PGY3). OPTIONAL COURSES: J. Kiffin Penry Epilepsy Mini-Fellowship; The Residents Course for Advancing Autonomic Medicine; National Residents Scholarship Program (Epilepsy); Vanderbilt University Focus on Common Movement Disorders; Vanderbilt University Neuromodulation Course; American Epilepsy Society Epilepsy Workshop; American Headache Society Resident Education Program. SIMULATION: Acute Stroke; Status Epilepticus - which 'occurs (without the residents' prior knowledge) in a deployed combat setting'; Brain Death Evaluation & Delivering Bad News. PROCEDURES: EMG performed and EEG interpreted independently by graduates; botulinum toxin injections and nerve blocks for headache; residents 'routinely score above the national mean on an EMG test which is typically only administered to fellows'; senior residents proctor lumbar puncture simulations. MILITARY-UNIQUE CURRICULUM: dedicated didactic time for 'supervising enlisted personnel, Air Force Medical Corps career pathways, the readiness implications of neurology care', plus coding and military clinic operations; a leadership curriculum with interpersonal communication, time management and leadership book clubs. RESEARCH: 'Research is emphasized... residents are expected to plan, organize, and conduct their own research projects', presented each May at the Neurology Education and Research Symposium ('Research Day') 'now jointly hosted by the BAMC Neurology Department and UTHSA Neurology Department'; SAUSHEC also runs an institutional Research Day competition each April. QIPS: IHI Open School certification on entry; quarterly departmental review of neurology patient-safety cases; a QIPS Faculty Champion; encouragement to complete Healthcare Safety Review certification. TEACHING: BAMC is a core clerkship site for the Uniformed Services University, so residents are the primary teachers for core neurology clerkship students; June-October brings audition rotators; transitional-year interns, psychiatry interns, internal medicine residents and pain fellows rotate through; residents deliver quarterly didactics to Internal Medicine. summary: ECFMG certification is required only of graduates of medical schools outside the US and Canada, and must be held before appointment. Graduates of LCME-accredited US schools, including those in Puerto Rico, are covered by a different eligibility criterion and do not need it.
raw_finding: HCA Healthcare GME 2026 Core Manual, 'Eligibility for Appointment - All candidates for Appointment must meet one of the following eligibility criteria', verbatim: 'A. Graduate of a medical school in the United States or Canada accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME) or, B. Graduate of a college of osteopathic medicine in the United States or Canada accredited by the American Osteopathic Association (AOA) or, C. Graduate from a medical school outside of the United States or Canada, and meeting one of the following additional qualifications: a. Holds a currently valid certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) prior to appointment, or b. Holds a full and unrestricted license to practice medicine in a United States licensing jurisdiction in his or her current ACGME specialty/subspecialty program.' The ECFMG requirement is therefore scoped strictly to criterion C - schools OUTSIDE the US and Canada. AMBIGUITY FLAGGED PER CONTRACT: criterion A reads 'a medical school in the United States or Canada accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME)' and does not enumerate US territories or name Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico is a United States jurisdiction and its LCME-accredited schools - Universidad Central del Caribe, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico, San Juan Bautista - are United States LCME-accredited medical schools, so a UCC graduate plainly satisfies criterion A and is NOT routed through criterion C or the ECFMG requirement. The ambiguity is low-severity (the policy says 'United States', not 'the fifty states'), but it is recorded because the policy never states the territorial question explicitly. The manual's glossary separately defines ECFMG as 'an organization that assesses' foreign medical graduates. Registry's 'IMG Step 2 Required: Yes' is consistent: IMGs need Step 1 and Step 2 CK passed prior to Appointment plus ECFMG certification.

value.determination: Three current published sources give three materially different answers about WHEN Step 2 CK is needed, and they cannot be reconciled from public text. (1) The program's own Application Information page ties only Step 1 to the application and makes Steps 1+2 a pre-start PREFERENCE: 'Step 1 is required with the initial ERAS application. Successful completion of Steps 1 and 2 is preferred prior to the start of residency training.' Read alone this is at most REQUIRES_STEP2_BEFORE_START, and arguably no barrier at all because the word is 'preferred'. (2) The SAME page's 'Application Requirements' list names 'USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 Scores' among the documentation that must accompany the ERAS application, which reads as REQUIRES_STEP2_WITH_APPLICATION against a stated deadline of October 23rd. (3) FREIDA's 2026 survey record - the newest of the three, received 2026-06-15 and published 2026-08-20, i.e. AFTER the registry release of 2026-07-09 - renders 'Must Have Passed USMLE Step 2 CK: Yes' for U.S. MD, IMG and DO applicants underneath the section heading 'Medical Exam Licensing Requirements for Interview Consideration', which reads as REQUIRES_STEP2_BEFORE_INTERVIEW. Separating the four questions the contract asks: required with ERAS submission - YES on reading (2), NO on reading (1); required before initial review - not addressed by any source; required before interview invitation - YES per FREIDA, not stated by the program; required before ranking - not addressed; required before start date only - YES per reading (1). The REQUIREMENT that Step 2 CK be passed is not in doubt in any source; only the TIMING is. This determination was NOT inferred from the program's 220 minimum-score rule, which is silent on timing. Comparing cycles: the registry's prior-cycle values ('US MD Step 2 Required: Yes', 'IMG Step 2 Required: Yes') already encoded the requirement, and the 2026 survey's field_usmle_us_md_pass_ck / field_usmle_img_pass_ck / field_usmle_do_pass_ck are all still true - so there is NO policy CHANGE between cycles here, only a framing that the registry did not capture (FREIDA files these answers under an interview-consideration heading). Separately, FREIDA's distinct fields field_usmle_step2_req_int and field_usmle_step_2_required are both FALSE in the 2026 payload, which cuts against the interview-consideration reading and is itself part of the conflict.

value.barrier_reasoning: A published barrier condition exists, but on Alejandra's actual calendar it is narrow rather than disqualifying, and the risk is concentrated in the deadline rather than the interview. Her Step 2 CK was sat late September 2026 with a result expected mid-October 2026. The program publishes 'Submit completed application by October 23rd' and 'Interviews are conducted from November to the end of January.' Under FREIDA's interview-consideration reading, a mid-October result lands roughly two to six weeks before interviews begin, so that reading would NOT bar her. Under the reading that Step 2 scores are required documentation at submission, a mid-October result leaves only days of margin against the October 23rd deadline, and any slip in score release would put her outside it. Under the program-page preference reading there is no barrier at all. Because at least one current published source conditions consideration on a passed Step 2 CK and the program's deadline is unusually early, this is scored as a published barrier that she should resolve by writing to the coordinator before submitting, not as an absence of a barrier. The additional and more consequential screen is the first-attempt rule: 'Applicants must pass USMLE Steps 1 and 2 on the first attempt with a score of 220 or higher' - a pending Step 2 must clear on the first sitting.

Nine named residents, matching FREIDA's 'Program Size 9 Current Residents'. ROSTER YEAR ESTABLISHED BY WAYBACK DIFFERENTIAL - this matters because the live page is one academic year stale. The 2026-02-17 Wayback snapshot of the same URL contains the IDENTICAL nine names in the identical PGY slots. The 2025-03-18 snapshot reads: PGY-4 Haroutiun Hamzoian, MD; Michel Abdelmasih, MD / PGY-3 Zisan Akcaag, MD; Brandon Donley, MD / PGY-2 Christine Ochoa; Bryan Velasco / PGY-1 Raneem Maqsood, MD; Ana Paraiso, MD (eight residents). The 2024-07-25 snapshot reads: PGY-4 Mekdes Ditamo, MD (Chief); Mina Gerges, MD (Chief) / PGY-3 Haroutiun Hamzoian, MD; Michel Abdelmasih, MD / PGY-2 Zisan Akcaag, MD; Brandon Donley, MD / PGY-1 Christine Ochoa; Bryan Velasco (eight residents). Akcaag and Donley are PGY-3 in the 2025-03-18 snapshot and PGY-4 in both the 2026-02-17 snapshot and the live page, which fixes the live roster as the AY2025-26 cohort. Akcaag and Donley would therefore have completed training in June 2026, and the AY2026-27 PGY-1 class is not listed. The live roster is consequently a carryover and does NOT name the program's current PGY-1s. COMPLEMENT VS CENSUS: NRMP quota has been exactly 2 categorical PGY-1 positions in each of 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 (8 positions across four years), yet the AY2025-26 roster shows nine residents with three in the PGY-2 class (Maqsood, Paraiso, Cannaday) - i.e. exactly one resident above the matched 2-per-year pattern, consistent with one off-cycle or transfer appointment. FREIDA's field_total_positions is 9 and FREIDA labels it 'Program Size 9 Current Residents', so FREIDA's own total is a census-style figure rather than a clean approved complement. FREIDA 2026 also reports resident gender at 66.7% female / 33.3% male (field_pct_female 66.7, field_pct_male 33.3), superseding the registry's 50/50.

named_faculty: Vikram Shivkumar, MD - division director of Movement Disorders; fellowship-trained in movement disorders (University of Toledo Medical Center); FAAN; member of the Movement Disorder Society
value.dedicated_clinic: Yes - 'the Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute Movement Disorder clinic', a named multidisciplinary clinic within the Neuroscience Institute with its own page, treating Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, dystonia, ataxia and chorea, plus atypical parkinsonian disorders (dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy) and motor/vocal tics
value.resident_elective: NOT a named elective. The program's published 'Current Available Electives' list is Headache, Multiple Sclerosis, Epilepsy, Stroke Clinic, Neuro Oncology, Neuro Ophthalmology, Neuro Rehabilitation, Pain Medicine - Movement Disorders is absent. Exposure would come from the narrative claim of rotations in 'all the major specialty areas' and from outpatient specialty-clinic blocks (PGY-2 three blocks, PGY-3 two blocks, PGY-4 one block), none of which is published as a movement-disorders assignment.
value.research: Documented and specific: 'Dr. Shivkumar also has served as the principal investigator for multiple clinical trials pertaining to treatment of Parkinson's disease and essential tremor, contributed to three book chapters, and published numerous peer-reviewed articles in medical journals. Additionally, he is a professional reviewer for eight medical journals and a frequent speaker at Parkinson's disease support groups.' Procedural capability includes 'deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's and botulinum toxin injections for dystonia, blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm and spasticity'; Deep Brain Stimulation is also listed among the Neuroscience Institute's specialties.
value.formal_designation: NONE. No Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence, no CurePSP Center of Care and no HDSA Center of Excellence is claimed by Orlando Health anywhere, and none was found on the awarding bodies' side either. See raw_finding for the two designation traps that were checked and refused.
value.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The institutional capability is real and named: a Movement Disorder clinic with a fellowship-trained division director, DBS and botulinum toxin programmes, and PI-level Parkinson's and essential-tremor trials. The resident exposure is materially weaker than that capability and is the honest limiting factor. Movement Disorders does not appear on the program's published elective list, no movement-disorders block appears in any PGY year of the published block schedule, and no movement-disorders continuity clinic is described. The only resident-facing claim is narrative: the welcome page says years two through four include rotations 'in all the major specialty areas of neurology such as Movement Disorders, Epilepsy, Neuro-Oncology, Neuro-rehab, Neuroimmunology, Headache Disorders and Neuro muscular disorders', and journal clubs are 'mentored by Neurology Faculty subspecialized in specific areas'. So a resident would encounter movement disorders through general outpatient specialty clinics and faculty mentorship rather than through a scheduled, named rotation. For an applicant whose stated interest is movement disorders, this is a question to put to the program directly, not something the published curriculum settles.
value.summary: Orlando Health has a named Movement Disorder clinic led by a fellowship-trained division director, Vikram Shivkumar, MD, with DBS, botulinum toxin and Parkinson's/essential-tremor clinical trials. But Movement Disorders is not on the program's published elective list and no movement-disorders block appears in the published schedule, so documented resident exposure lags the institutional capability.

But Movement Disorders is not on the program's published elective list and no movement-disorders block appears in the published schedule, so documented resident exposure lags the institutional capability.
raw_finding: DEDICATED CLINIC, VERBATIM from the Neuroscience Institute's Movement Disorders page: 'At the Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute Movement Disorder clinic, our multidisciplinary team uses the latest technologies, therapies, diagnostic tools and medications to treat a wide range of movement disorders, including Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, dystonia, ataxia and chorea.' and 'Our highly trained neurologists, neurosurgeons, nurses, neuropsychologists and rehabilitation specialists will work with you to develop a compassionate treatment plan designed around your unique needs.' The page's Conditions We Treat sections cover Ataxia, Parkinson's disease, Atypical Parkinsonism disorders (naming dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy), Chorea, Dystonia, Essential tremor, and Motor and vocal tics. NAMED FACULTY, VERBATIM from Vikram Shivkumar's official Orlando Health profile: 'Dr. Vikram Shivkumar is a neurologist with the Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute Neurology Group. He specializes in caring for patients with movement disorders such as: Parkinson's disease / Lewy body dementia / Essential tremor / Dystonia / Huntington's disease / Tourette syndrome. He also serves as the institute's division director of Movement Disorders. Some of Dr. Shivkumar's specialties include deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's and botulinum toxin injections for dystonia, blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm and spasticity.' Training, verbatim: 'He earned his medical degree from MGM Medical College and Maharashtra University of Health Sciences in India. He completed his postdoctoral training at the University of Toledo Medical Center in Ohio with a residency in neurology and a fellowship in movement disorders.' He is the only faculty member with a documented movement-disorders fellowship. RESIDENT EXPOSURE, MEASURED AGAINST THE PUBLISHED CURRICULUM: the program's Curriculum, Rotations, Electives page publishes 'Current Available Electives' as exactly - Headache; Multiple Sclerosis; Epilepsy; Stroke Clinic; Neuro Oncology; Neuro Ophthalmology; Neuro Rehabilitation; Pain Medicine. Movement Disorders is NOT among them. The published block schedule contains no movement-disorders block in any year. The residency welcome page nevertheless claims, verbatim, that years two through four include 'rotations in vascular neurology, inpatient neurology consultations, pediatric neurology, psychiatry, and in all the major specialty areas of neurology such as Movement Disorders, Epilepsy, Neuro-Oncology, Neuro-rehab, Neuroimmunology, Headache Disorders and Neuro muscular disorders.' That narrative claim and the published elective list are in tension, and the elective list is the more specific and more recently operational document. DESIGNATION TRAP 1 - PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION CENTER OF EXCELLENCE, CHECKED AND NOT CLAIMED: Orlando Health makes no Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence claim on any page opened. Verified from the awarding side that Florida's Parkinson's Foundation Centers of Excellence are the University of Florida (Norman Fixel Institute), the University of Miami and the University of South Florida. Orlando Health is not among them. Had such a claim appeared here it would have been a red flag; it did not, and none is asserted in this dossier. DESIGNATION TRAP 2 - HDSA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE, CHECKED AND REFUSED: the Huntington's Disease Society of America does have an Orlando-area presence, but it belongs to OTHER institutions. HDSA lists Florida Centers of Excellence at the University of Florida and the University of South Florida, plus an 'HDSA Center of Excellence Partner Site at Central Florida Center for Huntington Disease' located at AdventHealth Medical Group Neurology at Innovation Tower in Orlando and UCF. Those are the two sibling programs explicitly excluded from this ticket (AdventHealth Florida, ACGME 1801100008, and University of Central Florida / HCA Florida Healthcare, ACGME 1801100155). This trap is unusually easy to fall into because Shivkumar's own condition list names Huntington's disease. Orlando Health has NO HDSA designation and none is attributed to it here. CUREPSP: no CurePSP Center of Care claim was found on any Orlando Health page, and none is asserted. The Neuroscience Institute's published Awards list contains only: ALS Association Certified Treatment Center of Excellence; U.S. News Best Hospital and High Performing Hospital 2025-26 for ORMC; High Performing in National Back Surgery (Spinal Fusion) 2025-26; AACN Beacon Award for Excellence, Silver level, for the Neuro Step Down Unit; and Joint Commission Spine Center of Excellence. No movement-disorders designation appears in that list. FELLOWSHIP: no movement disorders fellowship exists - see domain 18. No fellowship was inferred from Shivkumar's specialty, per the contract's explicit prohibition.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - no movement disorders fellowship, no movement-disorders elective and no Parkinson's Foundation, HDSA or CurePSP designation could be established for Orlando Health; the Orlando-area HDSA Partner Site belongs to AdventHealth and UCF, not to this program.
conflict_notes: The welcome page claims rotations in Movement Disorders among 'all the major specialty areas of neurology', while the curriculum page's 'Current Available Electives' list omits Movement Disorders and no movement-disorders block appears in the published schedule.

value.dedicated_clinic: Yes - the 'Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center', a named centre with its own Neuroscience Institute page and a multidisciplinary team of 'neurologists, occupational therapists, physical therapists and psychologists', offering infusion, oral and injectable disease-modifying therapy, MS rehabilitation, speech therapy, and education and support groups. The residency's own welcome page describes it as one of ORMC's 'recognized outpatient practices of a Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center and ALS Center'.
value.resident_elective: YES - 'Multiple Sclerosis' is published by name in the program's 'Current Available Electives' list. Elective time is scheduled in PGY-2 (2 blocks), PGY-3 (3 blocks) and PGY-4 (2 blocks), and the welcome page adds that 'All residents will have a one-month elective rotation each year'.
value.research: Program-director-level MS trial leadership: 'Dr. Gutierrez has been the principal investigator for many research trials related to MS.' The Neuroscience Institute runs clinical trials and lists Multiple Sclerosis among its specialties; no MS-specific trial registry page was opened.
value.formal_designation: Claimed by Orlando Health and quoted verbatim from the page opened: 'The center has earned the prestigious designation as a "Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care" through the National MS Society, and we are also a member of the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers. Our therapy team members are designated Multiple Sclerosis Certified Specialists.' Cross-checked against the awarding body: the National MS Society's own 'Network of MS Healthcare Professionals' page confirms both tier names exist and describes them - 'Partners in MS Care are healthcare providers ... who have demonstrated knowledge and expertise treating people with MS' and 'Centers for Comprehensive MS Care deliver coordinated, multi-disciplinary services designed to meet the complex needs of people with MS.' The NMSS does NOT publish a public searchable roster of designees (it routes enquiries to an MS Navigator and to PartnersInMSCare@nmss.org), so the site-specific listing could not be independently confirmed. Separately, the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers member directory contains a record titled 'Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Care Center', but that directory loads its member data dynamically and the record's fields could not be read, so CMSC membership is corroborated only by the presence of the record.
value.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: This is the domain where capability and resident exposure actually line up, and it is the inverse of the movement-disorders picture at the same program - which is exactly why the two were tested separately. Institutional capability: a named Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center with a multidisciplinary team, MS-certified therapists, CMSC membership and a claimed NMSS Partner in MS Care / Centers for Comprehensive Care designation. Resident exposure: Multiple Sclerosis is one of only eight named electives the program publishes, and elective time is scheduled in each of PGY-2, PGY-3 and PGY-4. Mentorship: the centre's director IS the residency program director, so an MS-interested resident's elective supervisor and her program director are the same person - an unusually direct mentorship line, and the single strongest structural feature of this program for an MS-interested applicant. What is NOT established: no in-house MS or neuroimmunology fellowship exists, no MS continuity-clinic requirement is published, and no graduate has yet gone to an MS or neuroimmunology fellowship (documented placements are vascular, epilepsy and pain).
value.summary: MS is the strongest subspecialty alignment at this program: a named Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center directed by the residency's own program director, a Multiple Sclerosis elective published by name, and a claimed National MS Society 'Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care' designation quoted verbatim. There is no in-house MS fellowship.

summary: MS is the strongest subspecialty alignment at this program: a named Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center directed by the residency's own program director, a Multiple Sclerosis elective published by name, and a claimed National MS Society 'Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care' designation quoted verbatim. There is no in-house MS fellowship.
raw_finding: DESIGNATION, QUOTED VERBATIM FROM THE PAGE OPENED (Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute, Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center): 'At the Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center, our team of specialists will be at your side to help you live a full, active life. We provide patients and caregivers with access to leading-edge medications, treatments and specialty rehabilitation services. Our individualized and coordinated care draws on the expertise of multiple disciplines - including neurologists, occupational therapists, physical therapists and psychologists. The center has earned the prestigious designation as a "Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care" through the National MS Society, and we are also a member of the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers. Our therapy team members are designated Multiple Sclerosis Certified Specialists.' AWARDING-BODY CHECK, AS THE CONTRACT REQUIRES: the National Multiple Sclerosis Society's own page for its Network of MS Healthcare Professionals confirms the program and both tier names, verbatim: 'Partners in MS Care are healthcare providers - neurologists, physical therapists, mental health providers, urologists, neuro-ophthalmologists and other healthcare professionals - who have demonstrated knowledge and expertise treating people with MS' and, under its own heading, 'Centers for Comprehensive MS Care deliver coordinated, multi-disciplinary services designed to meet the complex needs of people with MS.' So the designation Orlando Health quotes maps onto real NMSS tiers under NMSS's own naming - this is NOT a fabricated or migrated credential. What could NOT be done is confirm Orlando Health's name on an NMSS roster, because the NMSS publishes no public searchable list of designees; its page directs enquiries to an MS Navigator and to PartnersInMSCare@nmss.org. The designation is therefore reported as the program's own verbatim claim, corroborated as to the credential's existence and exact naming at the awarding body, but not independently confirmed as to this site. Orlando Health's slight rewording ('Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care' vs NMSS's 'Partners in MS Care' and 'Centers for Comprehensive MS Care') is noted and not smoothed over. CMSC: a Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers member record exists under the title 'Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Care Center'. The CMSC member directory renders its 1,097 member records via client-side loading and the record's own fields could not be read, so this corroborates the membership claim only weakly. PROGRAM-DIRECTOR LINKAGE - THE KEY STRUCTURAL FACT: the residency's welcome page bylines its director verbatim as 'Amparo (Amy) Gutierrez, MD FAAN / Neurology Residency Director / Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Clinic Director'. Her official physician profile adds, verbatim: 'Dr. Gutierrez has been the principal investigator for many research trials related to MS. She has more than 20 years of clinical experience with MS and has held leadership roles with the National Multiple Sclerosis Society.' Those NMSS leadership roles are hers personally and are deliberately NOT converted into any designation of the site. RESIDENT EXPOSURE: the curriculum page lists 'Multiple Sclerosis' by name under 'Current Available Electives'. Elective blocks are scheduled PGY-2 two blocks, PGY-3 three blocks, PGY-4 two blocks. The welcome page also claims rotations in 'Neuroimmunology' among the major specialty areas. SITE CONTEXT: the residency welcome page states, verbatim, that ORMC has 'recognized outpatient practices of a Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center and ALS Center'. The Neuroscience Institute lists Multiple Sclerosis among its specialties and separately claims, verbatim, 'Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute has been recognized as ALS Association Certified Treatment Center of Excellence' - that ALS claim is Orlando Health's own and was not checked against the ALS Association. OTHER NEUROIMMUNOLOGY-ADJACENT FACULTY: Bahareh Hassanzadeh, MD, neuro-ophthalmology, whose published condition list includes 'demyelinating disorders', 'Multiple sclerosis' and 'Neuromyelitis optica'; and Naoir Zaher, MD, whose epilepsy work-up list includes 'Neuroimmunology evaluations and treatments'. Neither is described as an MS specialist and neither is presented as one here. NO MS OR NEUROIMMUNOLOGY FELLOWSHIP was found - see domain 18. DOMAINS 16 AND 17 WERE TESTED INDEPENDENTLY and came out asymmetric at this one program: MS has a named elective plus program-director-level mentorship (STRONG), while movement disorders has a named clinic and division director but no published elective (MODERATE).
conflict_notes: Orlando Health writes the designation as 'Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care'; the National MS Society's own naming is 'Partners in MS Care' (provider tier) and 'Centers for Comprehensive MS Care' (centre tier). The NMSS publishes no public designee roster, so the site-specific listing is unconfirmed.

raw_finding: Orlando Health's GME Fellowship Programs page states verbatim: 'Please click below for more information about specific medical education fellowship programs (*indicates ACGME accredited programs)' and then lists 33 entries. 'Neurology' is one of them. Two structural facts about that entry were established directly in the DOM: it is NOT a hyperlink (a query for a link whose text is exactly 'Neurology' inside the page's main element returned nothing, while every ACGME-marked entry is linked), and it carries no asterisk. The other non-linked entries are Bariatric Surgery, Emergency Medicine Clinical Informatics, Emergency Medical Research, Emergency Medicine Ultrasound, Emergency Medicine Simulation, Minimally Invasive Surgery - Colon and Rectal, Pediatric Craniofacial and Maxillofacial Surgery and Pediatric GI Nutrition. A direct fetch of the plausible URL /medical-professionals/graduate-medical-education/fellowship-programs/neurology returned a 404. THIS IS PRECISELY THE PATTERN THE CONTRACT WARNS ABOUT - a fellowship that is listed but may be aspirational, in development, non-ACGME, or an administrative placeholder. It is therefore NOT reported as an existing in-house neurology fellowship, and no fellows-in-post figure is asserted. NO FELLOWSHIP WAS INFERRED FROM ANY FACULTY MEMBER'S SPECIALTY, per the contract's explicit prohibition. Orlando Health has a fellowship-trained movement disorders division director (Shivkumar), a fellowship-trained epileptologist pair (Zaher, Dhingra, plus Nemade), a fellowship-trained neuromuscular division director (Tohidi), a fellowship-trained neuro-ophthalmologist (Hassanzadeh), a UCNS-certified neuro-oncologist (Santos), three vascular neurologists (Rosado, Velez, Chaudhary) and a headache/facial-pain fellowship graduate (Nohra Revilla) - and NONE of that is evidence of a fellowship at Orlando Health. The GME office states verbatim: 'We are the institutional sponsor of 8 residency and 29 fellowship programs.' The published fellowship list is dominated by emergency medicine, surgery, cardiology, pediatrics and critical care; no neurology subspecialty fellowship (vascular neurology, epilepsy, clinical neurophysiology, movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology, neuromuscular, headache, neuro-oncology) has a page. FREIDA 2026 reports field_match_nrmp_adv_fellow = false and field_participates_sf_match = false. AFFILIATED vs IN-HOUSE, KEPT STRICTLY SEPARATE: the three fellowships named above (Epilepsy at the University of Florida; Vascular in Toledo, OH; Pain in Wisconsin) are graduate DESTINATIONS drawn from the program's own alumni table. They are not Orlando Health fellowships, and residents have no institutional access to them by virtue of training here. They are recorded under 'affiliated' only because the contract requires relevant non-in-house fellowships be separated out, and each carries an explicit note saying so. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR ALEJANDRA: because there is no in-house MS/neuroimmunology or movement disorders fellowship, neither of her two stated subspecialty interests has an internal continuation pathway at this institution; both would require an external fellowship application.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - Orlando Health publishes no verifiable in-house neurology subspecialty fellowship. A plain-text 'Neurology' entry appears in its GME fellowship list without the page's own ACGME marker and without a page, and it could not be established as an operating program.

Recovered from the Internet Archive, snapshot 2026-02-14, the table reads verbatim with columns 'Last Name / First Name / Graduation Year / Fellowship / Fellowship Location / Full-Time Practice / City / State': 'Kahila / Roua / 2023 / Practice / Straight to Practice / Orlando Health / Orlando / FL'; 'Gerges / Mina / 2024 / Practice / Straight to Practice / Orlando Health / Orlando / FL'; 'Ditamo / Mekdes / 2024 / Vascular / Toledo, OH'; 'Abdelmasih / Michel / 2025 / Epilepsy / University of FL / / / FL'; 'Hamzoian / Haroutiun / 2025 / Pain / Wisconsin'. An earlier snapshot (2025-01-23) of the same page carried only the first three rows, so the Abdelmasih and Hamzoian rows were added during 2025 - the table was being maintained until the page was taken down, which is what makes the 2026-02-14 version the best available record. CROSS-CONFIRMATION OF THE TWO RETENTIONS, from sources independent of the alumni table: Roua Kahila and Mina Gerges both appear on the residency's current Leadership and Faculty page, and both appear on archived CURRENT-RESIDENT rosters of this same program (Gerges as a PGY-4 Chief in the 2024-07-25 snapshot alongside Ditamo). Their Orlando Health physician profiles independently record 'Residency: Orlando Health'. So two of five documented graduates were retained as faculty at the sponsoring institution - a concrete, verifiable retention signal for a program whose first NRMP match was 2022. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW FOR ALEJANDRA: 3 of 5 documented graduates entered subspecialty fellowship, which is a real signal that this small, young program places people into fellowship. But the three fellowships are vascular neurology, epilepsy and pain - NOT movement disorders and NOT MS or neuroimmunology, her two stated interests. There is no published instance of a graduate of this program entering a movement disorders or MS fellowship. That absence is stated plainly rather than smoothed over. CHRONOLOGY NOTE: graduation years 2023 and 2024 precede what a 2022-first-match cohort would produce in a four-year program, which is consistent with the early classes including residents who entered with prior GME or by transfer - Kahila's profile documents a prior neurology residency at Lehigh Valley Hospital, and Gerges completed an internal medicine residency at Orlando Health first. FREIDA 2026 reports field_requires_previous_gme = 'No', so prior GME is not a requirement now. NOT ESTABLISHED: no outcomes are published for the 2026 graduating class; no board-certification outcomes are attached to any graduate (see domain 20); no practice-setting detail beyond 'Orlando Health' is given for the two retained graduates.

summary: No ABPN board pass rate is published for this program by the program, by Orlando Health, or by FREIDA. The program's newest FREIDA survey in fact reports that it does NOT use graduates' board certification pass rates as a program-evaluation measure, which contradicts the registry.
raw_finding: Searched the program pages (welcome, about us, program information, curriculum, benefits, application information, people, residents, alumni including archived versions), the Orlando Health GME pages, FREIDA's full 2026 survey payload (210 fields) and the web generally for an ABPN pass rate attached to this program. None exists. The program is also very young - first NRMP match 2022, first documented graduates 2023 - so few cohorts have sat the examination. A DIRECTLY RELEVANT FREIDA FINDING THAT CONTRADICTS THE REGISTRY: FREIDA 2026 renders, under Program Evaluations, verbatim: 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements Yes / Graduates board certification pass rates No / Performance-based assessment scores (e.g. OSCE, patient or computer simulations) Yes'. The underlying field_program_evaluation_2019 array contains only 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements', 'Graduates' board certification pass rates' and 'Performance-based assessment scores' as the question's option set with the middle one unselected in the rendered output. The registry stored 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes' from the prior cycle; the current FREIDA record renders 'No'. Either way, FREIDA reports a program-evaluation METHODOLOGY, not a pass rate. TWO FALSE POSITIVES WERE REJECTED. First, a search result reporting a '100 percent first attempt pass rate on the Neurologic Clinical Specialist (NCS) board specialty examination' belongs to a DOCTOR OF PHYSICAL THERAPY neurologic residency at the University of Central Florida - a different profession, a different board and a different institution. Second, a national figure (roughly 84% first-time pass on the 2024 ABPN neurology certification examination, 151 of 972 first-time takers missing the mark) is a national benchmark and says nothing about this program; it is not attributed here.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - the program does not publish an ABPN board certification pass rate, and neither Orlando Health nor FREIDA publishes one for it.

summary: The curriculum is stroke-heavy: ten of the roughly thirty-nine neurology blocks across PGY-1 to PGY-4 are stroke or stroke-service inpatient, alongside general inpatient consults, three child-neurology blocks and a longitudinal outpatient clinic. Seven elective blocks across PGY-2 to PGY-4 draw on eight named electives that include Multiple Sclerosis but not Movement Disorders.
raw_finding: The Curriculum, Rotations, Electives page publishes the block schedule verbatim as recorded in the value object. Counting neurology-side blocks: stroke or stroke-service inpatient appears 2 (PGY-1) + 3 (PGY-2) + 2 (PGY-3) + 3 (PGY-4) = 10 blocks; general neurology inpatient consults 1 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 8; child neurology 1 (PGY-2 outpatient) + 1 (PGY-3 inpatient) + 1 (PGY-3 outpatient) + 1 (PGY-4) = 4; elective 0 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 7; psychiatry 1 (PGY-4). CHILD NEUROLOGY BLOCKS ARE LEGITIMATE ADULT CURRICULUM DATA under contract law 2 - they are rotations described on an ADULT program's own curriculum page, and no Child Neurology program's material was used anywhere in this dossier. Electives, verbatim: 'Current Available Electives - Headache / Multiple Sclerosis / Epilepsy / Stroke Clinic / Neuro Oncology / Neuro Ophthalmology / Neuro Rehabilitation / Pain Medicine.' Didactics, verbatim in part: 'There are a variety of conferences providing essential basic science and clinical instruction. The didactic curriculum is very flexible, and topics are adjusted frequently in response to the needs and interest of the residents. Bioethics, finances of medicine, and other contemporary subjects are integrated into the curriculum'; 'Residents attend monthly journal clubs which will be mentored by Neurology Faculty subspecialized in specific areas'; 'Residents are required to read the AAN Continuum publications which review in depth different disease states from bench to bedside. Residents are assigned grand rounds presentation dates'; 'Residents have specific lectures in this area and review these principles during their rotation in Pain Management Clinic and in the ALS Clinic'; 'Residents participate in lectures on this subject and will do at least one-month rotation in psychiatry.' Welcome page, verbatim: 'We offer a four -year ACGME general neurology residency program'; 'The residency structure consists of a first year spent engaged in learning internal medicine for nine months with an additional four months in neurology'; 'All residents will have a one-month elective rotation each year to ensure residents have the time to develop increased expertise in specific areas within neurology. Residents will participate in a longitudinal neurology outpatient clinic throughout their training. Residents will be encouraged to be involved in research which can be clinical, basic, or in social determinants of health care. Residents will meet all the required rotations to fulfill the American Academy Board of Neurology board requirements.' (The last phrase is a page error - the certifying board is the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology.) Program-information page, verbatim: 'If matched into our program, residents will complete the first year of internal medicine at the Orlando Health Orlando Regional Medical Center (OHORMC) Internal Medicine Residency Program, followed by three years of general neurology ... We accept two residents per year.' INTERNAL CONFLICT ON ELECTIVE VOLUME: the welcome page says every resident gets a one-month elective 'each year' (which would be four), while the block schedule gives PGY-1 none and PGY-2/3/4 two, three and two respectively. The block schedule is the more specific document. COMPREHENSIVE STROKE CENTER - VERIFIED AGAINST THE AWARDING BODY VIA A GOVERNMENT REGISTRY. Orlando Health's own wording varies across three pages and is loose in one place: the residency welcome page says 'OHORMC has an accredited Tertiary Comprehensive Stroke Center'; the Neuroscience Institute stroke page says 'Our Comprehensive Stroke Center is located at Orlando Health Orlando Regional Medical Center ... The nationally recognized center is designated to treat the most critical and complex strokes'; the ORMC facility page says 'Comprehensive Stroke Center is guided by AHA/ASA and The Joint Commission'. None of those three plainly names a certifying body for the CSC itself, and 'Tertiary Comprehensive Stroke Center' is not standard United States certification terminology - so the claim was checked independently. The Florida Agency for Health Care Administration's HOSPITAL STROKE PROGRAMS REPORT (Comprehensive Stroke Center: 53, report timestamped 4/8/2026 9:35 AM) lists, in Orange County: 'LIC NBR 4393 / FILE NBR 100006 / PROVIDER NAME ORLANDO HEALTH ORLANDO REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER / 52 W UNDERWOOD ST / ORLANDO / 32806 / (321) 841-5111 / QUALIFYING ORGANIZATION: JC / PROGRAM TYPE: Comprehensive Stroke Center / PROGRAM EFFECTIVE DATE: 10/16/2013'. 'JC' is The Joint Commission. The designation is therefore CONFIRMED with a named awarding body and an effective date. IDENTITY SEPARATION IN THE SAME GOVERNMENT TABLE: the row immediately above is 'LIC NBR 4369 / FILE NBR 100007 / ADVENTHEALTH ORLANDO / 601 E ROLLINS ST / ORLANDO / 32803 / (407) 303-5600 / DNVGL / Comprehensive Stroke Center / 4/19/2010'. That is a DIFFERENT Orlando hospital with a DIFFERENT certifying body and belongs to sibling program 1801100008, not to this one. A third row, 'HCA FLORIDA / 700 W OAK ST / KISSIMMEE / DNVGL / 9/10/2020', corresponds to the Kissimmee area of sibling program 1801100155. None of those was attributed here. Also distinct: 'ORLANDO HEALTH / 701 6TH ST S / SAINT [PETERSBURG] / DNVGL / 5/30/2013' is Orlando Health Bayfront in St. Petersburg - the same system, a different city, and not this program's site. AHA/ASA STROKE AWARDS, verbatim from the ORMC facility page: 'The American Heart Association and American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) have recognized ORMC with two distinct honors: Get with the Guidelines - Stroke GOLD PLUS / Target: Stroke Honor Roll Elite Plus.' NAEC LEVEL 4 EPILEPSY CENTER - VERIFIED AT THE AWARDING BODY'S OWN SITE. The National Association of Epilepsy Centers' own center page for the 'Orlando Health Epilepsy Program' reads: 'Level 4 / Adult Epilepsy Center / Medical Director: Naoir Zaher, MD / Co-Medical Director: Neelu Dhingra, MD' with phone 321-843-8621. Both named directors are on this
