summary: ECFMG certification is required before appointment, but only for graduates of medical schools outside the United States and Canada. As an LCME-accredited U.S. MD school graduate, Alejandra would not use this pathway.
raw_finding: UFCOM-J GME 'Trainee Eligibility and Selection Policy' (current) sets out three alternative Medical School Criteria verbatim: 'Graduation from a medical school in the United States or Canada, accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME); or Graduation from a college of osteopathic medicine in the United States, accredited by the American Osteopathic Association Commission on Osteopathic College Accreditation (AOACOCA); or Graduation from a medical school outside the United States or Canada who holds a valid certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) prior to appointment.' Universidad Central del Caribe is an LCME-accredited medical school located in Puerto Rico, a United States jurisdiction, so its graduates satisfy the FIRST bullet and the ECFMG bullet does not apply to them. FLAGGED AMBIGUITY, exactly the pattern the contract asks to be surfaced: the policy's wording is 'a medical school in the United States or Canada, accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME)' and it does NOT name Puerto Rico anywhere in the document. The correct reading plainly includes Puerto Rico's LCME-accredited schools, but the text leaves that to the reader rather than stating it, which is the kind of phrasing that can produce a mis-screen at the coordinator level. This is a real finding, recorded here and in alejandra_signals.eligibility_concerns rather than smoothed over. FREIDA separately records visa sponsorship as 'J-1 through ECFMG', which is the sponsorship mechanism for the third bullet, not an additional requirement for U.S. graduates.

summary: Applications go through ERAS only, with an unusually late December 31 deadline, 3-4 letters (at least one from neurology), and no supplemental materials. Adult neurology offers 8 program signals this cycle, but this program does not publish how it uses them.
raw_finding: DEADLINE: the program's own How to Apply page states verbatim 'The deadline for submitting your completed application is Dec. 31.' This SUPERSEDES the registry's 'Application Deadline: 2025-09-15', which was a prior-cycle value; the 2026 FREIDA survey now sets field_univ_spec_app_date_use=true with field_latest_date_current_year=null and field_application_period=null, i.e. the program defers to specialty universal dates in FREIDA while publishing Dec. 31 on its own site. A December 31 deadline is materially later than most programs and is the single most useful application-logistics fact here. DOCUMENTS: 'Our residency program only accepts applications through the AAMC's Electronic Residency Application Service (ERAS)... We do not require any materials beyond the ERAS requirements.' Required: ERAS common application form; personal statement; three current letters of recommendation ('One from a neurology physician at your medical school or a neurology physician who has been involved in your education. Two from physicians who are familiar with your work or abilities.'); Dean's letter; official transcript; USMLE or COMLEX score report; CV. FREIDA: min 3 / max 4 letters, 'Required Letter Writers: Letter(s) from someone within the specialty (e.g., faculty, attending)', 'Required Supplemental Information: No', field_chair_letter=false, field_pgm_dir_letter_req_ind=false, 'Program Offers: Does not offer open house or second look'. ADVANCED-PROGRAM APPLICATION MECHANIC, critical: 'If you are interested in applying for a PGY-1 in internal medicine and a PGY-2 in neurology, the following required documents must be provided to ERAS...' and 'We are an advanced program but do not require a separate interview for the preliminary PGY-1 internal medicine position. If you are interested in both programs, please make sure to check both programs under the tab 'Programs' of the ERAS application. Applicants who MATCH with our program are also guaranteed a PGY-1 position in internal medicine if they elect to conduct their preliminary year on our campus.' SIGNALING: the OPDA Guide for Residency Applicants - Adult Neurology 2026-2027 gives 'Number of signals: 8', 'Signal home institutions? No specialty guidance', and states verbatim 'Select Neurology programs may participate in program signaling (8 signals per adult neurology)' and 'Please note that there are no universal practices across programs in the use of program signals... or interview invitation release dates.' This program publishes nothing about whether or how it weighs signals - that specific sub-question is RESEARCHED_NOT_PUBLIC. INTERVIEW VOLUME comes from the 2026 survey's field_historical_interview_stats, which adds a 2025 row (56 interviews / 4 positions) absent from the registry; the registry's 'Interviews Conducted Last Year: 80' and 'Interviews Per First Year Position: 20.0:1' are one cycle stale. INTERVIEW FORMAT is a live contradiction preserved rather than resolved - see conflict_notes.
source_date: Program page current 2026 cycle; FREIDA survey 2026-06-16; OPDA guide 2026-06
conflict_notes: Interview format conflicts across three current sources. (1) The program's own How to Apply page describes an entirely virtual process: 'a virtual question and answer session with several of our neurology residents' the evening before, 'a virtual programmatic overview session that is conducted by the neurology chair and neurology program director from 12:30pm to 2pm EST', and three roughly 20-minute interviews in a 2pm-5pm EST window. (2) FREIDA's 2026 survey sets field_interview_type=1 with field_video_interview=false, which FREIDA/registry render as 'In Person'. (3) The OPDA Adult Neurology guide lists the specialty recommendation 'Interview format: Virtual'. Both program-level sources are current. The program's own narrative description is the more specific and is internally consistent (it names virtual sessions three times and gives EST time windows), but the FREIDA structured answer says the opposite and I am not resolving it. An applicant should confirm format directly with the coordinator.

raw_finding: SOURCE AND METHOD: the program's live Residents page no longer prints medical schools. An Internet Archive capture of the identical official URL, timestamped 2026-03-16, does print a 'Medical School:' line for each resident. The 8 residents who appear on both the archived roster and the live roster are the same people and their schools do not change, so those 8 are established at HIGH confidence from the program's own publication. The 4 residents who joined in July 2026 (Abedi, Dabbas, Nozari, Sehgal) appear only on the live page and have no published school. COMPLETE ARCHIVED AY2025-2026 ROSTER WITH SCHOOLS, as published: PRG 1 - Saaniya A Bagdadi D.O., Alabama College of Osteopathic Medicine; Imran Khan M.D., University of Texas Medical School at San Antonio; Hanna F Malik D.O., Kansas City University College of Osteopathic Medicine; Jade Thomas D.O., Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine, Auburn Campus. PRG 2 - Said El Hage M.D., Lebanese University Faculty of Medical Sciences; Kevin E Kleine D.O., Lincoln Memorial University DeBusk College of Osteopathic Medicine; Matthew L Moench M.D., University of Central Florida College of Medicine; Joshua D Perdue D.O., Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine, Carolinas Campus. PRG 3 (graduated June 2026) - Manali Desai D.O., Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine; Junaid M Essa D.O., Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine, Bradenton; Rochelle M Kinssies D.O., Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine, Bradenton; Ashley Lefebvre D.O., M.P.H., Alabama College of Osteopathic Medicine. INDEPENDENT CROSS-VALIDATION, which is why confidence is high: that archived 12-person roster resolves to 9 U.S. DO, 2 U.S. MD and 1 IMG (Lebanon). This also explains and retires an apparent contradiction: the LIVE roster shows 6 D.O. and 6 M.D. degrees, which does not match 75% DO, because FREIDA's percentages describe the PREVIOUS academic year's cohort, not the current one. SCHOOL CLASSIFICATION IS A PROPERTY OF THE INSTITUTION, never of any person, and no inference about anyone's nationality, ethnicity or immigration status is drawn from any name. PUERTO RICO / UCC RESULT: zero graduates of Universidad Central del Caribe, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico or San Juan Bautista appear in the archived roster, and zero graduates of offshore for-profit Caribbean schools (Ross, St George's, AUC, Saba and similar) appear either.

summary: Of the 12 current residents, 6 are U.S. osteopathic graduates, 2 are U.S. MD graduates, 1 is a non-Caribbean IMG, and 3 remain unknown because the program stopped publishing schools. No Universidad Central del Caribe or Puerto Rico graduates.
raw_finding: CURRENT COHORT (AY2026-2027), denominator 12 = actual census by head-count of the published roster, NOT the approved complement (both happen to be 12 this year but are established separately - see domain 11). Bucket assignment, resident by resident: US_MD = 2 (Imran Khan, University of Texas Medical School at San Antonio; Matthew L Moench, University of Central Florida College of Medicine). US_DO = 6 (Saaniya A Bagdadi, Alabama COM; Hanna F Malik, Kansas City University COM; Jade Thomas, Edward Via COM Auburn; Kevin E Kleine, Lincoln Memorial University DeBusk COM; Joshua D Perdue, Edward Via COM Carolinas - these five have published schools; plus Maleeha Abedi, whose school is unpublished but whose degree is published as D.O.). CARIBBEAN = 0. OTHER_IMG = 1 (Said El Hage, Lebanese University Faculty of Medical Sciences, Lebanon). UNKNOWN = 3 (Jood Dabbas M.D.; Andre Joseph A Nozari M.D., M.S.; Rohan Sehgal M.D. - all three hold M.D. degrees with no published school, so they could be US_MD, CARIBBEAN or OTHER_IMG and are not guessed). SUM CHECK: 2+6+0+1+3 = 12, exactly the denominator. REASONING FOR PLACING ABEDI IN US_DO: the degree 'D.O.' is published by the program, and the UFCOM-J 'Trainee Eligibility and Selection Policy' admits osteopathic physicians only via 'Graduation from a college of osteopathic medicine in the United States, accredited by the American Osteopathic Association Commission on Osteopathic College Accreditation (AOACOCA)', so an appointed D.O. here is necessarily a U.S. osteopathic graduate. Confidence on that single placement is MEDIUM; the other five US_DO placements are HIGH. OVERLAY COUNTS, which per the contract are NOT buckets and are NOT added into the sum: ucc_residents = 0 and puerto_rico_school_residents = 0. These are counts of zero established, resting on eight fully resolved schools plus three unresolved M.D. schools - so 'none found' rather than 'proven none'. PUERTO RICO CLASSIFICATION RULE APPLIED AS INSTRUCTED: had any resident held a degree from Universidad Central del Caribe, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico or San Juan Bautista, that resident would have been counted US_MD, never CARIBBEAN and never OTHER_IMG, because those are LCME-accredited United States MD schools. CARIBBEAN in this dossier means offshore for-profit schools (Ross, St George's, AUC, Saba and similar) and none appear on the resident roster. PRIOR-YEAR COHORT, fully resolved and reported separately because it is a different population: AY2025-2026 was 9 US_DO, 2 US_MD, 1 OTHER_IMG, 0 CARIBBEAN, 0 unknown, denominator 12 - which matches the program's own FREIDA figures of 75.0% DO / 16.7% US MD / 8.3% IMG to the person. NOTE ON THE REGISTRY: the registry's 'US Graduates: US MD 16.7%; DO 58.3%' and 'International Graduates: 25.0%' came from the older 2025 survey and describe yet another, earlier cohort; they are superseded by the 2026 survey figures and should not be applied to either cohort above.

summary: Three fellowship-trained movement disorders faculty, a DBS and botulinum toxin program, roughly ten weeks of dedicated outpatient neurodegenerative rotation across the three years, and movement disorders fellowship placements in five of the last six graduating classes. There is no in-house movement disorders fellowship and no formal external designation.
raw_finding: RESIDENT EXPOSURE, quoted from the program's own Curriculum page and deliberately separated from institutional capability: 'The neurodegenerative diseases rotation is outpatient oriented. This rotation incorporates exposure to patients with movement disorders and demyelinating diseases. Under the supervision of our movement disorder specialists, residents evaluate and treat patients with Parkinson's disease, Parkinsonian syndromes, dystonia and hyperkinetic disorders. In addition residents have exposure to Deep Brain Stimulation and botulinum toxin treatment of dystonia.' The rotation is scheduled, not optional: the PGY-2 block table lists 'Neurodegen/TBI 2 weeks'; the PGY-3 table lists 'Neurodegen/TBI 2 weeks' twice; the PGY-4 table lists 'Neurodegen/TBI 4 weeks'. The PGY-2 narrative adds 'During the outpatient subspecialty rotation, residents evaluate patients in clinics for stroke, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, movement disorders and neuromuscular diseases.' Didactics are structured into blocks, and the 'Subspecialty Block' is described as 'Focusing on outpatient subspecialties (Neuromuscular, Movement disorders, Neuroimmunology / Multiple Sclerosis, Dementia, Headache, Neuro-Otology, Neuro-Ophthalmology, etc)'. PGY-4 electives include 'Behavioral neurology / Dementia'. So this is genuine, calendared resident time in movement clinics with named supervising specialists, not merely a department that treats Parkinson's. NAMED FACULTY, all three fellowship-trained in movement disorders, from their official UF profiles: (1) Jesse S Cohen, MD - 'Dr. Cohen received his medical degree from Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. He completed his neurology residency and subspecialty training in movement disorders at the University of Pennsylvania.' He holds an M.S. in translational research from Penn where 'his thesis used neuroimaging to identify the brain areas responsible for cognitive and sleep dysfunction in Parkinson disease and other Lewy body disorders', and publishes in the field (e.g. 'Microstructural Changes in the Tuberal Hypothalamus Correlate with Daytime Sleepiness in Lewy Body Disorders', Movement Disorders 2025;40(9):1919-1929). Assistant Professor 2024-current. (2) Joseph D Legacy, MD - 'Dr. Legacy received his medical degree from the University of Central Florida in Orlando, Florida. He completed an internal medicine internship, a neurology residency and fellowship training in movement disorders and deep-brain stimulation at the University of Florida College of Medicine in Gainesville, Florida.' Areas of interest published on his profile include Parkinson Disease, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Multiple System Atrophy (both cerebellar and parkinsonian subtypes), Huntington's Disease, dystonia, essential tremor, Tourette Syndrome and tic disorders, tardive dyskinesia, Wilson Disease, Friedreich ataxia and restless legs syndrome. His profile lists an active movement-disorders trial grant: 'A Phase 2, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Dose Range Finding Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Tolerability, Safety, and Efficacy of PRAX-944 in the Treatment of Adults with Essential Tremor'. Assistant Professor 2021-current. (3) Kartik Mangipudi, MD - movement disorders and DBS fellowship at Mayo Clinic Arizona, research focus on gait and balance in Parkinsonian disorders, and Associate Program Director of this residency since 2025. INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY, quoted from the residency Faculty page under the 'Movement Disorders' heading: 'The Movement Disorders and Parkinson's Program at the UF Health Neuroscience Institute at Jacksonville delivers comprehensive care for Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders, including advanced diagnostics, medical management, and state-of-the-art neurosurgical treatment options. This program offers residents valuable exposure to both common and complex movement disorders within a multidisciplinary neuroscience environment.' There is no Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence, no HDSA Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence and no CurePSP Center of Care at Jacksonville. NO IN-HOUSE MOVEMENT FELLOWSHIP: the complete UFCOM-J GME program list shows Vascular Neurology as the institution's only neurology fellowship. I did not infer a movement fellowship from the presence of three movement-trained faculty, which is exactly the error the contract warns against.

summary: Vascular Neurology is the only neurology fellowship at this institution, with three fellows currently in post. There is no movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology, epilepsy, neurophysiology or neurocritical care fellowship here.
raw_finding: DEFINITIVE SOURCE: the UFCOM-J Graduate Medical Education office publishes a complete list of every residency and fellowship it sponsors. Under 'ACGME-Accredited Programs / Fellowships' the entire 'Neurology' subsection contains exactly one entry: 'Vascular Neurology'. The other fellowship subsections on that page are Emergency Medicine, Medicine, Pathology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry and Surgery, plus CODA, CPME, EUFAC and non-accredited lists (the non-accredited list includes a Neurosurgery 'Neurotrauma & Spine Fellowship', which is a neurosurgery programme, not neurology). So the absence of movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology, epilepsy, clinical neurophysiology and neurocritical care fellowships is established from the institution's own affirmative enumeration, not merely from failure to find them. The same list confirms there is NO Child Neurology programme at UFCOM-J, which removes any adult/child contamination risk from within this institution. IN-HOUSE FELLOWSHIP DETAIL: the department's own Vascular Neurology Fellowship section publishes a Fellows page listing three fellows in post - 'Fell 1: Jessica Canosa, M.D., Vascular Neurology Fellow; Tyler Cochran, M.D., Vascular Neurology Fellow' and 'Fell 2: Aaron Seifer, D.O., Vascular Neurology Fellow'. Leadership: Scott L Silliman, M.D. is titled 'Professor; Program Director, Vascular Neurology Fellowship; Medical Director, Comprehensive Stroke Program' with his profile recording 'Program Director 2005-Current - Vascular Neurology Fellowship'; Ryan K Crooks, MD is titled 'Assistant Professor; Associate Program Director, Vascular Neurology Fellowship'. FREIDA's 2026 survey sets field_match_nrmp_adv_fellow=true. GENUINE RESIDENT ACCESS to this fellowship is documented, not assumed: two graduates of this residency entered this very fellowship - 2023 Andres Arciniegas M.D. and 2022 Yessenia Marquez M.D., both recorded on the Alumni page as 'Vascular Neurology Fellowship, University of Florida College of Medicine - Jacksonville, Jacksonville, FL', and Marquez is now faculty here. The FREIDA special-features text also invites residents to 'Collaborate with our vascular fellowship'. AFFILIATED FELLOWSHIPS - DELIBERATELY LEFT EMPTY. FREIDA lists 'Shands Hospital at the University of Florida-Gainesville' as a participating institution for this program, and residents do spend 6 weeks in each of PGY-3 and PGY-4 at UF Health Shands Children's Hospital in Gainesville for pediatric neurology with lodging provided. The Gainesville campus hosts the Norman Fixel Institute and its movement disorders fellowships. But a participating institution for a rotation is NOT fellowship access, the Gainesville campus is a separate sponsoring institution with a separate adult neurology accreditation, and no page published by this program offers its residents preferential access to any Gainesville fellowship. Listing a Gainesville movement fellowship as 'affiliated' would blur exactly the line the contract forbids blurring, so the affiliated array is empty and this reasoning is recorded instead. The only documented instance of a Jacksonville graduate entering a Gainesville UF fellowship is 2024 Hayley Shade M.D. to 'Sports Neurotrauma Fellowship, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL' - a single alumni outcome, not a structural affiliation. NO FELLOWSHIP WAS INFERRED FROM A FACULTY MEMBER'S SPECIALTY: three movement-trained faculty and two neuroimmunology-trained faculty practise here, and none of that was converted into a fellowship claim.

summary: Neither the program nor the institution publishes an ABPN neurology board pass rate, although the program confirms it tracks graduates' pass rates as a formal program-evaluation measure.
raw_finding: I searched the program's residency landing page, Program Director's Welcome, Curriculum, Mission/Aims/Goals/Objectives, Residents, Alumni, Benefits and How to Apply pages; the department home page; the UFCOM-J GME site including 'About & Mission' and 'Benefits, Requirements and Resources'; and the full FREIDA 2026 survey record. No numeric ABPN pass rate for this program is published in any of them, and I ran a targeted web search for a program-specific ABPN pass rate which returned nothing program-specific. WHAT IS PUBLISHED, and it is not a pass rate: FREIDA's 2026 survey field_program_evaluation_2019 lists the measures the program uses to evaluate ITSELF, which include verbatim 'Graduates' board certification pass rates' alongside 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements' and 'Performance-based assessment scores (e.g. OSCE, patient or computer simulations)'. That confirms the program tracks the metric internally; it does not disclose the number. The registry's 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes' is therefore a SEMANTIC MISMATCH if read as a pass rate - it is a yes/no answer about whether the program uses pass rates as an evaluation input, not a rate. Separately, the program's 'at a glance' panel publishes a '90% Board-certified faculty rate', which is a FACULTY certification statistic and must not be mistaken for a resident board pass rate; ABPN itself publishes aggregate national neurology pass rates but not per-program rates. So the number a student would want does not exist publicly for this program.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - The program does not publish an ABPN neurology board pass rate. It does confirm that it uses graduates' board certification pass rates as an internal program-evaluation measure, and separately publishes a 90% board-certified FACULTY rate, which is a different statistic.

summary: A block-scheduled three-year curriculum with heavy stroke and neurocritical care volume, a dedicated outpatient neurodegenerative rotation in all three years, 40 half-days of continuity clinic per year, 21 weeks of elective time, and chief-resident roles in PGY-4.
raw_finding: All block tables above are transcribed from the program's own Curriculum page. KEY NARRATIVE PASSAGES, verbatim. Service structure: 'Our inpatient experiences are divided into a Vascular Neurology Service (all things stroke) and General Neurology Service (everything else). Both of these services are a combination of primary service inpatient and consultation services. Each service has a combination of a PGY2 resident and a senior (PGY3 or PGY4) resident. The resident conducts consults on inpatients and emergency department patients... Within the emergency department, residents assist in managing patients with acute stroke who may be candidates for interventions including intravenous TNK and/or thrombectomy.' Neurocritical care: 'A two week rotation in neurocritical care medicine provides residents with exposure to the management of patients with mass occupying lesions, intracerebral hemorrhage, spinal cord disorders, acute neuromuscular emergencies and neuro-trauma.' PGY-2 subspecialty clinics: 'During the outpatient subspecialty rotation, residents evaluate patients in clinics for stroke, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, movement disorders and neuromuscular diseases. They gain required early experience to outpatient subspecialty rotations, which helps the resident identify early areas of interest for future electives and career choices.' Neurodegenerative rotation (the movement/MS rotation): 'The neurodegenerative diseases rotation is outpatient oriented. This rotation incorporates exposure to patients with movement disorders and demyelinating diseases. Under the supervision of our movement disorder specialists, residents evaluate and treat patients with Parkinson's disease, Parkinsonian syndromes, dystonia and hyperkinetic disorders. In addition residents have exposure to Deep Brain Stimulation and botulinum toxin treatment of dystonia. Under the supervision of our multiple sclerosis attendings, residents have opportunities to diagnose and to treat patients with demyelinating and autoimmune disorders of the central nervous system.' PGY-4 leadership: 'The resident also develops supervisory and teaching skills, as they manage the vascular neurology team, general neurology team, and help to organize departmental conferences. Residents also actively engage in team-based quality improvement initiatives.' Research: 'The one-week research rotation aims to make the resident competent to write a research study proposal and complete the study over the course of his/her training... Residents also participate, as sub-investigators, in departmental clinical trials.' Conferences: 'Teaching conferences are incorporated into the curriculum, with didactics scheduled 12-1pm every weekday... Our conferences are in a modified block format, taking advantage of consecutive lectures to build on knowledge, and incorporating pre- and post-testing to track gains and areas needing further review. We also incorporate patient-focused, interactive weekly sessions on imaging and EEG review: Neuroradiology rounds on Tuesday mornings... and EEG Reading Fridays...'. Electives: 'In conjunction with the program director, residents can create an elective that suits an educational need not outlined above.' Simulation: 'Residents receive training in managing neurological emergencies, breaking bad news and patient safety at the UF Center for Simulation Education and Safety Research (CSESaR).' PEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY - LEGITIMATE ADULT CURRICULUM DATA, NOT CHILD-NEUROLOGY CONTAMINATION: the Program Director's Welcome states verbatim 'Residents spend their required pediatric neurology rotations at the UF College of Medicine campus in Gainesville at UF Health Shands Children's Hospital. Residents see pediatric patients with a wide variety of neurologic disorders while being supervised and taught by UF physicians from the division of pediatric neurology. Our program provides lodging while on this rotation.' items.title: Three fellowship-trained movement disorders faculty for a four-per-year program
items.student_explanation: Jesse Cohen (movement disorders, University of Pennsylvania), Joseph Legacy (movement disorders and deep-brain stimulation, UF Gainesville) and Kartik Mangipudi (movement disorders and DBS, Mayo Clinic Arizona) all practise here. Mangipudi is also an Associate Program Director, so a movement specialist sits in program leadership and on your interview panel.

items.title: A calendared outpatient movement and demyelinating rotation in all three years, not an elective you have to fight for
items.student_explanation: The Neurodegen/TBI block appears in every year of the published block schedule - 2 weeks in PGY-2, 4 weeks in PGY-3 and 4 weeks in PGY-4. The program states you will 'evaluate and treat patients with Parkinson's disease, Parkinsonian syndromes, dystonia and hyperkinetic disorders' and get 'exposure to Deep Brain Stimulation and botulinum toxin treatment of dystonia', plus MS and autoimmune CNS care under the MS attendings in the same rotation.

items.title: Movement disorders fellowship placements in five of the last six graduating classes
items.student_explanation: The program's own alumni list shows graduates going to movement disorders fellowships at the University of Washington, Medical College of Georgia, The Queen's Medical Center in Honolulu, Emory and OHSU between 2021 and 2025. For a program graduating four people a year, that is an unusually dense track record into the exact fellowship you want.

items.title: A National MS Society Center for Comprehensive Care in the same building and on the same floor as the residency office
items.student_explanation: The National MS Society's own provider directory lists the UF Health Jacksonville Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center at 580 W 8th St, Tower I, 9th Floor with both a 'Partner in MS Care' and a 'Center for Comprehensive Care' designation. That address is the residency's own department address, so the designated centre is not a separate campus you visit - it is where you work.

items.title: Two neuroimmunologists trained at Harvard and the NIH, both hired in 2025
items.student_explanation: Alexander Carvajal Gonzalez did autoimmune neurology subspecialty training at Harvard, a neuroimmunology research fellowship at Johns Hopkins and a PhD in clinical neurology at Oxford. William Frazier did neuroimmunology and neurovirology fellowship training at NINDS/NIH. Both joined in 2025, so the MS and neuroimmunology side of the department is actively being built out, and 'Neuroimmunology' is a named senior elective.

items.title: A December 31 application deadline, which is unusually late
items.student_explanation: The program states 'The deadline for submitting your completed application is Dec. 31.' Most programs close far earlier. If any part of your file - a Step 2 CK score, a letter - lands in October or November, this program is still open and still reviewing.

items.title: A guaranteed preliminary PGY-1 year on the same campus, with no separate interview
items.student_explanation: Because this is an advanced program you must also match a PGY-1 year. The program states 'We are an advanced program but do not require a separate interview for the preliminary PGY-1 internal medicine position' and 'Applicants who MATCH with our program are also guaranteed a PGY-1 position in internal medicine if they elect to conduct their preliminary year on our campus.' NRMP data confirm the paired Med-Prelim/Neurology track (code 1101140P1) matched 4 of 4 in 2026. That removes most of the usual risk and extra interviewing burden of an advanced program.

items.title: A program director who trained in this program and has won five teaching awards
items.student_explanation: Shannon LaBoy completed this very residency, returned as faculty, and has been program director since 2021 while also serving as neurology clerkship director. Her published awards include Exemplary Teacher in 2024 and 2021, a departmental Golden Apple Award in 2024, and Excellence in Student Education in 2018. Education is visibly her job, not a side duty.

items.title: High-acuity stroke volume through a Level I trauma centre, a mobile stroke unit and a DNV Comprehensive Stroke Center
items.student_explanation: UF Health Jacksonville is the only Level I trauma centre in Northeast Florida and Southeast Georgia, runs a Mobile Stroke Treatment Unit and telestroke service, and draws stroke patients by TraumaOne helicopter from a 12-county area. DNV Healthcare recertified the downtown programme as a Comprehensive Stroke Center in December 2025. You spend 12 weeks on the vascular service in PGY-2 alone and help manage thrombolysis and thrombectomy decisions in the ED.

items.title: A required research rotation with sub-investigator roles on real trials, including a movement disorders trial
items.student_explanation: The research rotation is required, and the program states residents 'participate, as sub-investigators, in departmental clinical trials' with on-campus biostatistics support. One movement faculty member's published grant list includes a Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial of PRAX-944 in essential tremor, so there is an active movement-disorders trial you could plausibly join.

items.title: The only in-house neurology fellowship takes its own graduates
items.student_explanation: Vascular Neurology is the institution's single neurology fellowship, currently with three fellows. Two recent graduates of this residency went straight into it, and one of them, Yessenia Marquez, is now on the faculty. It is a genuine internal pathway rather than a nominal one.

items.title: Documented graduate placements into Houston teaching hospitals
items.student_explanation: Two 2020 graduates went to UTHealth Houston - one for vascular neurology and one for neurocritical care. This is a factual placement record, not a claim about convenience: Jacksonville is roughly 860 road miles from Houston and any visit is a flight.

summary: The residency has no Medical Spanish curriculum and no faculty member documents Spanish-language ability. What does exist is institution-level: UF Health Jacksonville is the city's only safety-net hospital and staffs three certified Spanish interpreters plus remote interpreting, in the same buildings where residents train.
raw_finding: WHAT WAS ESTABLISHED. (1) FORMAL MEDICAL SPANISH - ABSENT, verified fresh rather than inherited. FREIDA's question is worded verbatim 'Instruction in medical Spanish or other non-English language' and the program's own 2026 survey answer renders verbatim as 'No'. The underlying array field_resident_fellow_offer_2019 contains seven selections - health systems leadership, interprofessional teamwork, alternative/complementary medicine, debt management, retreats, off-campus electives, hospice/home care - and the medical-Spanish option is NOT among them. The registry recorded 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: No'; that value is CONFIRMED against a survey the program submitted on 2026-06-16, not carried forward. A string search of the entire FREIDA program payload for 'Spanish' returns only the question label itself. (2) SPANISH-SPEAKING NEUROLOGY FACULTY - NONE DOCUMENTED. I fetched and read all 37 published profiles in the department's own profile directory and searched every one for 'Spanish', 'bilingual', 'habla', 'languages spoken' and 'interpreter'. Zero matches. Not one neurology faculty profile documents any language capability. (3) INTERPRETER SERVICE - PRESENT and program-adjacent. UF Health Jacksonville's own published account states verbatim: 'For in-person services, patients can work with one of our staff interpreters. We currently have three certified staff interpreters who speak Spanish along with a host of other employees who are bi-lingual and qualified interpreters. For all other languages, we use two local vendors who provide access to over 80 different languages.' and 'Cyracom and Language Line Solutions are also tools used to help provide video and audio remote interpreting.' It also documents an operational Limited English Proficiency workflow: 'In the Emergency department, staff use what is called Limited English Proficiency (LEP). This is signified by placing an orange wrist band on a patient who has limited English skills' and 'Employees in the ED can also place a globe sticker on the patient's door.' Residents rotate through that ED and those clinics, so this is infrastructure they will actually use - but it is a hospital service, not residency training, and it is Spanish-inclusive rather than Spanish-specific. (4) SAFETY-NET SITE - PRESENT and stated by the program itself. The program's own FREIDA special-features text states verbatim: 'As the only safety net hospital in Jacksonville, we serve a diverse population.' UF Health Jacksonville is one of Florida's statutory teaching hospitals. The program's Mission page commits to 'elimination of health disparities' and its Program Aims include providing care 'to all patients, regardless of their socioeconomic background'. This is the genuine, program-level, safety-net evidence the ticket anticipated might exist here - and it is socioeconomic in framing, not Latino-specific. WHY THE STRENGTH IS LIMITED AND NOT MODERATE: there is no Spanish-language clinic, no Spanish-language continuity panel, no bilingual track, no Medical Spanish curriculum, no documented Spanish-speaking neurology faculty or resident, and no published Latino community partnership. A fluent Spanish speaker would find her language useful here through interpreter-free direct communication with patients, but the program offers her nothing structured to build on and would not be a place where Spanish fluency is formally developed or credentialled.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - The residency publishes no Medical Spanish curriculum and no neurology faculty profile documents Spanish-language ability. What exists is hospital-level interpreter service at the safety-net site where residents train.

raw_finding: SEARCH METHOD, across six populations. (1) CURRENT RESIDENTS - all 12 named on the live roster; schools established for 8 via the program's own archived page, none Puerto Rican; 3 M.D. schools unpublished so 'none found' rather than 'proven none'. (2) PRIOR-YEAR RESIDENTS - the complete AY2025-2026 roster of 12 with every medical school published, recovered from the 2026-03-16 capture: Alabama COM, UT Medical School at San Antonio, Kansas City University COM, Edward Via COM Auburn, Lebanese University Faculty of Medical Sciences, Lincoln Memorial DeBusk COM, University of Central Florida COM, Edward Via COM Carolinas, Philadelphia COM, Lake Erie COM Bradenton (x2), Alabama COM. No Puerto Rico school. (3) GRADUATES 2020-2026 - 29 named graduates on the Alumni page with destinations; no Puerto Rico institution appears as a destination and the page publishes no medical schools for graduates. (4) CURRENT FELLOWS - Jessica Canosa M.D., Tyler Cochran M.D., Aaron Seifer D.O.; the Fellows page publishes no medical schools, so no Puerto Rico tie could be established or excluded. (5) FACULTY - I fetched and read all 37 published profiles in the department's own profile directory and grep-searched every one for 'Puerto Rico', 'del Caribe', 'Ponce', 'San Juan Bautista', 'Bayamon', 'UPR' and 'Recinto'. Exactly one hit surfaced and it was a false positive: the substring 'upr' inside 'Progressive Supranuclear Palsy' in Joseph Legacy's published areas of interest. ZERO real matches. Faculty medical schools where published span the Philippines, Jordan (x3), Colombia, Ireland, India (x3), Grenada, Dominica, Lebanon and a range of US MD and DO schools - no Puerto Rico institution among them. (6) LEADERSHIP - the PD, both APDs and the chair have published training histories and none includes Puerto Rico. THE DISTINCTION THE CONTRACT INSISTS ON, applied here: two faculty hold degrees from offshore for-profit Caribbean schools - Program Director Shannon M LaBoy from St. George's University School of Medicine in Grenada, and Lintu Ramachandran from Ross University School of Medicine. These are NOT Puerto Rico ties and are NOT equivalent to Universidad Central del Caribe. Puerto Rico's LCME-accredited schools are United States MD schools; Ross and St George's are offshore for-profit institutions. Recording LaBoy or Ramachandran as a 'Caribbean tie' relevant to Alejandra would be precisely the misclassification the contract warns misclassifies her own school. I also confirmed I am not confusing Universidad Central del ESTE (Dominican Republic) with Universidad Central del CARIBE (Bayamon, Puerto Rico) - neither appears anywhere in this program's published material. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR ALEJANDRA, stated plainly: she would be the first Universidad Central del Caribe graduate in this program as far as its public record shows, and there is no Puerto Rico alumnus, mentor or faculty member here to serve as a precedent or an advocate. That is a genuine absence, not a disqualification, and it is worth her knowing before she applies. One partial counterweight: the program has demonstrably appointed graduates of medical schools outside the US mainland - a Lebanese University graduate currently in PRG-3 - and its own program director is an offshore Caribbean graduate who rose to lead the program, so the program has no visible pattern of screening against non-mainland training.

raw_finding: Mayo Clinic School of Graduate Medical Education Application Process page, verbatim: 'Valid ECFMG certificate required if you graduated from a medical school outside the United States. Canadian medical school graduates who completed their studies before July 1, 2025, do not need ECFMG certification. However, graduates after this date must obtain full ECFMG certification.' The general admissions requirements page sets residency-interview eligibility as being 'currently enrolled in or a graduate of' one of: 'A medical school in the United States accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME); or, A college of osteopathic medicine in the United States, accredited by the American Osteopathic Association Commission on Osteopathic College Accreditation (AOACOCA); or, An accredited dental school; or, An accredited doctoral program applicable to the training program; or, Medical school outside of the United States, including Canada, and meeting one of the following additional qualifications: Be verified by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) prior to appointment; or, Hold a full and unrestricted license to practice medicine...'. It also states the ranking gate: 'Applicants in the process of obtaining ECFMG certification may be interviewed, but may not be placed on a rank match list, or appointed, unless they have received full ECFMG certification.' ALEJANDRA ANALYSIS, and this is a deliberate finding rather than an assumption: Universidad Central del Caribe is an LCME-accredited medical school located in Puerto Rico, a United States territory. It therefore satisfies Mayo's first eligibility limb, 'A medical school in the United States accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME)', and she is NOT a graduate of a 'medical school outside the United States'. No ECFMG certificate is required of her. AMBIGUITY FLAGGED AS INSTRUCTED: Mayo nowhere names Puerto Rico. Its wording is actually BETTER than the pattern the contract warned about - Mayo says 'in the United States accredited by the LCME' rather than 'in the U.S. and Canada', so the territory is covered by the plain words. However, one later sentence on the same page reads 'Medical and surgical residencies are open to qualified graduates of accredited U.S. and Canadian medical schools' and another reads 'All graduates from medical schools outside the U.S. and Canada must be certified by ECFMG'. A coordinator reading only those sentences would still reach the correct answer for a Puerto Rico LCME graduate, but the absence of an explicit Puerto Rico mention is a residual documentation gap she may wish to pre-empt in her application materials.

Program Department and Faculty page: 'Dr. Marin Collazo is an autoimmune neurologist who leads our multidisciplinary multiple sclerosis clinic. Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship (Florida) Overview page: 'Autoimmune neurology is one of the most rapidly evolving and treatable fields in neurology. IN-HOUSE FELLOWSHIP, verbatim: 'The Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship is a one-year program at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, designed to provide an opportunity to participate in contemporary autoimmune neurology clinical management and translational activities.' Program history, verbatim: 'The Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship will accept its first fellow to begin training in July 2024. We anticipate that one fellow will complete this program each year.' Its program director is Sebastian Lopez, M.D. (Sebastian Lopez Chiriboga), with coordinator Kathryn Thoman. Fellows_in_post is recorded as null rather than 1 because 'we anticipate one fellow per year' is a capacity statement, not a verified current head count, and no named current fellow was found. FELLOWSHIP CURRICULUM, verbatim: 'During the Autoimmune Neurology Clinic, working with a neurology consultant, you will focus on the diagnosis, investigation, and management of autoimmune neurological disorders.' and 'Additional clinical activities in a template custom-tailored to match the career goals of the trainee including frequent rotations in MS clinic, behavioral neurology, epilepsy, movement disorders, neuro-ophthalmology, rheumatology, immunology, and pediatric neurology.' and 'Fellows will actively participate in clinical trials for antibody-mediated diseases.' FACULTY DEPTH, verbatim: 'Dr. Irani is an autoimmune neurologist and scientist who has extensive expertise in conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis, neuromyelitis optica, stiff person syndrome, and paraneoplastic syndromes.' The fellowship faculty page adds, verbatim: 'Dr. Irani is a clinician-scientist and consultant neurologist. He has discovered LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies, faciobrachial dystonic seizures and associated treatment responses, and has described the underlying immunobiology of autoantibody-mediated diseases.' On Marin Collazo, verbatim from the fellowship faculty page: 'Dr. Marin Collazo is a neurologist with a special interest in multiple sclerosis. Her clinical focuses include the diagnosis and management of demyelinating/autoimmune diseases of the central nervous system, multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, traverse myelitis, and neurosarcoidosis.' On Day, verbatim: 'Dr. Day is the Director of the Division of Behavioral Neurology and Vice Chair of Research for the Department of Neurology... He is a founding member and Clinical Director of the Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis Foundation, and a project PI of the ExTINGUISH Trial - the first multi-site randomized controlled trial for patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.' On Lopez Chiriboga, verbatim from the residency page: 'Dr. Lopez is an autoimmune neurologist who attends on the general neurology inpatient service and staffs the resident continuity clinic. He is the program director of the Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship.' RESIDENT ACCESS: 'Multiple sclerosis and demyelinating diseases' is a named elective option among 8.5 elective blocks; there is no required MS block in the published rotation schedule. However two of the MS/autoimmune faculty are embedded in required resident experiences - Lopez Chiriboga attends the general neurology inpatient service and staffs the resident continuity clinic, and Marin Collazo 'works closely with our residents in the outpatient clinic' - so baseline contact does not depend on electing it. INTERNAL PIPELINE, which is the single most distinctive feature here: both of the program's MS/autoimmune clinical leads are graduates of this very residency. Marin Collazo is quoted on the Overview page as 'Vanessa Marin Collazo, M.D., class of 2016' and Lopez Chiriboga as 'Sebastian Lopez Chiriboga, M.D., class of 2017'. Secondary profiles add that Lopez Chiriboga did his neurology residency at Mayo Clinic Florida 2013-2017, served as chief resident for administration 2016-2017, then a one-year Autoimmune Neurology fellowship 2017-2018 and a Neuroimmunology/Multiple Sclerosis fellowship at Mayo Clinic Rochester 2018-2019, and is Director of the Multiple Sclerosis and Autoimmune Neurology Division at Mayo Florida - recorded at MEDIUM confidence as SECONDARY because mayoclinic.org bios returned HTTP 403. What I DID find is that the NMSS-designated 'Center for Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Care' in Jacksonville belongs to UF HEALTH JACKSONVILLE - a different institution, and specifically the other adult neurology program in this city (ACGME 1801112154), which this ticket explicitly warned not to mix in. raw_finding: Searched the program Overview, Curriculum, Department and Faculty, Alumni, Resident Life and Application Process pages, Mayo's GME pages, and FREIDA's 210-field survey record; no numeric board pass rate appears anywhere. What IS published is adjacent but not a rate. Program Overview page, verbatim under the heading Certification: 'Graduates are eligible to take the board examination of the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology.' Under Accreditation: 'The Adult Neurology Residency is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME).' Under Program history: 'The Adult Neurology Residency at Mayo Clinic's campus in Florida began in July 2002 and has received maximum ACGME accreditation every cycle since its inception.' FREIDA's 2026 survey records that the program USES board results as an evaluation input - field_program_evaluation_2019 = ['Aggregate resident Milestone achievements', 'Graduates' board certification pass rates', 'Performance-based assessment scores (e.g. OSCE, patient or computer simulations)'] - which CONFIRMS the registry's 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes'. That is a statement that the metric is tracked internally, NOT a published value, and the registry field should not be read as implying a disclosed rate. ABPN publishes aggregate pass rates by specialty and by programme size bands but the program-level figure for 1801113148 is not public. This is a genuine non-publication after meaningful searching, not a failure to look, and it must not be converted into any claim about pass performance in either direction.

summary: Mayo pays by 'Graduate Level', not PGY: $75,105 at Level 1 rising to $85,398 at Level 4, effective 11 March 2026. Twenty vacation working days a year, medical leave up to 13 weeks including six weeks paid maternity leave, ten days paid parental leave for either parent, free parking, on-call meal subsidy. raw_finding: PRIMARY SOURCE is Mayo's own GME Stipend and Benefits page, which publishes a full table headed 'Resident and fellow educational stipends: Effective March 11, 2026': Graduate Level 1 $75,105 ($2,889 biweekly); Level 2 $77,721 ($2,989); Level 3 $80,936 ($3,113); Level 4 $85,398 ($3,285); Level 5 $89,036; Level 6 $92,376; Level 7 $95,417; Level 8 $99,058; Level 9 $102,594; Level 10 $106,096. Footnote, verbatim: 'Annual compensation applies to Mayo Clinic School of Graduate Medical Education residents and fellows but does not apply to Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery (OMS) residents.' and 'Mayo Clinic payroll runs on an every-other-week schedule. The annual amount is only an approximation due to Mayo's payroll structure.' REGISTRY IS STALE AND SEMANTICALLY MISMATCHED. The registry stored Salary PGY1 75093, PGY2 75093, PGY3 78199, PGY4 82510 - an older cycle, and note that it lists PGY1 and PGY2 at the identical figure, which no Mayo Graduate Level table does. Mayo does not pay by PGY at all; it pays by Graduate Level, and for THIS program the PGY-1 internal medicine preliminary year is Graduate Level 1 while the three neurology years are Levels 2, 3 and 4. FREIDA's 2026 survey independently confirms the level mapping in a way that also confirms the program's structure: field_graduate_year_statistics = [{salary: null, ...}, {salary: 77121, paid_vacation: 20, paid_sick: 91}, {salary: 80936, ...}, {salary: 85398, ...}] - the FIRST program year carries a NULL salary (because the PGY-1 year sits in the internal medicine preliminary program, not this one) and years two, three and four carry 77121, 80936 and 85398. The last two match Mayo's Graduate Levels 3 and 4 exactly. field_first_year_salary = 77121 differs from Mayo's published Level 2 figure of $77,721 by $600 - a transposition or a pre-increase value in FREIDA; Mayo's own HR table is preferred. BENEFITS, verbatim from the same page: paid benefits are 'Vacation (20 working days a year)', 'Short-term disability (medical leave up to 13 weeks - includes six weeks of paid maternity leave)', 'Paid parental leave (ten days - applies to both the birthing and non-birthing parent(s), in addition to the above six weeks of maternity leave)' and a 'Dental assistance plan'. Insurance: comprehensive medical care plan; voluntary basic life, disability and family life insurance; voluntary additional life; voluntary AD&D; excess personal liability. Other: dependent and healthcare reimbursement accounts, adoption reimbursement, Mayo Employees Credit Union resident and fellow housing loans, paid and unpaid leaves of absence, tax-deferred annuity plans, 'Meal subsidy for on-call residents', and 'Free parking and intercampus bus shuttle'. Also 24/7 free access to the Bill Hewitt Employee Wellness Center (opened summer 2024, 6,700 square feet) and, in Jacksonville specifically, a discount with the YMCA. FREIDA CONFIRMS the registry's cost-sharing structure across all benefit lines (major medical for residents, dependents and domestic partners; outpatient and inpatient mental health; group life; dental; disability - all 'Institution & Resident Share Cost'), field_salary_paid_nonprofit = Yes, field_leave_paid = 84 and field_allows_moonlighting = false (registry 'Moonlighting: No' CONFIRMED). Note field_leave_unpaid = 999, a FREIDA null sentinel that the registry correctly rendered as 'NGO'/Negotiable.
conflict_notes: Registry salary figures (PGY1/PGY2 both 75093; PGY3 78199; PGY4 82510) are one cycle stale AND expressed per-PGY where Mayo pays per Graduate Level. summary: Thirteen four-week blocks a year. The three neurology years carry 20.5 blocks of adult neurology, 8.5 elective blocks, 3 blocks of child and adolescent neurology, and 2 each of clinical neurophysiology, neurocritical care and the epilepsy monitoring unit, plus 1 of psychiatry. Night float replaces 24-hour call entirely.
raw_finding: STRUCTURE, verbatim from the Rotation Schedule page: 'Each year is divided into 13 four-week blocks.' PGY-2: Adult neurology inpatient 6.5 blocks; Adult neurology outpatient 2; Electives 2; Night float 1.5; Neurocritical care unit 1. PGY-3: Adult neurology inpatient 3; Electives 3.5; Clinical neurophysiology 2; Child and adolescent neurology 2; Night float 1.5; Epilepsy monitoring unit 1. PGY-4: Adult neurology inpatient 3.5; Electives 3; Night float 1.5; Adult neurology outpatient 1; Epilepsy monitoring unit 1; Neurocritical care unit 1; Child and adolescent neurology 1; Psychiatry 1. Published totals: Adult neurology inpatient and outpatient 20.5; Electives 8.5; Child and adolescent neurology 3; Clinical neurophysiology 2; Neurocritical care unit 2; Epilepsy monitoring unit 2; Psychiatry 1. PGY-1 AND THE TRANSITION COURSE, verbatim: 'The American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) requires that you spend one year in an accredited internal medicine program in the U.S. or Canada, or in a transitional program that has been approved by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) and includes at least six months in internal medicine. No neurology residency credit will be given for time spent in a residency program for another medical specialty.' / 'Applicants who match in our Neurology Residency Program are guaranteed a position in our one-year Internal Medicine Preliminary Residency Program.' / 'A unique feature of the Adult Neurology Residency in Florida is the Transition to Neurology course. This course occurs during May and June of the PGY-1 year. The first month is built on a program of didactics on a variety of topics in neurology and neuroanatomy, simulations of emergent neurological conditions including brain attacks and status epilepticus, and lumbar puncture training. In June, you are immersed into the inpatient service where you will learn the workflow and get acquainted with the multidisciplinary care teams. You will spend time with the general neurology, vascular neurology, and neurocritical care teams.' CONTINUITY CLINIC: 'One half-day a week throughout the three years.' CALL: night float in two-week blocks, Monday to Friday 6 p.m. to 7 a.m.; PGY-2 residents share weekend day coverage while PGY-3 and PGY-4 share weekend night responsibilities; NO 24-hour shifts. FREIDA CONFIRMS field_night_float = true and field_night_float_y1 = true (registry 'Night Float: Yes' CONFIRMED), field_avg_hours_on_duty_y1 = 60 (registry 60 hours/week CONFIRMED), field_max_hours_on_duty_y1 = 16, field_avg_24hr_off_duty_y1 = 1.50, field_avg_hrs_lecture_conf_y1 = 6 (registry recorded 5 structured didactic hours for PGY1 - the 2026 survey says 6, a minor update), field_train_ambulatory_nonhospit = 30 and field_training_outpatient_clinic = 30 (registry clinic structure CONFIRMED), field_research_rotation = 'Optional' (CONFIRMED) with field_research_rotation_duration = 0, field_beyond_accredited_length = false, field_next_away_rotation_in = false, field_special_tracks = ['Academic or clinician educator'] (CONFIRMS registry 'Clinician Educator Track: Yes' and 'Research Track: No'). PEDIATRIC ROTATION - THIS IS LEGITIMATE ADULT CURRICULUM DATA, taken solely from the adult program's own curriculum pages, verbatim: 'Mayo Clinic has a formal affiliation for teaching and research with Nemours Children's Clinic, Jacksonville, and Wolfson Children's Hospital in Jacksonville. Your training in caring for children and adolescents occurs under the direction of the pediatric neurology division. During PGY-3 (two-month rotation) and PGY-4 (one-month rotation), your child and adolescent neurology assignments are divided between hospital and outpatient clinic services.' No child neurology PROGRAM page was opened to obtain this. CLINICAL NEUROPHYSIOLOGY, verbatim: two months in PGY-3 covering 'Electromyography (EMG); Nerve conduction studies; Electroencephalography (EEG); Evoked potentials; Autonomic function testing; Polysomnography', after which 'you can choose to spend additional elective time in the EMG lab if desired'. ELECTIVES - the full published option list, which is the key structure for Alejandra's interests: 'Autonomics; Behavioral neurology; Brooks Rehabilitation Hospital; Cerebrovascular disease; Clinical epilepsy and epilepsy monitoring unit; Clinical neurophysiology; Clinical neuropsychology; Electroencephalography (EEG); Headache; Movement disorders; Multiple sclerosis and demyelinating diseases; Neurointensive care; Neuromuscular; Neuro-oncology; Neuro-ophthalmology; Neuro-otology; Neuroradiology; Pain medicine; Palliative care; Research; Sleep disorders; Speech pathology; Telestroke.' DIDACTICS AND SCHOLARSHIP: weekly academic half-day conferences, journal clubs, formal courses, a weekly 'Professor Rounds' led by Benjamin Eidelman, a PGY-2 Neuroanatomy course directed by Lindsy Williams, and a weekly multidisciplinary epilepsy education conference led by Seyed Mirsattari. All residents must conduct scholarly activity (chart review, case report or original investigation). Off-campus electives are available at the Rochester and Phoenix/Scottsdale campuses - noted here as a resident opportunity, and NOT used as a source of any Florida programme claim.

raw_finding: RESIDENTS: all 18 current residents have a published medical school and none is Universidad Central del Caribe, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico or San Juan Bautista. ucc_residents = 0 and puerto_rico_school_residents = 0. These are OVERLAY counts and are deliberately NOT added into the five-bucket composition partition. Note the classification rule that would apply if one existed: a Puerto Rico LCME-accredited school graduate counts as US_MD, not CARIBBEAN and not OTHER_IMG - the single resident classified CARIBBEAN here is a graduate of the University of Medicine and Health Sciences in St. Kitts, an offshore for-profit school, which is a different category entirely despite the shared geography. FACULTY: no Puerto Rico tie could be established for any of the 48 faculty. This is an evidentiary limit, not a finding of absence. The program publishes roles and subspecialties but not medical schools or training histories for faculty, and Mayo's individual physician biography pages on mayoclinic.org - which would carry medical school and sometimes languages - returned HTTP 403 to every automated request and were NOT bypassed. Critically, and in direct compliance with law 4: several faculty surnames on the roster could invite a guess about Puerto Rico origin, and no such guess was made. School classification is treated strictly as a property of the institution, never of the person, so ucc_faculty and puerto_rico_faculty are reported empty-because-unverifiable and the section status reflects that a claim was tested rather than assumed. ELIGIBILITY, which is the part that actually matters for her: Mayo's published residency-interview eligibility rule is being 'currently enrolled in or a graduate of ... A medical school in the United States accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME)'. Universidad Central del Caribe is an LCME-accredited medical school located in a United States territory and satisfies that limb on its plain words. She therefore needs no ECFMG certification and faces no IMG ranking gate. The residual issue is documentation rather than eligibility: Mayo nowhere names Puerto Rico, and one sentence on the same page narrows to 'graduates of accredited U.S. and Canadian medical schools'. That phrasing still covers her, but the ambiguity is flagged as instructed because it is the kind of wording that produces avoidable coordinator queries.

summary: Twenty-six domains completed on 21 successfully opened URLs across 7 domains, with 20 official sources. The decisive freshness finding is that FREIDA held a complete newer survey cycle (received 2026-06-15) than the registry snapshot carried, which corrected the graduation-recency cap, the accepting-applications flags and the resident composition percentages.
raw_finding: FRESHNESS. The registry release is rise_registry_2026-07-09_f51f0643a2d9 and records 'Survey Received: 2025-06-18' with 'FREIDA Last Updated: 2026-02-19'. Reading FREIDA's server-rendered ng-state payload directly (the public page is an Angular dead end) produced a node--survey_2026 record whose field_date_received is 2026-06-15, with node created 2026-08-20 and changed 2026-08-20T03:24:44Z. That is a FULL SURVEY CYCLE NEWER than the registry's substrate, and comparing the two is what surfaced the material corrections catalogued in registry_reconciliation - most importantly the five-year graduation-recency cap (registry: no cap), the inverted accepting-applications flags, and the resident-composition percentages that were computed on a stale denominator of 16. The program's own web pages are current for the 2026 ERAS cycle: the Application Process page references 'the 2026 ERAS cycle' and an in-person second look 'in February 2027', which is precisely Alejandra's cycle. Mayo's stipend table is dated 'Effective March 11, 2026'. Nothing used here is STALE_NEEDS_REFRESH. ACCESS BOUNDARIES, all recorded and none bypassed. (1) mayoclinic.org returned HTTP 403 to every automated request, including its robots.txt, blocking Mayo's individual physician biography pages for Elizabeth Mauricio and Sebastian Lopez Chiriboga and the Florida interpreter-services page. This is the single largest evidentiary gap in the dossier: it is why faculty and leadership medical schools, training histories and documented languages are null, and why Puerto Rico faculty ties could not be established in either direction. One request with a standard browser user agent was made and also refused; no further circumvention was attempted. (2) als.org returned HTTP 403, so the ALS Association's own certification wording for a Mayo Clinic Florida ALS centre could not be read and the certification is therefore not asserted. (3) ACGME's public program data was attempted at apps.acgme.org/ads/Public/Programs/Detail?programId=1801113148 and returned HTTP 404; ACGME's public program search is CAPTCHA-gated and was NOT bypassed, per law 3. Consequently ACGME-sourced accreditation status, accreditation dates and approved complement are UNAVAILABLE_DUE_TO_ACCESS_BOUNDARY; the program's own statement that it 'has received maximum ACGME accreditation every cycle since its inception' is reported as the program's claim. (4) NRMP program-level historical fill and unfilled/SOAP data is not published per program; NRMP's List of Unfilled Programs is restricted to registered users during SOAP week, so historical SOAP is RESEARCHED_NOT_PUBLIC rather than negative. TECHNIQUES THAT PAID OFF, for reuse. The FREIDA ng-state extraction was decisive and produced a 210-field record newer than the registry. Reading the program's raw HTML to enumerate sub-page hrefs recovered the roster, which had 404'd at the guessed URL /meet-our-residents/ and actually lives at /meet-our-trainees/ - without that, the entire named roster, the composition partition and the school mapping would have been RESEARCHED_NOT_PUBLIC. Going to NRMP's program directory directly resolved the position type that FREIDA's own contradictory flags could not. AGGREGATORS QUARANTINED: residencyadvisor.com, matcharesident.com, residencyprogramslist.com, admit.org, doximity.com, healthgrades.com, webmd.com, medicalnewstoday.com, us news doctors and md.com all surfaced in searches for this program. NONE was opened and NONE is cited as authority. The only secondary-derived statements in the dossier are the training histories of Mauricio and Lopez Chiriboga and Uitti's DBS research activity, each explicitly labelled SECONDARY at MEDIUM confidence with the reason (the primary Mayo bio host is 403-blocked) stated in place.

summary: The program sponsors J-1 visas through ECFMG and has publicly stopped sponsoring H-1B visas for housestaff. This is irrelevant to Alejandra, who as a Puerto Rico LCME-school graduate is a US medical graduate requiring no sponsorship.
raw_finding: The program's Application Requirements page states verbatim under 'Visas': 'Due to recent changes at the state and federal level, our department is no longer able to sponsor H-1B visas for housestaff. We will continue to support and sponsor J-1 visas for eligible applicants. We will provide updates if additional guidance becomes available.' The FREIDA survey_2026 record carries field_visa_status = ['J-1 through ECFMG'] only. The registry (from the older 2025 survey) stored 'J-1 through ECFMG; F-1' and 'F1 OPT First Year: Yes'; the 2026 survey cycle no longer carries F-1, so the F-1/OPT pathway is not currently confirmed. summary: The program publishes no Step 2 timing requirement of any kind, and states affirmatively that no single metric can preclude interview consideration. A mid-October 2026 Step 2 CK result therefore creates no published barrier at this program, and rolling interview invitations run from mid-October to mid-December.
raw_finding: Three independent sources were checked separately for the four possible timing gates. (1) The program's own Application Requirements page, current for the 2026-2027 season, contains no sentence requiring Step 2 at submission, before review, before interview, or before ranking. Its operative sentence is verbatim: 'All applications are reviewed and considered for interview, utilizing a holistic review process as recommended by the AAMC... No individual metric will preclude consideration for interview, but applicants ideally should have passed the USMLE/COMLEX exams on first attempt and have completed their medical training no more than five years before application.' It also states 'Because the holistic structure naturally slows the overall review process, interview invitations are sent on a rolling basis throughout the interview season' and 'Interviews are generally conducted from mid-October through mid-December. Rank order lists must be submitted to the NRMP by mid-February.' (2) FREIDA survey_2026 fields field_usmle_step2_req_int = false and field_usmle_step_2_required = false, with field_usmle_step_2_minimum_score = null - so no requirement AND no interview-stage flag. (3) The UF GME institutional eligibility policy places Step 2 only inside the foreign-graduate/ECFMG branch, not in the LCME branch that applies to a Puerto Rico LCME graduate. The UF GME USMLE/COMLEX Policy governs Step 3, not Step 2. NO inference was drawn from any minimum-score rule, because none exists. This is a genuine absence of a published timing gate, not an unfound one: the program publishes a detailed, specific screening-philosophy paragraph and that paragraph disclaims metric-based exclusion.

value.puerto_rico_ambiguity_flag: The UF GME policy's LCME branch reads 'United States or Canadian medical school accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME)' and does not name Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico is part of the United States and Universidad Central del Caribe is LCME-accredited, so UCC falls inside this branch on the policy's own wording. summary: ECFMG certification is required of foreign medical graduates by the time of rank-list submission. As a Universidad Central del Caribe graduate - a US LCME-accredited school - Alejandra does not need ECFMG certification and falls inside the UF GME policy's LCME branch.
raw_finding: The program's Application Requirements page states verbatim: 'We welcome all qualified applicants from the United States and abroad. Applicants must have an M.D., D.O. or M.B.B.S. degree, or be in their senior year of medical school. Foreign medical graduates must comply with all requirements of the Accreditation Committee for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) and must obtain certification from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) by the time of rank-list submission.' The UF GME Housestaff Recruitment, Selection, Eligibility and Appointment Policy (rev. 9/12/2024), section V.a, lists appointment eligibility as graduation from one of: '(i) United States or Canadian medical school accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME); (ii) United States college of osteopathic medicine accredited by the American Osteopathic Association; (iii) Medical school outside the United States or Canade [sic] with: 1. A valid certificate from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) and have a passing score for Step 1, Step 2, and Step 3, as applicable, of the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) or hold a full and unrestricted license to practice medicine in the United States licensing jurisdiction in which the program is located.' AMBIGUITY FLAGGED PER CONTRACT: the LCME branch does not enumerate Puerto Rico. It also contains no wording that would exclude a US territory, and the operative test is 'United States ... medical school accredited by the LCME', which Universidad Central del Caribe satisfies. The residual risk is clerical (a screener mis-sorting a Puerto Rico school into the foreign-graduate branch), not policy-based. A second institutional note: the same policy includes 'Selective Service Registration (Male Applicants Only) - As part of the program, Housestaff may be required to rotate through the VA hospital', confirming the VA rotation is an institutional expectation; it does not apply to Alejandra.

value.formal_designation: THREE designations verified against the awarding bodies' own listings, plus one distinct research award. (1) PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Parkinson's Foundation's own Global Care Network listing reads verbatim 'FL- University of Florida, Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases' and states 'The Parkinson's Foundation has designated 59 Centers of Excellence around the world, including 46 in the U.S and 13 internationally. These designated Centers of Excellence must meet and maintain rigorous care, clinical research, professional training, community education and outreach criteria.' The only other Florida entries are University of Miami and University of South Florida Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center. FORM OF THE AWARD: this is a single-site institutional designation. The same page defines the separate multi-site construct: 'A Network of Excellence is comprised of multiple, independent medical sites that together provide high-quality, patient-centered and multi-disciplinary care to people with PD within a specific country or region.' UF is listed as a Center, not as part of a Network. (2) PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION RESEARCH CENTER OF EXCELLENCE - A SEPARATE AND DIFFERENTLY SHAPED AWARD. The Foundation's own research-centers page lists five: Columbia University Medical Center; Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai; University of Florida 'in collaboration with Emory University'; University of Michigan 'in collaboration with The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center'; and Yale School of Medicine, funded at $500,000 annually for four years ($2 million per center). This is a MULTI-INSTITUTION RESEARCH GRANT, not a site care designation, and it must not be conflated with item (1). (3) TOURETTE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Tourette Association's own Centers of Excellence Locations page lists 'University of Florida Health (Gainesville, Florida)', 'Directors: Irene A. Malaty, MD and Carol A. Mathews, MD', 'Coordinator: Heather Simpson, OTD, OTR/L', and states 'The UF Health Tourette Center of Excellence is comprised of two world-renowned clinical care centers. The Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases (FIND) and the Center for OCD, Anxiety and Related Disorders (COARD)...'. The TAA page lists 21 Centers of Excellence and uses the phrase 'Center of Excellence (CofE)'. (4) HDSA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Huntington's Disease Society of America's own page is titled 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Florida' and gives the site as 'UF Health Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases, Gainesville, FL 32608', 'Director: Nikolaus McFarland, MD, PhD'. CUREPSP CENTER OF CARE: searched and NOT established - no CurePSP listing naming UF was opened, and UF's own pages do not claim one. The program does hold an endowed professorship in PSP/atypical parkinsonism (McFarland), which is not a designation.
value.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: This is the rare case where institutional capability and resident exposure line up. The institutional capability is exceptional: a 25,000-square-foot interdisciplinary Fixel Institute, 12 movement-disorders neurology faculty, a 2-year in-house fellowship, an NIH T32, the DBS Think Tank, and four independently verified third-party designations. But the distinguishing fact for Alejandra is that movement disorders is one of only five ASTERISKED SELECTIVE rotations - one month is required of every resident, not merely available. The residency overview page also places residents at the Fixel Institute by name as a training site ('residents care for a broad population of patients at our two affiliated teaching hospitals: Shands/UF Health and the Malcom Randall VA Medical Center, as well as the Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases'), and offers optional 'participation in deep brain stimulation cases in the operating room'. A movement-disorders APD (Dr. Rawls) sits in residency leadership. COUNTERWEIGHT, reported plainly: across the five published graduating classes (2022-2026, 40 graduates) exactly two entered movement disorders fellowships - Leonid Gozman (class of 2026, University of Pennsylvania) and Marcos Santana Firme (class of 2025, Emory University) - and NEITHER entered UF's own movement disorders fellowship. The program publishes no current movement fellow roster, so fellows_in_post is null.
value.summary: Movement disorders is the strongest identifiable asset of this program and is backed by four independently verified third-party designations at the Norman Fixel Institute, 12 movement-disorders faculty, a 2-year in-house fellowship and an NIH T32 - and crucially, a one-month movement-disorders rotation is REQUIRED of every resident, not optional.

value.formal_designation: NMSS COMPREHENSIVE CARE CENTER - PROGRAM SELF-CLAIM, NOT CONFIRMED AGAINST THE AWARDING BODY. The claim appears verbatim on UF's own MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship page: 'The National MS Society (NMSS) estimates that over 20,000 persons with MS live in Florida. Our center offers highly coordinated, competent and accessible care to over 2,000 individuals with MS and is recognized as a Comprehensive Care Center by the NMSS.' I could not corroborate this against the National MS Society's own current listing: the NMSS provider directory at nationalmssociety.org/resources/get-support/find-doctors-and-resources is rendered entirely through a Salesforce Experience Cloud application (nmss.my.site.com), returning 2.2 MB of HTML containing about 1,600 characters of text and no server-rendered center list, and no public JSON endpoint was available; that is an access boundary I did not attempt to bypass.
