IMPORTANT CROSS-CAMPUS FINDING: the only NMSS-authored page I could open naming a 'UF' comprehensive MS center is the retired National MS Society North Florida chapter page 'NMSS Affliated Comprehensive MS Centers: UF Hospital', which names 'UF Medical Center', Jacksonville, and states 'The Comprehensive MS Center at Shands Jacksonville is dedicated to diagnosing, treating and educating MS patients, as well as conduction clinical drug trails and researching new treatment techniques.' with a Jacksonville, FL 32256 address. That page now 301-redirects to the generic NMSS find-a-provider tool; the archived copy is dated 2022-01-21. That designation belongs to UF Health Jacksonville / UF College of Medicine Jacksonville (ACGME 1801112154), a DIFFERENT campus and a DIFFERENT residency program, and must not be credited to this Gainesville program. The Gainesville claim is therefore recorded as PARTIALLY_VERIFIED at the level of the designation while everything else in this domain is verified.
value.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The institutional capability is real and independently substantiated: a named MS Program with a dedicated Fixel Institute clinic, an endowed MS research professorship, a one-year in-house fellowship with a published fellow history, over 2,000 MS patients under care, and a fellowship curriculum with an explicit health-inequities focus. But resident exposure is weaker than in movement disorders in two measurable ways. First, the MS/neuroimmunology rotation is an ELECTIVE, not one of the five required asterisked selectives. Second, the faculty complement is two physicians against twelve in movement disorders, and MS is not its own division - it sits inside the combined 'Neuromuscular/General Neurology/Multiple Sclerosis/Headache' division, whereas Movement Disorders & Neurorestoration is a standalone division. AGAINST THAT, the strongest pro-MS evidence at this program is a graduate-outcome signal that runs the OPPOSITE way from the faculty counts: across the five published classes (2022-2026), three graduates entered MS/neuroimmunology fellowships - Karina Maria Rodriguez (class of 2026, Neuroimmunology Fellowship, University of Florida), Elsa Rodriguez (class of 2023, MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship, University of Florida) and Aisha Elfasi (class of 2023, MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship, Johns Hopkins, now faculty at USF) - MORE than the two who entered movement disorders fellowships, and two of the three entered UF's OWN MS fellowship, which no graduate did for the movement fellowship. There is also direct residency-leadership representation: Dr. Montalvo Perero is simultaneously an Associate Program Director of the residency and of the MS fellowship, and she and Dr. Rempe both have UF-documented Spanish.
value.summary: MS/neuroimmunology is genuinely built out at UF Gainesville - a named MS Program at the Fixel Institute, an endowed MS research chair, a one-year in-house fellowship, over 2,000 MS patients - but it is a two-physician faculty, it is not its own division, and the resident rotation is an elective rather than a required selective. The 'NMSS Comprehensive Care Center' label is the program's own claim and could not be confirmed against the National MS Society's own current listing.

The correct state for Gainesville is UNCORROBORATED BEHIND AN ACCESS BOUNDARY - not disproven. Status remains PARTIALLY_VERIFIED, which was the right call; only the reasoning is corrected.

summary: The program publishes complete named placement lists for five consecutive graduating classes (40 graduates), and 33 of 40 entered a named fellowship. Notably for Alejandra, MS/neuroimmunology placements (3, two of them into UF's own fellowship) slightly outnumber movement-disorders placements (2, neither at UF).
raw_finding: The Residency Alumni page is titled 'Residency Alumni - Past 5 years' and lists Classes of 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2022, each with exactly eight named graduates and a specific placement, so each row is a complete cohort rather than a selected example. Distribution of first fellowships across the 40 graduates: vascular neurology 9 (Pirwani 2026-UF, Hernandez 2025-UF, Johnson 2024-UF, Korenblit 2024-UF, Tirado Castro 2024-UF, Wasserstrom 2024-Brown, Yu 2023-UF, Kincaid 2022-UF, Rohrbough 2022-UF, Metha 2022-UC Irvine - 10 counting Metha), clinical neurophysiology 6 (Alex 2026-Minnesota, Remley 2026-Mayo Jacksonville, Aboudan 2025-Miami, Figeuredo-Rivas 2024-UF, Humbert 2023-UF, Sadasivan 2023-UF), neurocritical care 5 (Patel 2026-UF, Weston 2026-UCSD, Bin Zahid 2022-Hopkins, Coffey 2022-Boston University, Nelson 2022-UF), neuromuscular 3 (Abraham 2025-UF, Vasquez 2023-UF, Jain 2022-UF), MS/neuroimmunology 3 (K.M. Rodriguez 2026-UF, E. Rodriguez 2023-UF, Elfasi 2023-Hopkins), epilepsy 2 (Farrukh 2025-Duke, Hu 2023-UT Health Houston), movement disorders 2 (Gozman 2026-Penn, Santana Firme 2025-Emory), vestibular 1 (Panic 2024-Hopkins). Sixteen of the fellowship entrants stayed at UF, consistent with the research-track page's statement that 'Residents in this track are strongly encouraged to remain at UF for fellowship in order to finalize their research projects in depth.' HONEST COUNTERWEIGHT FOR DOMAIN 16: despite UF's exceptional movement-disorders institutional profile, only two graduates in five years entered movement disorders fellowships and NEITHER entered UF's own two-year movement fellowship. Conversely the MS side, with only two faculty, placed three graduates into MS/neuroimmunology fellowships, two of them at UF. One 2023 graduate (Calvin Hu, MD) went to an epilepsy fellowship at UT Health in HOUSTON, Texas - a single data point of a UF-to-Houston pathway, offered as a fact rather than as a pattern.

FREIDA's field_program_evaluation_2019 lists 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements', 'Graduates' board certification pass rates' and 'Performance-based assessment scores (e.g. OSCE, patient or computer simulations)' as the methods by which the program evaluates itself, and field_evaluate_res_fellow_2019 lists 'Patient surveys', 'Portfolio system' and 'Objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE)' as resident evaluation methods - the registry mirrors both as 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes'. That is a statement that the program tracks pass rates, NOT a published rate. No numeric rate was found. The American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology does not publish program-level first-time pass rates publicly, and ACGME's public search is CAPTCHA-gated and was not attempted. This is recorded as RESEARCHED_NOT_PUBLIC, not as a failure or a zero.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - the program does not publish an ABPN board certification pass rate. FREIDA confirms the program tracks graduates' board pass rates internally as a program-evaluation method, but no rate is published by the program, the department, UF GME or FREIDA.

summary: A four-year categorical curriculum with unusually early neurology exposure in PGY-1 (only 8 of 12 months are internal medicine), five required one-month selectives including movement disorders, a large elective menu that includes MS/neuroimmunology, continuity clinics at both Shands and the VA, and two optional tracks (research academician, medical education).
raw_finding: From the curriculum page verbatim on PGY-1: 'Neurology interns spend 8 months on internal medicine inpatient rotations, as required by the ABPN, but the remainder of the year is spent on neurology rotations. Interns rotate on an inpatient neurology service for 1.5 months (usually Stroke, Consult and/or VA), spend 1 month in a general neurology outpatient clinic and on Epilepsy/EEG, and use the rest of the time on their choice of a wide selection of neurology electives. Although they do not yet have their own continuity clinics, they spend time with a PGY4 in clinic to gain familiarity with the longitudinal clinic process, become certified in lumbar punctures in a low-stress environment, and meet the patient population they will be caring for as residents.' On senior years: 'Residents spend 3 months over their final two years rotating on pediatric neurology and also complete their psychiatry rotation on one of the inpatient wards at the VA.' (Per contract law 2 this pediatric neurology ROTATION inside an adult program's curriculum is legitimate adult curriculum data; no Child Neurology program page was used.) THE SELECTIVE/ELECTIVE DISTINCTION, which is the single most decision-relevant curricular fact for Alejandra, verbatim: 'Residents spend one month on each selective rotation (noted with * below) over the course of the residency to ensure a well-rounded neurology education. The remainder of time may be spent on their choice of a wide variety of other electives, including:' followed by the list in which Behavioral*, Epilepsy (including EEG and Epilepsy Monitoring Unit)*, General Clinic*, Movement disorders* and Neuromuscular disease (including electromyography/nerve conduction studies)* carry asterisks and 'Multiple sclerosis/neuroimmunology' does not. On the stroke service: 'Two neurology residents (generally one junior and one senior) rotate on the vascular neurology service, led by a board-certified vascular neurologist. The team also includes fellows from our ACGME-accredited vascular neurology fellowship program, dedicated stroke ARNPs, off-service rotators from neurosurgery, anesthesia, and pediatric neurology, and medical students.' On night float: 'Two residents cover the inpatient services (with the exception of the Neuro-ICU) from 6 pm - 7 am daily and see new consults and stroke alerts.' On off-site rotations: 'Off-site rotations may be set up, provided there is sufficient lead time to obtain a formal agreement with the other institution and for the resident to obtain a state-specific training license if the rotation is outside of the state of Florida' - relevant to Alejandra because it is the published mechanism by which a Houston-area rotation could in principle be arranged. FREIDA survey_2026 corroborates: field_accredited_length 4, field_program_start_dates ['July'], field_research_rotation 'Optional', field_research_rotation_duration 0, field_special_tracks ['Research track/fellowship (non-ACGME accredited)', 'Academic or clinician educator'], field_training_outpatient_clinic 25 (percent hospital outpatient), field_train_ambulatory_nonhospit 999 (a FREIDA null/negotiable sentinel, which the registry correctly rendered as 'NGO'), field_call_schedule four entries of 'N/A' and field_beeper_home_call [99,99,99,99] (also sentinels - the actual call structure is the published night float system, not an absence of call).

value.title: A required one-month movement disorders rotation - not an optional elective
value.student_explanation: UF's curriculum page names five 'selective' rotations that every resident must complete for one month each, and Movement disorders is one of them. At many programs movement disorders is something you have to choose to seek out; here it is built into everyone's four years, so your Parkinson's and movement-disorder exposure is guaranteed rather than negotiated.

value.title: Four separately verified national movement-disorder designations at one building
value.student_explanation: The Norman Fixel Institute holds a Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence (one of 59 worldwide, one of only three in Florida alongside Miami and USF), a Tourette Association of America Center of Excellence, and an HDSA Center of Excellence for Huntington's disease. Each of these was confirmed on the awarding organization's own directory, not just on UF's website.

value.title: Both of your subspecialty interests have a residency Associate Program Director
value.student_explanation: Dr. Ashley Rawls (Stanford-trained movement disorders) and Dr. Mayra Montalvo Perero (Mayo Clinic-trained autoimmune neurology, and Director-level in the MS fellowship) are the two associate program directors of this residency. Whichever of movement disorders or MS you lean toward, the person shaping the residency has already walked that path.

value.title: Two UF residents in the last four years went into UF's own MS/neuroimmunology fellowship
value.student_explanation: The alumni page shows Elsa Rodriguez (class of 2023) and Karina Maria Rodriguez (class of 2026) both entering the University of Florida Neuroimmunology fellowship, and a third graduate going to Johns Hopkins for MS. That is a concrete, repeated in-house pathway from this residency into MS, which matters more than a brochure claim.

value.title: The two leaders of the MS program both have UF-documented Spanish
value.student_explanation: UF Health's own provider directory lists 'Additional languages: Spanish, German' for Dr. Torge Rempe, who directs the UF Health Multiple Sclerosis Program and its fellowship, and 'Additional languages: Spanish' for Dr. Montalvo Perero. If you want to use your Spanish in MS clinic, these are the attendings you would be working beside.

value.title: Virtual interviews for the 2026-2027 season - no travel cost from Houston
value.student_explanation: The program states it will conduct virtual interviews this cycle 'to ensure equity across all applicants, regardless of ability to pay for travel'. For a Florida program you are considering from Houston, that removes a flight from the interview decision entirely; the only in-person option is a voluntary, explicitly non-evaluative second-look visit in late January or early February.

value.title: A published screening philosophy that says no single number can shut you out
value.student_explanation: The application page says in so many words: 'No individual metric will preclude consideration for interview.' With your Step 2 CK result not arriving until mid-October 2026, this is the sentence that matters most - the program publishes no Step 2 requirement, no minimum score, and no rule that a score must be in hand before review or before an interview invitation.

value.title: Ten in-house fellowships in one department, including both of yours
value.student_explanation: Movement Disorders (2 years), MS & Neuroimmunology (1 year), Vascular Neurology, Epilepsy, Clinical Neurophysiology, Neurocritical Care, Neuromuscular, Behavioral Neurology and Neuropsychiatry, Headache Medicine and Critical Care EEG are all run by this same department. Sixteen of the last 40 graduates stayed at UF for fellowship, so 'staying put' is a real option rather than a theoretical one.

value.title: Unusually early neurology in the intern year
value.student_explanation: Only 8 of 12 PGY-1 months are internal medicine - the ABPN minimum - and the other four are neurology: 1.5 months on an inpatient neurology service, a month of general neurology clinic and Epilepsy/EEG, and free neurology electives. You also shadow the PGY-4 whose continuity clinic you will inherit and get certified in lumbar punctures in your first year.

value.raw_finding: WHAT WAS FOUND, and from where. (1) DOCUMENTED BILINGUAL ATTENDINGS IN ALEJANDRA'S SUBSPECIALTY. UF Health's own provider directory records 'Additional languages: Spanish, German' on the page for Torge Rempe, MD, PhD - Director of the UF Health Multiple Sclerosis Program and Program Director of the MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship - and 'Additional languages: Spanish' on the page for Mayra J. Montalvo Perero, MD, who is simultaneously Associate Program Director of this residency and Associate Program Director of the MS fellowship. These are institutional data fields on the health system's provider directory, not self-description in a narrative bio. This is genuine, non-demographic, subspecialty-aligned evidence. The same directory renders no additional-languages field for Michael S. Okun or Christopher W. Hess; provider pages for several other movement-disorders faculty (Malaty, Rawls, McFarland, Wagle Shukla) could not be located under the slugs tested, so their language status is unestablished rather than negative. One further faculty language datum: Carolina B. Maciel is listed with 'Additional languages: Portuguese', and Bhavana Patel with 'Hindi, Gujarati' - recorded for completeness, not as Spanish evidence. (2) PUBLISHED DISPARITY CURRICULA. The residency program page states: 'Understanding the environment in which we practice and our patients live has measurable benefits for patient care, and our residency training includes a longitudinal curriculum to learn the impact of local socioeconomic, demographic, and cultural factors on health and illness.' The MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship page states: 'A particular focus of the fellowship curriculum will be education in inequities in the field of MS including difficult access to healthcare and disease-modifying therapy for patients due to their socioeconomic status and ethnical background. In particular, UF's patient population includes a large number of patients that due to their geographical location and socioeconomic status have only limited access to specialized healthcare.' The fellowship also frames itself geographically: 'Due to our strategic location, our center is ideally located to address health disparities in the rural areas of North Florida.' Note that this is framed around RURAL and socioeconomic disparity, not around a Spanish-speaking or Latino population. (3) SAFETY-NET / OUTREACH SITE. The residency page states residents 'have the opportunity to give back to our community by providing neurological care on the UF Mobile Outreach Clinic.' This is a resident-accessible outreach vehicle; I could not open a UF Health page for the Mobile Outreach Clinic itself within this session, so its patient-population profile and whether it provides Spanish-language services are unestablished. WHAT WAS NOT FOUND. A department-wide search of the WordPress search API on neurology.ufl.edu returned zero results for 'bilingual'. Queries for 'Spanish' returned eight records, of which the two faculty profiles (Bruzzone Giraldez, Montalvo Perero) contain no rendered Spanish-language statement in their visible text at all, and the remainder are research publications about ethno-racially diverse cohorts. A query for 'interpreter' returned twenty records, every one of which is a false positive matching the stem 'interpret' (EEG interpretation, MRI interpretation) - there is no interpreter-service statement on the department site. No Medical Spanish curriculum, elective, or certificate exists on the residency, curriculum, tracks or GME pages. FREIDA survey_2026 has no Medical Spanish field at all and field_curriculum is an empty array, so the registry's 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: No' cannot be re-derived from the current source (see registry_reconciliation).
value.explicitly_rejected_evidence: REFUSED AS EVIDENCE, per contract laws 4 and 5: (a) Alachua County and Gainesville Hispanic-population demographics - not consulted and not counted in either direction. Gainesville's Hispanic share being smaller than South Florida's is not evidence against this program any more than Miami's share would be evidence for another. (b) Every resident and faculty surname on the roster and directory. No language, nationality, ethnicity or immigration inference was drawn from any name, including names that a careless reader would treat as Spanish-speaking. (c) Medical school country as a proxy for language. Several faculty and residents hold degrees from Spanish-language institutions (Universidad San Francisco de Quito, Universidad de la Republica, Universidade de Fortaleza, Escola de Medicina Souza Marques) and two residents' biographies state they were born in Cuba or grew up in Brazil - none of this was counted as program Spanish-language capability, because school country and personal biography are not a program service. Dr. Montalvo Perero counts ONLY because UF Health's provider directory carries an explicit Spanish language field for her, not because of her degree. (d) The department's research output on 'ethnically diverse' and 'Hispanic and non-Hispanic' Alzheimer's cohorts. This is epidemiological research, not a clinical Spanish-language service, and Alejandra would not learn Spanish clinical skills from it. (e) Any UF or UF Health institution-wide language-access or interpreter program outside the neurology residency training environment - none was located, and had one been located it would not have counted as residency-level evidence. (f) The word 'interpreter' appearing in twenty site-search results, all of which were the stem 'interpret' in an EEG or imaging context.

Alejandra would be the first UCC representation at this program. | [value relocated from `value` field, which the contract requires to be null for absence states] {"status": "RESEARCHED_NOT_FOUND", "ucc_residents": 0, "puerto_rico_school_residents": 0, "puerto_rico_schools_represented": [], "ucc_faculty": [], "puerto_rico_faculty": [], "puerto_rico_training_ties": null, "ucc_alumni": 0, "ucc_fellows": 0, "where_searched": ["All 32 current resident profile pages on neurology.ufl.edu", "The five-year Residency Alumni page (40 named graduates, classes of 2022-2026)", "The full department Faculty Directory (65 active faculty plus 3 emeritus and 4 in memoriam)", "The Movement Disorders Faculty page", "The MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship page's published fellow history (7 named fellows, 2018-2026)", "The Epilepsy Fellowship Recent Graduates page", "The department-wide WordPress search API for 'Puerto Rico', 'Caribe', 'Ponce', 'San Juan' and 'Universidad'", "Residency leadership bios on the program page"], "summary": "No Universidad Central del Caribe and no Puerto Rico medical school connection of any kind was found among current residents, five years of alumni, the 65-member faculty directory, the MS fellowship's published fellow history, or residency leadership."}
raw_finding: SEARCH METHOD AND RESULTS. The department's public WordPress search API (neurology.ufl.edu/wp-json/wp/v2/search) was queried across the whole site. 'Puerto Rico' returned ZERO results. 'Caribe' returned ZERO results. 'Ponce' returned one result, the page 'Activities Outside of Gainesville' under /living-in-gainesville/, which concerns recreation (Ponce de Leon area springs) and not Ponce Health Sciences University. 'San Juan' returned two results, neither a Puerto Rico school: the Epilepsy Fellowship Recent Graduates page, where the match is a 2023 graduate now practising at Mercy San Juan Medical Center in Carmichael, CALIFORNIA, and a Wilder Center research page. 'Universidad' returned six results - the Wilder Center affiliated-faculty page, the Neurocritical Care Lab page, the residency program page, and the profiles of Carolina B. Maciel, Mayra J. Montalvo Perero and Maria Bruzzone Giraldez; the named institutions are Universidad San Francisco de Quito (Ecuador) and Universidad de la Republica (Uruguay), neither of which is in Puerto Rico. Separately, all 32 current resident profiles were individually retrieved and read: the identified schools are Florida Atlantic, Philadelphia COM, UT Southwestern, Lincoln Memorial-DeBusk COM (x2), Kansas City University, Nova Southeastern, Geisinger Commonwealth, Touro COM, RCSI Ireland, Tsinghua, FSU, Escola de Medicina Souza Marques, Burrell COM, Texas Tech, VCOM-Carolinas, VCOM-Virginia, University of Florida (x2), FIU (x2), University of Washington, West Virginia University, VCOM-Auburn, Wake Forest, Drexel, Augusta/UGA Medical Partnership, Universidade de Fortaleza and Medical College of Georgia - no Puerto Rico school among them, and three residents' schools are unpublished (see domain 12). The 40 named graduates across the classes of 2022-2026 are listed with placements but not medical schools, so a graduate's Puerto Rico origin could not be excluded from that page alone; however the site-wide 'Puerto Rico' and 'Caribe' searches returning zero results covers alumni pages as well. The MS fellowship's seven named past fellows (Misbah Azeem, Brinda Bhaskar, Freddy Escobar, Elsa Rodriguez, Laura Snider, Carlos Vervloet Sollero, Buse Sengul) carry no Puerto Rico affiliation on that page. The 65-entry faculty directory contains no Puerto Rico institution. CONTRACT COMPLIANCE NOTE: I deliberately did NOT treat any surname on the roster, alumni list or faculty directory as evidence of a Puerto Rico connection, in either direction - several alumni and faculty names would invite that inference and law 4 forbids it. This is recorded as RESEARCHED_NOT_FOUND, not as an affirmative institutional 'no': the program simply publishes no Puerto Rico or UCC tie, and for the 40 alumni it publishes no medical schools at all, so an unpublished tie cannot be excluded with certainty. ALEJANDRA'S ELIGIBILITY IS UNAFFECTED: Universidad Central del Caribe is LCME-accredited and located in the United States, which places her inside branch (i) of the UF GME eligibility policy ('United States or Canadian medical school accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education'), not the foreign-graduate/ECFMG branch. She is a US MD graduate for every eligibility purpose here.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - no Universidad Central del Caribe or Puerto Rico medical school connection was found among current residents, five years of published alumni, the 65-member faculty directory, the MS fellowship's fellow history, or residency leadership. Note that the program does not publish medical schools for its alumni, so an unpublished tie cannot be ruled out.

summary: The only timing rule the program and its sponsoring institution publish is that Steps 1 and 2 must be passed before the residency starts. Nothing published gates initial application review, interview invitation or ranking on a Step 2 result, and FREIDA records Step 2 as not required before interview.
raw_finding: See the structured step2_timing record at the top level of this dossier for the full determination. Decisive verbatim language, Jackson GME neurology page, Program Requirements: 'All residency applicants must successfully complete United States Medical Licensing Examination or Comprehensive Medical Licensing Examination Steps 1 and 2 before the start of the residency program. USMLE or COMLEX Step 3 must be successfully completed prior to the start of the clinical neurology curriculum in the second year of the residency.' FREIDA survey_2026 (received 2026-06-12): field_usmle_step2_req_int = False and field_usmle_step_2_required = False. Counter-pressure: the program's Application Information page, verbatim: 'The application requires a personal statement, your medical school transcript, USMLE scores for steps 1 and 2, three letters of reference (a 4th "chair" letter is optional), and the Medical Student Performance Evaluation (MSPE).' That sentence is a list of application contents, not a timing rule, and the contract forbids inferring timing from a non-timing statement; it is preserved as a conflict rather than promoted to the final code. SEPARATE and material scheduling finding, program FAQ verbatim: 'We suggest that all your application materials are submitted through ERAS by September 15th. The absolute deadline for completed applications is the 15th of November, although earlier applications are given priority. We typically have filled our available slots by October 15th.' Interview slots filling by about October 15 is an application-timing pressure that exists independently of any Step 2 rule, and Alejandra's result is expected mid-October 2026.
conflict_notes: UNRESOLVED after adversarial review. Two primary-tier readings conflict and neither can be dismissed: (a) Jackson GME publishes only a before-start rule ('must successfully complete ... Steps 1 and 2 before the start of the residency program') and FREIDA's survey sets field_usmle_step2_req_int = False, which together imply no interview-stage gate; (b) FREIDA's own public page renders, under the heading 'Medical Exam Licensing Requirements for Interview Consideration', 'Must Have Passed USMLE Step 2 CK => Yes' for both US MD and IMG applicants, with field_usmle_us_md_pass_ck = True, and the canonical registry carries 'US MD Step 2 Required = Yes'. Two sibling Florida programs coded that identical rendering AS a barrier. Treat as unresolved and confirm with the coordinator before relying on either reading.

summary: Two official sources give different deadlines: the program's own pages say the absolute ERAS deadline is November 15, while the Jackson GME page says applications are accepted from September 15 until November 1. The program separately notes it typically fills its interview slots by about October 15, and interviews are virtual from early November to late January.
raw_finding: Program Application Information page, verbatim: 'Application deadline thru ERAS is November 15th, but the earlier the application is in, the better.' Program FAQ, verbatim: 'We suggest that all your application materials are submitted through ERAS by September 15th. The absolute deadline for completed applications is the 15th of November, although earlier applications are given priority. We typically have filled our available slots by October 15th. If you wish to cancel your interview, we ask that you provide us with notice 7 days prior.' Jackson GME neurology page, verbatim: 'Deadline: Applications are accepted from September 15 until November 1. Interviews are conducted from November to January.' Registry stored 'Application Deadline: 2025-11-01', matching Jackson GME and one cycle old. BOTH SIDES PRESERVED - the conservative planning date is November 1, and the early-October practical pressure is stronger than either. Interviews page, verbatim: 'Interviews for invited applicants will be held virtually and take place from early November through end of January.' The interview day is structured with a Thursday evening Zoom welcome, morning and afternoon groups, 4 interviews per candidate, Grand Rounds at 12:15 PM and Chairman's remarks at 1:30 PM; virtual tours are offered in lieu of a campus tour. Also verbatim: 'When invited for the interview, applicants are encouraged to indicate any special clinical or research interests so that we can try to match you with interviews, if possible.' This is a concrete, actionable hook for Alejandra's Movement Disorders and MS interests. Letters: program page says 'three letters of reference (a 4th "chair" letter is optional)'; FREIDA field_min_letters_req = 3, field_max_letters_req = 4, field_chair_letter = False, field_other_letters_req_ind = True with field_other_letters_detail = 'Those that know you best.' Program Statistics: '~1000' applications, '100-120' invited interviews, 7 interview dates; FAQ says 'over 950 applications, and from these we select (~10%) for interviews'. FREIDA survey_2026 field_interviews_conducted = 90 and field_second_look_ind = True. Signaling: Neurology participates in ERAS program signaling for the 2027 season with 8 signals per applicant (AAMC, Neurology row: 'Neurology | 8'); this is Alejandra's cycle. The program itself publishes no statement about how it uses signals, and FREIDA field_nxt_supplement = False. FREIDA field_participates_in_eras = True, which supersedes the registry's incorrect 'ERAS Participates: No'.
conflict_notes: Program pages state an absolute ERAS deadline of November 15; the sponsoring institution's GME page states an application window closing November 1; the registry stored 2025-11-01. Neither official source was silently preferred. Separately, the registry and FREIDA field_interview_type record an In-Person interview format, which the program's own Interviews page contradicts by stating interviews are held virtually.

summary: The program's own current FREIDA survey reports 48.9% US MD, 6.7% DO and 44.4% IMG, which resolve to 22 US MD, 3 DO and 20 IMG over a denominator of 45. The 20 IMG cannot be split between offshore-Caribbean and other-IMG because no individual schools are published, so they are carried as unknown.
raw_finding: FREIDA survey_2026 for this program (field_date_received 2026-06-12): field_pct_usmd = '48.9', field_pct_do = '6.7', field_pct_img = '44.4', field_pct_female = '62.2', field_pct_male = '37.8', field_total_positions = 45. These resolve exactly over 45: 22/45 = 48.9%, 3/45 = 6.7%, 20/45 = 44.4%, 28/45 = 62.2%, 17/45 = 37.8%. CORROBORATION: the survey's 3 DO matches exactly the three DO degrees on the published 2025-2026 named roster (Arvelo, Fasciano, Hughes), which is meaningful independent support for the survey's DO count. REGISTRY IS STALE HERE: the registry's 'US MD: 56.8%; DO: 4.5%; IMG: 38.6%' and 'Resident Gender Female Percent 56.8%' resolve over a denominator of 44 (25 + 2 + 17 = 44), coming from the older survey received 2025-06-18. The two cycles disagree and the newer one is used. BUCKET DISCIPLINE: the five buckets are a mutually exclusive, exhaustive partition summing to the denominator - 22 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 20 = 45. caribbean = 0 and other_img = 0 mean NOT IDENTIFIED, not 'none present'; the 20 IMG residents are held in `unknown` precisely because FREIDA reports IMG as one undifferentiated bucket and the program publishes no individual schools. Do not read caribbean = 0 as a finding that no offshore-Caribbean graduate trains here. COMPLEMENT VS CENSUS: approved complement is 45 and the named 2025-2026 roster census is 48; the composition denominator here is the complement-based FREIDA figure, not the census, and the two are deliberately not blended. The registry's per-year row 'Residents Per Year: PGY-1: 8; PGY-2: 12; PGY-3: 13; PGY-4: 12' equals FREIDA field_program_size [8, 12, 13, 12], which sums to 45 and is the complement distribution - it does NOT match the live roster's 12/13/12/11. ucc_residents and puerto_rico_school_residents are overlay counts and are NOT added into the five buckets; both are reported as 0 in alejandra_signals meaning none could be identified, since no resident's school is published.

summary: Movement Disorders is a genuinely strong, independently verifiable division: nine faculty, a two-position fellowship, a required two-week PGY-3 rotation plus elective time, and two designations confirmed against the awarding bodies' own listings. The residency program director is himself a movement disorders specialist.
raw_finding: TESTED INDEPENDENTLY OF MS, NOT ASSUMED FROM INSTITUTIONAL REPUTATION. Division page verbatim: 'The Division of Movement Disorders is a subsection of the Department of Neurology within the Leonard M. Miller School of Medicine (MSM) of the University of Miami (UM). The Division was founded in 1984 by Dr. William J Weiner who served as Division Chief until 2000, followed by Dr. William Koller. The division was been under the direction of Dr. Carlos Singer from2002 to 2020. He was succeeded by the current Division Chief, Dr. Ihtsham Haq.' [sic] Also verbatim: 'The center employs six fellowship-trained movement disorders faculty, one Advanced Registered Nurse Practitioner, one Licensed Clinical Social Worker, four study coordinators, and a support staff of eight.' DESIGNATION LANGUAGE, QUOTED VERBATIM FROM THE PAGE I OPENED: 'The Center received the designation as a Center of Excellence from the Parkinson's Foundation in 2007. Since then additional designations have included the Huntington Disease Center of Excellence and the Wilson Disease Center of Excellence. The center also partners closely with the Department of Psychiatry's Tourette Center of Excellence.' AWARDING-BODY VERIFICATION (contract guard 8): (1) The Parkinson's Foundation's own Centers of Excellence listing includes 'University of Miami' among three Florida entries, alongside 'University of Florida, Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases' and 'University of South Florida Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center' - CONFIRMED, and note the awarding body's listing names it 'University of Miami', not 'Miller School of Medicine'. (2) The Huntington's Disease Society of America hosts a dedicated page headed verbatim 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Miami' naming Carlos Singer, MD as Director - CONFIRMED against the awarding body. (3) The Wilson Disease designation is corroborated only within UM's own content, though UM's faculty bio for Dr. Margolesky names the awarding body directly, listing him as 'Co-Director of Wilson Disease Association Center of Excellence'; I did NOT open the Wilson Disease Association's own directory, so this is program-asserted with the awarding body named, not independently verified. (4) The Jackson GME page makes a much broader claim, verbatim: 'Our department is designated as a Center of Excellence for: Multiple Sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Epilepsy, Huntington's disease, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Tourette syndrome, Multiple System Atrophy, Ataxia, Wilson Disease, and Dementia with Lewy Bodies research'. That sentence names no awarding bodies. I verified only Parkinson's Foundation and HDSA against awarding bodies and I explicitly do NOT assert a CurePSP Center of Care, a National Ataxia Foundation center, an LBDA Research Center of Excellence or any NAEC epilepsy level, none of which I confirmed and none of which the program names as such. FACULTY: Ihtsham ul Haq, M.D., FAAN - Division Chief, Cornfeld-Hurowitz Endowed Chair in Movement Disorders, Associate Director of the Evelyn F. McKnight Brain Institute; Carlos Singer, M.D. - Professor of Neurology; Division Chief 2002-2020; Director, HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Miami; Corneliu Luca, M.D., Ph.D. - Professor of Clinical Neurology; Director, Movement Disorders Fellowship Program; Jason Margolesky, M.D., FAAN - Associate Professor; Neurology Residency Program Director; Director, Functional Movement Disorders Clinic; Vice Chair for Education; Co-Director, Wilson Disease Association Center of Excellence; Danielle Shpiner, M.D. - Associate Professor of Clinical Neurology; Associate Program Director, Movement Disorders Fellowship; Henry Moore, M.D. - Associate Professor of Clinical Neurology; Matthew Feldman, M.D. - Assistant Professor of Clinical Neurology; Zufe Rizvi, M.D. - Assistant Professor of Clinical Neurology; Yusen Wu, Ph.D. - Research Assistant Professor of Neurology. The fellowship page describes a '1 or 2-year fellowship', first year 80% clinical / 20% scholarly, second year 50/50, with training in 'botulinum toxin injections, deep brain stimulation patient selection, interoperative assessment, and post-operative programming', and states 'The University of Miami participates in the Movement Disorders Fellowship (MODIF) Match Network conducted by SFMatch.' It names six board-certified movement disorders neurologists running general movement disorders clinics: Haq, Singer, Moore, Luca, Margolesky and Shpiner. RESIDENT EXPOSURE, distinguished from institutional capability: the Jackson GME Year 3 curriculum states residents 'will complete 2-week Neuro-oncology and Movement Disorder rotations', which is a REQUIRED rotation, and the UM Core Curriculum PGY-3 elective list separately includes 'movement disorders' among available electives. So a resident gets a required two-week block plus the option of dedicated elective time - concrete exposure, not merely a department that treats Parkinson's disease. MENTORSHIP SIGNAL: the residency Program Director, Jason Margolesky MD FAAN, is a movement disorders specialist who directs the Functional Movement Disorders Clinic, trained in this very program (UM MD 2012, UM/Jackson neurology residency 2016 as administrative Chief Resident, UM/Jackson movement disorders fellowship 2017) and is Vice Chair for Education.

summary: MS and neuroimmunology is independently strong: a dedicated MS Center of Excellence clinic with six MS neurologists, a two-position fellowship, 17 active MS clinical trials, and an MS curriculum that residents receive. One of the residency's associate program directors is an MS specialist.
raw_finding: TESTED INDEPENDENTLY OF MOVEMENT DISORDERS. The Texas finding that these two domains were systematically inverted at a single program does NOT reproduce here: both are strong, and each was verified from its own division pages, its own faculty roster and its own fellowship listing. MS Division page verbatim: 'The Multiple Sclerosis Center of Excellence is a National MS Society of South Florida affiliated program which offers services in a state-of-the-art clinic. Patients are seen by one of six MS neurologists by appointment. An infusion lab where patients receive intravenous drug therapy and neurological imaging that uses MRI to track the disease are available.' MS Education page verbatim: 'We provide excellent care to patients with MS and other neuroimmunological disorders at our dedicated MS Center of Excellence at the University of Miami, a site by the National MS Society.' [the sentence is garbled in the source, apparently omitting a word such as 'recognized'] DESIGNATION DISCIPLINE - THIS IS THE HIGH-CONSEQUENCE POINT: 'MS Center of Excellence' is the University of Miami's OWN branding for its clinic. The only affiliation language the program publishes is 'a National MS Society of South Florida affiliated program'. I searched for, and did NOT find, any National MS Society designation of this center as a 'Center for Comprehensive MS Care' or a 'Partners in MS Care' partner; no NMSS page confirming either designation for the University of Miami surfaced. I therefore assert NO formal NMSS designation. Anyone reading this dossier should treat 'MS Center of Excellence' as institutional branding plus a stated Society affiliation, NOT as an NMSS Comprehensive Care Center. FELLOWSHIP: Fellowship Programs page lists 'Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology, 2 positions, Program Director: Dr. Silvia Delgado, Apply via SF Match'. The MS Education page describes 'one to two -year advanced training', requires that 'fellows must have completed an ACGME-accredited program in neurology and be eligible for a full Florida Medical license', covers MS, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, neuromyelitis optica, ADEM, CNS sarcoidosis and CNS lupus/Sjogren's, teaches intrathecal baclofen testing and botulinum toxin for spasticity, and states verbatim 'Currently, the division conducts 17 clinical trials in MS.' Teaching hospitals listed for the fellowship: 'University of Miami Hospital, Sethi Desai Medical Center, Jackson Memorial Hospital, and Veterans Affairs Medical Center.' RESIDENT EXPOSURE, distinguished from institutional capability: the MS fellowship curriculum requires fellows to 'Teach medical students and residents one-on-one or in a lecture-hall setting, and assist Neurology Chief Residents with the MS curriculum' - direct evidence that an MS curriculum exists inside the residency. The UM Core Curriculum PGY-3 elective list includes 'multiple sclerosis'; the Jackson GME Year 3 description lists 'neuroimmunology' among electives; and the Jackson GME education section names 'biweekly neuromuscular and neuroimmunology conferences'. Unlike Movement Disorders, MS is an ELECTIVE rather than a required rotation, which is a real difference between the two domains and is stated rather than smoothed over. FACULTY: Silvia R. summary: No numeric ABPN board pass rate is published for this program. The program asserts a consistently excellent pass rate without giving a figure, and FREIDA confirms it uses board pass rates internally as a program-evaluation measure.
raw_finding: Jackson GME Program Director's Welcome, verbatim: 'We are proud of our team's contributions to our education program, reflected in our consistently excellent board pass rate and fellowship match records.' That is an unquantified claim and is reported as such - it is NOT evidence of any particular rate. Searched the Program Statistics page (which publishes applications, interviews, positions, USMLE ranges and fellowship placements but no board pass rate), the Program Overview, Program Strengths, the Jackson GME program page, and general web search for a UM/Jackson neurology ABPN pass rate; nothing program-specific was found. ABPN publishes aggregate national figures rather than per-program rates, so the absence here is normal for the specialty and is not a mark against the program.

value.salary_source: Jackson Health System GME (employer of record)

summary: Jackson Health System pays the residents under a collective bargaining agreement with the Committee of Interns and Residents. The current 2026-2027 scale is $73,622 at PGY-1 rising to $83,778 at PGY-4, with 28 days off, 14 sick days, a $1,500 meal card and a $2,500 professional allowance.
raw_finding: SALARY - REGISTRY IS ONE CYCLE STALE AND SO IS FREIDA. Jackson Health System's own GME salary page publishes for 2026-2027, verbatim: 'PGY-1: $73,622 / PGY-2: $76,542 / PGY-3: $79,661 / PGY-4: $83,778 / PGY-5: $87,091 / PGY-6 $90,743 / PGY-7: $94,540 / PGY-8*: $99,515' with PGY-8 limited to specific ACGME-accredited specialties such as neurosurgery and plastic surgery. The registry stored 70790 / 73598 / 76597 / 80556, and FREIDA survey_2026 STILL reports field_first_year_salary = 70790 and field_graduate_year_statistics salaries of 70790 / 73598 / 76597 / 80556 despite being received 2026-06-12 - so the employer's own HR page is fresher than the program's FREIDA answer. The employer page is authoritative for pay and is used here; the registry figures are marked STALE. Additional compensation, verbatim: 'a $75 biweekly pay supplement' for all housestaff; chief residents receive an annual stipend of $2,900 plus $700 for committee participation. Salaries 'follow our collective bargaining agreement with the Committee of Interns and Residents' - the residents are union-represented, a material fact absent from the registry entirely. TIME OFF: Jackson lists vacation as '28 days annually (includes holidays and weekends)' and 14 sick days including one designated wellness day. This confirms the registry's Vacation 28 and Sick Days 14, but the parenthetical matters - 28 days inclusive of holidays and weekends is materially less generous than 28 weekdays, and the program's own Core Curriculum page describes '4 weeks of vacation - to be taken in 2-week blocks' in both PGY-2 and PGY-3. ALLOWANCES: the program FAQ, verbatim: 'Each resident receives $2500 per year as an educational allowance, and $1500 per year for meals... In addition, three new lab coats and scrubs are also provided each year.' Jackson's page corroborates: '$1,500 per year' meal card, '$2,500' annual professional allowance, three lab coats and scrubs yearly. The registry recorded 'Educational Stipend: On-call meal allowance' and 'Technology Allowance: On-call meal allowance', which is a field-mapping error - FREIDA's field_program_offers_2021 list contains the string 'On-call meal allowance' and the registry copied it into three unrelated benefit fields. The real educational allowance is $2,500/year. INSURANCE: Jackson First HMO medical at zero employee premium; Delta Dental free; $50,000 basic life at no cost; long-term disability covering 60% of monthly earnings up to $3,500/month; 'Unlimited, no-cost access' to therapists via a Tava and Aetna partnership. FREIDA benefit fields for this program: group life and disability 'Fully Paid by Institution'; major medical for residents, dependents and domestic partners, outpatient and inpatient mental health, and dental all 'Institution & Resident Share Cost' - the FREIDA sharing labels for medical and dental are contradicted by Jackson's own page stating zero-premium HMO and free dental, so Jackson's page is preferred. Other confirmed FREIDA values: field_leave_paid = 42 days paid family/medical leave (field_leave_unpaid = 999, a null sentinel the registry correctly rendered as negotiable); field_allows_moonlighting = True; on-site child care and placement assistance listed in field_program_offers_2021; field_salary_paid_nonprofit = 'Yes'.
conflict_notes: Jackson Health System's 2026-2027 published scale ($73,622 PGY-1) supersedes both the registry's $70,790 and FREIDA survey_2026's $70,790, the latter being stale despite a June 2026 receipt date. FREIDA labels medical and dental as cost-shared; Jackson's own page states a zero-premium HMO option and free dental.

summary: PGY-1 is an internal medicine internship with two months of neurology; clinical neurology runs PGY-2 to PGY-4, with continuity clinics at Jackson's Ambulatory Care Center and the Miami VA throughout. PGY-3 includes a required two-week Movement Disorders rotation, PGY-4 residents serve as chief residents, and a competitive research track offers protected blocks in all three neurology years.
raw_finding: PGY-1, Jackson GME verbatim: 'Trainees will predominantly rotate with our internal medicine colleagues through inpatient and outpatient settings. Two months will be spent on Neurology rotations including the inpatient consult service, the inpatient stroke service and the neuroscience intensive care unit.' PGY-2, UM Core Curriculum verbatim: 'The PGY-2 Neurology resident schedule is the most intense of the training program with q4 call while on the JMH stroke and NH services.' Published sample PGY-2 block schedule: 4-6 weeks Neuro-critical Care at Jackson (eight 12-hour shifts); 4-6 weeks Epilepsy (EMU and clinic), no call; 4-6 weeks VA inpatient, no call; 4-6 weeks Jackson inpatient Neurology, no call; 4-6 weeks UHealth Tower consults, no call; 10-12 weeks Stroke at Jackson on night float with 12-hour shifts; 6-8 weeks night float at UHT (alternating one week on, one week off, six nights per on-week); 2 weeks Headache; 2-4 weeks elective/research; 2-4 weeks Neuromuscular; 4 weeks vacation in 2-week blocks. Jackson GME adds that PGY-2 residents 'will start working in their outpatient continuity clinics at the Jackson Memorial Hospital Ambulatory Care Center and at Miami VA Healthcare System outpatient clinics.' PGY-3 sample schedule: 4-6 weeks Neurocritical Care; 4-6 weeks Elective/Research; 4-6 weeks VA consults (home call split with PGY-4); 16-18 weeks Jackson consults on night float roughly 1 in 4 weeks; 4-6 weeks UHealth Tower vascular neurology, no call; 4-6 weeks Pediatric Neurology with home call split among 2-3 residents; 2 weeks neuro-oncology; 2 weeks cognitive neurology; 4 weeks vacation. Jackson GME's Year 3 description adds verbatim that 'The PGY3 resident will cover the stroke service at UHT and will complete 2-week Neuro-oncology and Movement Disorder rotations' - a REQUIRED movement disorders block. Elective list, UM Core Curriculum verbatim: 'A wide range of elective rotations are available including neuroradiology, neuropathology, neurorehabilitation, neuro-ophthalmology, neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, psychiatry, neurophysiology, sleep medicine, multiple sclerosis, movement disorders, and basic neuroscience research.' PGY-4, Jackson GME verbatim: 'Fourth-year residents serve as chief residents with a greater degree of independence in formulating plans for patients encountered and have a primary responsibility for the education of the junior residents and students on the team. Residents will complete their pediatric neurology rotations, a rotation in psychiatry, neuro-oncology, and epilepsy. The PGY4 will complete 1-2 weeks of UHT night float and the remaining time will be elective rotations.' Note the UM Core Curriculum page publishes detailed sample schedules only for PGY-2 and PGY-3; the PGY-4 description comes from the Jackson GME page. The pediatric neurology rotation is legitimate ADULT-program curriculum content (a required rotation for adult residents) and is not imported from UM's separate Child Neurology program. CALL, Jackson GME: 'Year 1 (Internship) - NSICU night float, 3 nights x 2 weeks and 0-2 weeks of VA night float. Year 2 - Overnight call every fourth night for approximately five out of 12 months. NSICU night float, 4 nights x 2 weeks. Year 3 - NSICU night float, 4 nights x 3 weeks, and about four to five weeks of night float (7 p.m. to 9 a.m., Monday to Saturday) on the neurohospitalist (consult) service. Year 4 - Night float coverage for consult team approximately 2-3 times throughout the year (7 p.m. to 9 a.m.) on Sunday night.' This supersedes the registry's 'Call Schedule: Year 1: N/A; Year 2: N/A; Year 3: N/A; Year 4: N/A', which merely reproduced FREIDA's unanswered field_call_schedule. DIDACTICS, Jackson GME verbatim: 'Attendance is expected for all "academic half-day" (AHD) didactics (topically organized in blocks), Grand Rounds, Journal Club, and our quarterly M&M conferences. Other educational offerings can be attended when available: weekly "morning reports" and ICU conferences, biweekly neuromuscular and neuroimmunology conferences.' FREIDA field_special_features verbatim: 'Our robust didactic curriculum features simulation-based and lumbar puncture infusion training for ALS.' Jackson GME: 'Our grant-funded simulation curriculum provides residents with expansive, hands-on training in high-stakes neurologic care through immersive, skills-based educational experiences.' RESEARCH TRACK (RCRT): 1 resident selected per year; protected research blocks PGY-2 1-2, PGY-3 1-2, PGY-4 2; application at end of PGY-1 with an April 1 deadline via CV, application form and personal statement; evaluation committee named as Gillian Gordon-Perue MD FAAN (founder and Research APD), Tatjana Rundek MD PhD (Vice Chair for Research), Jason Margolesky MD FAAN (Program Director), Ayham Alkhachroum MD, Leticia Tornes, Hannah Gardner PhD plus the research chief resident. Curriculum adds linear and logistic regression, survival analysis, practical statistics, causal inference and advanced clinical trials; milestones run from project identification in PGY-2 to peer-reviewed publication in PGY-4, with K08 application encouraged. FREIDA field_special_tracks = ['Research track/fellowship (non-ACGME accredited)'] and field_research_rotation = 'Optional'. HOURS: FREIDA field_avg_hours_on_duty_y1 = 60, field_max_hours_on_duty_y1 = 24, field_avg_24hr_off_duty_y1 = 1.50, field_night_float = True, field_night_float_y1 = True. Registry's 'Structured Didactic Activities PGY1 Hours: 5' is superseded by field_avg_hrs_lecture_conf_y1 = 4 in the newer survey. Registry's 'Hospital Outpatient Percent: 30' is superseded by field_training_outpatient_clinic = 20.
conflict_notes: Movement Disorders appears as a REQUIRED 2-week PGY-3 rotation on the Jackson GME curriculum page but only as an elective on the UM Core Curriculum page. Both are reported. Registry's outpatient percentage (30) and PGY-1 didactic hours (5) are superseded by the newer FREIDA survey (20 and 4).

summary: Eleven student-ready reasons are recorded in the why_this_program array at the top level of this dossier, each tied to a named clinic, a specific rotation, a designation verified against its awarding body, or a published number.
raw_finding: See the top-level why_this_program array. Every item is anchored to a specific verifiable mechanism rather than to atmosphere: the program director's own movement disorders subspecialty and his Functional Movement Disorders Clinic; a required two-week PGY-3 Movement Disorders rotation; a Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence and an HDSA Center of Excellence, both confirmed against the awarding bodies' own listings; an MS-fellowship-trained associate program director; an MS clinic with six MS neurologists and 17 active clinical trials; ten in-house fellowships totalling 24 positions; a research track with quantified protected blocks; a continuity clinic at a named county safety-net site carrying over 4,500 adult neurology visits a year; three hospitals with published bed counts on one campus; a published 31-institution fellowship placement list that includes University of Texas/Houston; and two distinct entry routes both fully filled in every Match year 2022-2026. The banned formulations 'diverse patient population', 'strong academics', 'supportive faculty' and 'collegial environment' were deliberately excluded even though the program's own Program Strengths page and FREIDA special-features text use several of them - specifically 'Wide spectrum of neurological disorders across diverse patient populations', 'A close-knit atmosphere among faculty and residents' and 'Multicultural city and high-quality lifestyle'. summary: The program-level Spanish evidence here is real but thin. Residents hold their continuity clinic at a county safety-net hospital whose published mission is to treat every Miami-Dade resident regardless of ability to pay, and the program checks a FREIDA box for non-English language instruction, but no named Spanish-language clinic, no described Medical Spanish curriculum and no bilingual track is published anywhere.
raw_finding: See the structured spanish_latino_clinical_relevance record at the top level. WHAT I ACCEPTED, all program- or institution-level rather than demographic: (1) SAFETY_NET_SITE WITH A SPECIFIED RESIDENT ROLE. Hospital and Clinic Sites page verbatim: 'Jackson's Ambulatory Care Clinic (the ACC) services over 4500 adult neurology outpatient visits per year and serves as our primary resident continuity clinic.' Jackson GME confirms residents work in continuity clinics at the Jackson ACC and the Miami VA in PGY-2, PGY-3 and PGY-4. Jackson Health System's own About page establishes the safety-net character verbatim: 'Jackson Health System ensures that all residents of Miami-Dade County receive a single high standard of care regardless of their ability to pay', 'Governed by the Public Health Trust, a team of citizen volunteers acting on behalf of the Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners', and 'Jackson Health System is a nonprofit academic medical system offering world-class care to any person who walks through its doors.' That is a documented public safety-net site plus a specific, recurring, three-year resident role - the strongest item available. (2) A DIVISION-LEVEL LATIN AMERICA CLINICAL ROLE. Movement Disorders Division page verbatim: 'As a leading tertiary referral center, we serve a diverse patient population from the South Florida community and beyond, establishing ourselves as the premier destination for patients from Latin America and the Caribbean seeking expert care for Parkinson's disease and related disorders.' The residency's own Program Strengths page states 'Large tertiary care center, referral center for tri-county area, Caribbean, and Central/South America', and the Jackson GME Program Director's Welcome describes faculty 'serving Miami, South Florida, the Caribbean, Latin America, and beyond'. These are program- and division-level statements about referral catchment, not city demographics - but they describe where patients come from, not a Spanish-language service or a defined resident language role, and they are weighted accordingly. (3) A PROGRAM SELF-REPORT OF LANGUAGE INSTRUCTION. FREIDA survey_2026 field_resident_fellow_offer_2019 includes the option 'Instruction in medical Spanish or other non-English language'. This is the program answering for itself about its own training environment, so it is program-level evidence and not inherited. But note carefully what it is: a checkbox whose own wording does not even specify Spanish, with no curriculum, no hours, no instructor and no description published anywhere on the program's or the department's website. The registry's flattening of this into 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: Yes' overstates it materially, and that field was wrong at 3 of 16 Texas programs, so it was verified rather than inherited. I searched the Program Overview, Program Strengths, Core Curriculum, Hospital and Clinic Sites, FAQ, Wellness, RCRT and Interviews pages and the MS and Movement Disorders division pages, and text-scanned every page I downloaded: the ONLY Spanish-language artifact found anywhere in the department's own content is a 'PD101 Symposium in Spanish' video resource on the Movement Disorders Division's Outreach and Resources page, which is patient education, not resident training. WHAT I REFUSED TO COUNT is recorded in explicitly_rejected_evidence at the top level. NET ASSESSMENT: LIMITED. Alejandra's fluent Spanish would be clinically useful at the Jackson ACC continuity clinic on the published record, and that is a defensible thing to tell her. It would be fabrication to tell her this program runs a Spanish-language clinic, a Medical Spanish curriculum or a bilingual track, because no source says so.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · The program does not publicly describe a Spanish-language clinic, a Medical Spanish curriculum or a bilingual track. What is documented is a resident continuity clinic at Jackson's county safety-net Ambulatory Care Center and a FREIDA checkbox for non-English language instruction with no published detail.
conflict_notes: The registry records 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: Yes'. The underlying FREIDA option is 'Instruction in medical Spanish or other non-English language', which does not specify Spanish and is not elaborated on any program page. The registry value is a semantic overstatement of its own source.

summary: No resident's medical school is published, so UCC or other Puerto Rico representation among residents cannot be established either way. On the faculty side, one neurology faculty member is a University of Puerto Rico medical graduate and directs an in-house fellowship, and a second faculty member has Puerto Rico university training.
raw_finding: RESIDENTS: the program publishes 48 names but no medical schools, so no resident can be identified as a UCC, Ponce Health Sciences University, University of Puerto Rico or San Juan Bautista graduate. The reported counts of 0 mean NONE COULD BE IDENTIFIED, not none present. Per contract law 4, no resident's Puerto Rican identity or medical school was inferred from any name, and several names on the roster would invite exactly that error. FACULTY, established from institutions rather than names: (1) Enrique Serrano, M.D., M.Sc. - his UM faculty bio states verbatim 'He received his medical degree from the University of Puerto Rico' (San Juan, PR, 1998). The University of Puerto Rico School of Medicine is LCME-accredited, so he classifies as US_MD, never CARIBBEAN - the same classification that applies to Alejandra's own UCC degree. He is an Associate Professor of Clinical Neurology, board certified in neurology, epilepsy and clinical neurophysiology, an epileptologist and neuro-hospitalist at Jackson Health System, and the Fellowship Programs page lists him as Program Director of the Clinical Neurophysiology (ACGME) fellowship. His internship was at Walter Reed, his neurology residency and clinical neurophysiology fellowship at the Medical College of Georgia, and he holds an MS in Clinical and Translational Investigation from UM (2020); he also served four years in the military including a Navy deployment to Iraq. NOTE a discrepancy: his bio describes him as 'Former fellowship director for Epilepsy and Clinical Neurophysiology Fellowship Programs' while the current Fellowship Programs page lists him as the Clinical Neurophysiology PD and Dr. Naymee Velez-Ruiz as the Epilepsy PD; the fellowship list is treated as current. (2) Annelly Bure-Reyes, Ph.D. - Assistant Professor of Clinical Neurology, a neuropsychologist, not a physician. Her bio states she 'was born in the Dominican Republic and relocated to Puerto Rico with her family at the age of 14', earned her bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of Puerto Rico (UPR-Rio Piedras), a master's at UNC Wilmington and her PhD in Florida. Reported as a Puerto Rico training tie, not as a Puerto Rico medical-school graduate. NO UCC-GRADUATE FACULTY were identified in the Department of Neurology. AN IDENTITY HAZARD I REJECTED: a search surfaced Rafael Baez-Bonilla, M.D., a Universidad Central del Caribe graduate on University of Miami faculty - but at UM/Holy Cross in INTERNAL MEDICINE, a different program at a different site (the NRMP report lists 'U Miami MSOM/Holy Cross-FL' as a separate sponsoring institution). He is NOT a faculty member of this neurology residency and was excluded. COVERAGE LIMIT, stated honestly: the Department of Neurology faculty directory exposes 113 profiles but renders only truncated biography snippets, and most do not name a medical school in the directory view. I text-scanned the full rendered directory for 'Puerto Rico', 'Central del Caribe', 'Ponce' and 'San Juan Bautista' and opened the individual bios the scan implicated, but I did not open all 113 profiles individually. A complete faculty-wide Puerto Rico audit is therefore not claimed. TRAINING TIES: no Puerto Rico institutional affiliation, exchange, or rotation agreement was found for this program, and none is claimed. Florida did NOT show materially greater Puerto Rico medical-school representation than Texas in this program's published record, because the determinative data - resident medical schools - is simply not published here.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · The program publishes no resident medical schools, so Puerto Rico or UCC representation among its 48 residents cannot be determined. summary: Of 35 named residents, 13 are confirmed US MD graduates and 7 are US DO graduates; 15 have no published medical school and are recorded as unknown. No Universidad Central del Caribe or other Puerto Rico school graduate appears among any published school, and no offshore Caribbean school appears either.
raw_finding: Bucket partition over the 35 named residents, summing exactly to the denominator. US_MD = 13: the eleven PGY-1 MDs with published US MD schools (Arora, Cole, Demers, Karimi, Spicer, Tenney, Von Hoffmann - all USF; Reyes - Nova Southeastern MD; Sirvisetty - Louisville; Varigala and Yoon - UCF) plus two PGY-4s whose schools are published in the archived capture (Hong - Wayne State; Merkher - USF). US_DO = 7: Halle Root DO (Lincoln Memorial, PGY-1); Michael Benrubi DO (PGY-3); Elise Sandberg DO (Lake Erie COM, PGY-4); and the four PGY-2 DOs Shirley Chua, Anna-Katherine Escoto, Maya Rodriguez and Charles Spoeneman. A published DO degree is treated as sufficient to place a resident in US_DO because the DO degree is awarded only by US colleges of osteopathic medicine; Escoto is counted here on the live page's 'DO' while the archived capture's 'MD' is preserved as a conflict. CARIBBEAN = 0 and OTHER_IMG = 0: no offshore Caribbean school and no non-US school appears in any published school field. UNKNOWN = 15: Saikrishna Sriraman, Caroline St.Peter, George Tarantino (PGY-2); Isabella Birmingham, Muhammad Chaychi, Anu Khanna, Snow Li, Ashley Mason, Ariel Miller, Riley Payne (PGY-3); Husam Abuhayyeh, Sina Aghili-Mehrizi, Hannah Enyart, Valeria Fagundo, Kelsey Stefan (PGY-4). Sum check: 13 + 7 + 0 + 0 + 15 = 35. OVERLAY COUNTS, NOT BUCKETS: ucc_residents = 0 and puerto_rico_school_residents = 0, established over the 20 residents whose schools are published and unestablished for the other 15. COMPLEMENT VERSUS CENSUS: FREIDA 2026 field_program_size=[12,12,8,8] / field_total_positions=40 are positions per level; the registry stored 'Total Residents: 32' and 'Residents Per Year: PGY-1: 8; PGY-2: 8; PGY-3: 8; PGY-4: 8' from the older survey. Neither figure is the census. The actual named census is 35. Separately, FREIDA 2026's composition percentages describe the PRIOR academic year: field_pct_usmd=61.3, field_pct_do=25.8, field_pct_img=12.9, field_pct_female=58.1, field_pct_male=41.9. Those percentages resolve to exactly 19 US MD + 8 DO + 4 IMG over a denominator of 31, which matches AY2025-26 (7 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 31, before the twelve-person Class of 2030 arrived). FREIDA's 12.9% IMG figure therefore implies four international graduates in AY2025-26 whose schools the program does not publish; those individuals are within the 15 UNKNOWN here and the program publishes nothing that would let them be identified. This is why the unknown bucket is large rather than zero, and it is the correct handling: the program has residents FREIDA classifies as IMG, but it does not publish who they are or where they trained.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - the program publishes medical schools for its PGY-1 class only, so 15 of 35 residents cannot be classified; FREIDA separately reports 12.9% international graduates for the prior academic year without naming them.

raw_finding: Every page in the residency's secondary navigation was crawled: Overview, Faculty, Chief Residents, PGY1/PGY2/PGY3/PGY4 Residents, Credentialing/Verification Information, Stipend Benefits & Leave Policies, Letter to Applicants, Application Information, Salary & Benefits, Fellowships, 4th Year Medical Student Electives, Visit Tampa Bay, Prospective PMR Residents, Program Structure, Where We Train, Contact Information. None is an alumni or outcomes page and none lists graduate fellowship placements or first jobs. By contrast the department's PM&R residency - a different residency administratively housed in the same department - does publish an alumni page, which confirms that the site architecture supports such a page and that Adult Neurology has simply not created one. The Overview page offers only a qualitative claim: 'As a result of this exposure, graduates of the program are prepared for both private clinical practice and academic neurology careers.' SELECTED EXAMPLES VERSUS COMPLETE COHORT: the eleven MS fellowship alumni listed on the MS Clinical Fellowship page appear to be a complete list for that fellowship ('Past Fellows'), but they are MS fellowship graduates and several (Robertson, Moreo) were already USF faculty; none is identified as a USF neurology RESIDENCY graduate, and it would be wrong to present them as residency outcomes. Two of them - Demetrios Konstas MD and Chetan Gandhy MD - are described as medical director of the VA MS Center of Excellence at James A Haley VA, which is one of this residency's core training sites.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - the Adult Neurology residency does not publish a graduate placement list, alumni page, or career-outcomes data anywhere on its website. The eleven named alumni that do appear belong to the department's MS fellowship, not to the residency.

summary: The four-year categorical curriculum delivers its own internal-medicine PGY-1 with three months of neurology, then 36 months of core neurology split about evenly between inpatient and outpatient. Roughly half of PGY-2 to PGY-4 is subspecialty or elective time, with published outpatient rotations in both movement disorders and multiple sclerosis, two months of neuro-oncology at Moffitt, and continuity clinic every week.
raw_finding: From the Program Structure page, verbatim: 'The Neurology residency at USF is a categorical program that consists of a 12 month preliminary year medicine training (which includes 3 months of neurology rotations during PGY1) followed by 36 months of core neurology rotations, divided evenly between inpatient and outpatient training experiences (approximately 18 months in each setting). ... Each rotation is 3 weeks long with 17 distinct rotations per year. We provide our residents as much flexibility as possible to shape their individual training experience.' On wards: 'Inpatient neurology responsibilities occur in high proportion at Tampa General Hospital. With remaining inpatient training to occur the VA Hospital and both account for approximately 17 months of training'; 'Morning report occurs at each hospital every Wednesday'; 'TGH Vascular Neurology Radiology conference and Epilepsy Surgical Conferences occur weekly'; 'Ancillary duties are handled by hospital staff at all of the training facilities. Residents are not responsible for blood draws, transport, etc.'; 'The average team census at both hospitals is approximately 12-16 patients per service.' At Tampa General: 'There are 3 teams, each comprised of 1 senior resident (PGY3 or PGY4), 1 PGY 2 resident, and 2-3 medical students'; 'Night Float is Sunday to Friday 6 pm to 7 am except for Sunday which is 9 pm until 7 am Monday morning, 3 weeks per year for each PGY 2 and PGY3 resident'; 'There is no overnight call for PGY 4 residents'; 'Resident cap are absolute at 15 patients per resident per call. It is extremely rare to utilize the cap system. A back-up system is place to relieve a resident on call who has reached the cap.' At the James A. Haley VA: 'There is 1 team that comprises inpatient, consult, and the epilepsy monitoring unit ... the on call resident starts at 5 pm and takes call at home for both the VA and Moffitt Cancer Center. This average number of home calls per month is usually 1-2 per resident.' At Moffitt: 'Neurology residents spend 2 months during the PGY3 academic year at Moffitt Cancer Center. This is an incredible opportunity for our residents to gain exposure to a unique population of patients, and work with world renowned neuro-oncologists at an NCI-designated comprehensive cancer center.' On subspecialty time: 'Approximately 1/2 of PGY2-PGY4 training will take place on subspecialty or elective rotations' and 'The outpatient subspecialty rotations include neuromuscular, epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, interventional pain, headache and facial pain, movement disorder, and pediatric neurology.' On continuity: 'PGY 1 continuity clinics are at Tampa General outpatient clinic. PGY 2-4 continuity clinics are at the James A Haley VA Hospital. Both comprise one half day per week.' The Where We Train page adds that the Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital rotation 'provides trainees with essential pediatric neurology experience' - this is a PEDIATRIC ROTATION INSIDE AN ADULT CURRICULUM, which the contract expressly treats as legitimate adult curriculum data; no child neurology program content was used. Bay Pines VA: 'During the first and second years of our residency program, trainees rotate through the Bay Pines VA Healthcare System ... First-year residents complete a dedicated rotation on the psychiatry consult service.' summary: There is one real, primary-source Spanish link: USF's own Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence page states that Spanish-speaking families from Puerto Rico seek its services. Beyond that the program documents no Medical Spanish curriculum, no Spanish-language clinic, and no bilingual staffing - and the registry's 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: No' was re-verified rather than inherited.
raw_finding: See the structured spanish_latino_clinical_relevance record at the top level, including the explicitly_rejected_evidence field. The single positive finding is from USF Health's own Movement Disorders services page, in the section headed 'USF Health Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence', verbatim: 'Our HDSA HD Center of Excellence serves the entire state of Florida, from the panhandle to the Keys with a few families in southern Georgia and Spanish-speaking families from Puerto Rico also seeking our services.' This is a statement about the documented referral population of a specific named USF Neurology clinic, not a demographic inference about Tampa. It is also narrow: it documents that Spanish-speaking Puerto Rican families seek care there, and does NOT document Spanish-language care delivery, bilingual providers, interpreter provision, or any residency-level language training. MEDICAL SPANISH VERIFIED FRESH, NOT INHERITED: the registry recorded 'Medical Spanish Curriculum: No'. That registry value derives from FREIDA's multi-select field_resident_fellow_offer_2019. The 2026 survey answers that field as ['Formal program to foster interprofessional teamwork', 'Alternative/complementary medicine curriculum', 'Debt management/financial counseling', 'Academic support for USMLE Step 3 preparation', 'Resident/fellow retreats'] - no Medical Spanish item, in a survey received 2026-07-08, one cycle newer than the registry's substrate. The mapping was validated by checking that every other registry curriculum flag matches the same list: 'Complementary Medicine Curriculum: Yes' corresponds to the 'Alternative/complementary medicine curriculum' entry that IS present, while 'Integrative Medicine Curriculum', 'Health Systems Leadership Curriculum', 'Healthcare Economics Curriculum', 'Global Health Experience' and 'Hospice Home Care Experience' are all 'No' and all absent from the list. Independently, all seventeen residency pages plus the department faculty, fellowships, MS and movement-disorders service pages were searched for 'Spanish', 'bilingual', 'interpret', 'Hispanic' and 'Latino'; the only hits were the Huntington's sentence above and one PGY-1's personal hobby list. So 'No' is positively supported from two directions rather than carried over. FACULTY LANGUAGE: the shared USF Health / Tampa General provider directory carries a structured 'Languages' field, and the three neurology faculty profiles reachable by direct slug (Robert Hauser, Theresa Zesiewicz, John Ciotti) all list 'English' only. A complete language sweep of the faculty was not possible because the directory's list endpoint returns bare NPIs and its name search runs client-side. No faculty member is documented as Spanish-speaking; equally, none is documented as not speaking Spanish.
student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - the program publishes no formal Medical Spanish curriculum, no Spanish-language clinic and no bilingual-staffing statement. The one documented Spanish link is that USF's Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence reports Spanish-speaking families from Puerto Rico among the patients who seek its care.

summary: The program suggests a USMLE Step 1 score above 220 achieved in one attempt, and accepts COMLEX Level 1 as the equivalent. This is published as a suggestion, not as a hard cutoff.
raw_finding: Program page, How to Apply list, verbatim: 'USMLE Step 1 Transcript & Score > 220 is suggested with one (1) attempt/ COMLEX Level equivalent.' The IMG section repeats it: 'USMLE Step I Transcript & Score > 220 is suggested with one (1) attempt'. Note the word 'suggested' — the program publishes no absolute minimum and no automatic screen-out threshold. Step 1 has been pass/fail since January 2022, so a numeric '>220' expectation is by construction legacy language that can only apply to applicants with a pre-2022 three-digit score; the program has not updated this text. Alejandra passed Step 1 on the first attempt in the pass/fail era, so the attempt expectation is met and the numeric expectation is not applicable to her transcript. FREIDA 2026 survey reports field_usmle_step_1_required=false and field_usmle_step1_req_int=false, which contradicts the registry snapshot's 'US MD Step 1 Required: Yes' / 'IMG Step 1 Required: Yes'; FREIDA's 'required' fields appear to encode a required minimum score rather than a required score report, and the program page is the operative source.

raw_finding: See the structured step2_timing record at the top level of this dossier for the full determination, the exact paraphrase, and the barrier reasoning. Short form: the operative sentence is 'Must have USMLE /COMLEX Step 2 Score Report uploaded into ERAS prior to the deadline of the Rank List submission. If you do not have a Step 2 Score Report uploaded, you will not be ranked (assuming you were invited for an interview).' The parenthetical '(assuming you were invited for an interview)' is decisive: it positively contemplates an interview invitation being issued to an applicant who does not yet have a Step 2 score uploaded, which rules out an interview-stage barrier. FREIDA 2026 gives the current-year interview window as 2026-10-01 to 2027-02-28 (field_interview_period_curr_year), so interviews open the same month Alejandra's score is released and run four more months.
